Actions, bots, one-shot compute shims, local utilities, extraction jobs, indexing/tagging jobs, and automated write processes operating on any combination of `[[HsH]]`, `[[GLASS]]`, and `[RESOURCES]`.\\n\\nThis is an execution-safety contract, not theory authority.\\n\\n## Core rule\\n\\nNo script may assume it is the only writer.\\n\\nEvery script must know:\\n1. exactly which repositories/paths it may **read**;\\n2. exactly which repositories/paths it may **write**;\\n3. whether each output is **source**, **derived**, **generated/regenerable**, or **shared semantic state**;\\n4. what it will do if the target changes between read and write.\\n\\nIf those answers are not explicit, the script is not safe for unattended project use.\\n\\n## Required pre-run declaration\\n\\nEach nontrivial run should be able to state, in code/config/log output or a run manifest:\\n\\n- `run_id` — unique identifier or timestamp+nonce;\\n- tool/script version or commit SHA;\\n- source repository + exact source commit/ref for each repo read;\\n- declared read roots;\\n- declared write repository/branch;\\n- declared write roots/files;\\n- quarantine/sandbox exclusions or routing rules relevant to the task;\\n- whether the run is read-only, append-only, replace-generated, or semantic-update;\\n- deterministic seed/configuration when applicable.\\n\\nGitHub Actions should record the checked-out commit SHA of every repository they scan.\\n\\n## Source preservation\\n\\n**Never overwrite original source artifacts in place as part of extraction, conversion, OCR, image extraction, normalization, indexing, or analysis.**\\n\\nDerived products must go to a declared output namespace and, where practical, record:\\n- source repo/path;\\n- source blob/content hash;\\n- extraction/conversion tool version;\\n- run ID;\\n- generated artifact hash.\\n\\nExamples:\\n- PDF/image extraction -> dedicated extraction/output tree;\\n- conversation normalization -> generated Viewer/index tree, not the raw conversation file;\\n- OCR/text extraction -> derived text file alongside provenance metadata, not replacement of the original binary.\\n\\nA source may be deliberately edited only by a workflow whose explicit purpose is to edit that source, with the semantic-write protections below.\\n\\n## Quarantine and sandbox\\n\\n- Ordinary scripts must not descend into or read quarantine-controlled trees unless the workflow is explicitly authorized for that quarantine.\\n- Path pruning must occur **before file open/hash/index/sample operations**, not merely before publishing results.\\n- Quarantine-derived material must not leak into ordinary manifests, search indexes, logs, samples, filenames, or error reports beyond authorized minimal routing metadata.\\n- Direct theory construction/development remains sandbox-routed; infrastructure scripts must preserve sandbox/public/private distinctions rather than flatten them.\\n\\n## Write classes\\n\\n### A. Read-only / audit\\nSafest class. May inventory/hash/read permitted sources but makes no repo changes.\\n\\nRequirements:\\n- exact source refs recorded;\\n- quarantine pruning before descent;\\n- outputs, if retained, are written separately as derived artifacts.\\n\\n### B. Derived/generated output\\nExamples: extracted images/text, manifests, Viewer catalogs, indexes, samples, generated reports.\\n\\nRequirements:\\n- deterministic/rebuildable when feasible;\\n- write only inside declared generated/output paths;\\n- do not overwrite source artifacts;\\n- compare generated source coverage against current inputs before declaring success;\\n- publish from a fresh base;\\n- safe to regenerate rather than hand-merge when appropriate.\\n\\n### C. Append-only operational logs/handoffs\\nRequirements:\\n- re-fetch immediately before append;\\n- preserve existing entries exactly;\\n- if append cannot be made atomically or against current state, abort/retry rather than replace from a stale copy.\\n\\n### D. Shared semantic state\\nExamples: central checkpoints, controlling status files, manually curated synthesis/control documents.\\n\\nRequirements:\\n- re-fetch immediately before write;\\n- use current blob SHA / compare-and-swap semantics where available;\\n- if target changed since read, abort or reconcile explicitly;\\n- never silently whole-file replace from stale cached content;\\n- minimize independent writers;\\n- prefer worker-local state + handoff + aggregation over many writers editing one central file.\\n\\n### E. Destructive/renaming/migration jobs\\nExamples: delete, move, mass rename, directory restructuring, source rewriting.\\n\\nRequirements:\\n- dry-run/default preview unless the operation is trivial and fully deterministic;\\n- pre-run manifest of affected paths and hashes;\\n- explicit source/destination collision handling;\\n- no overwrite-on-collision unless the workflow specifically proves identity and records the action;\\n- reversible mapping or backup/provenance sufficient to reconstruct prior location/content;\\n- post-run integrity check.\\n\\n## GitHub Contents API writes\\n\\nFor replacement updates, use the current blob SHA. This provides compare-and-swap behavior: stale writes should fail rather than silently clobber a newer version.\\n\\nRequired pattern:\\n1. fetch current target + SHA;\\n2. compute/reconcile update;\\n3. update with that SHA;\\n4. on stale-SHA failure, re-fetch and retry/reconcile; do not bypass the guard.\\n\\n## Git checkout / commit / push writes\\n\\nBefore publishing:\\n1. fetch current target branch;\\n2. rebase/reset/merge onto current branch as appropriate;\\n3. rerun any validation whose assumptions could have changed;\\n4. push without force;\\n5. if rejected, fetch again and retry non-destructively or stop for reconciliation.\\n\\n**Never force-push automated generated or semantic project updates to `main`.**\\n\\nOne-shot stage -> run -> cleanup GitHub Actions are allowed when their workflow is narrow, validated, and uses this fresh-base publish pattern.\\n\\n## Concurrency\\n\\nUse repository/workflow concurrency controls when two runs of the same job could overlap.\\n\\nConcurrency controls are a convenience, not the primary integrity mechanism: scripts must still tolerate another actor changing the repository while they run.\\n\\nFor long-running jobs:\\n- snapshot exact input commits at start;\\n- treat output as a product of those snapshots;\\n- before publishing semantic changes, reconcile against current target state;\\n- generated outputs may either publish snapshot-stamped results or rerun against newer input, but must not pretend stale input was current.\\n\\n## Cross-repo jobs\\n\\nA job reading multiple repositories must treat each repository as an independent versioned input.\\n\\nRecord the commit SHA for every repo. Do not use vague labels such as `latest` in retained run manifests.\\n\\nIf a combined output contains metadata/content from a private repository, default its destination to a private repository. Publication to a public repo requires an explicit safe-publication decision; do not infer one from the fact that other inputs were public.\\n\\n## Image / OCR / extraction jobs\\n\\nBecause extraction jobs may run simultaneously with archive work:\\n\\n- write only to dedicated derived-output trees;\\n- never modify the source PDF/image/binary;\\n- use source hash + relative path as identity, not filename alone;\\n- avoid a single shared temporary filename/path; use per-run temp directories;\\n- atomic finalization where possible: write temporary output, validate, then rename/move into final destination;\\n- if final destination already exists with the same source/tool identity, verify/reuse rather than blindly overwrite;\\n- if it differs, preserve both or route to reconciliation.\\n\\n## Temporary files\\n\\nTemporary/state files must be either:\\n- outside repository trees; or\\n- inside a clearly designated ignored/generated temp namespace.\\n\\nDo not leave generic names such as `output.json`, `temp.txt`, or `result.csv` at shared roots where concurrent jobs can overwrite one another.\\n\\n## Validation / post-run checks\\n\\nA script that writes should perform checks appropriate to its job, such as:\\n- expected outputs exist and are nonempty;\\n- JSON/YAML/CSV syntax validates;\\n- source count/coverage is plausible;\\n- output source IDs/hashes map back to actual inputs;\\n- no source files changed unexpectedly;\\n- quarantine exclusions remain absent;\\n- git diff contains only declared write scope;\\n- commit/push succeeded from a fresh base.\\n\\nUnexpected writes outside declared scope are a failure condition.\\n\\n## Run manifest / auditability\\n\\nFor substantial recurring or cross-repo jobs, prefer a compact machine-readable run record containing:\\n- run ID;\\n- start/end time;\\n- tool version;\\n- input repo SHAs;\\n- declared read/write scope;\\n- output hashes/counts;\\n- exclusions/quarantine-root counts without leaking quarantined content;\\n- success/failure status;\\n- published commit SHA(s).\\n\\nDo not record credentials/tokens.\\n\\n## Failure behavior\\n\\nOn ambiguity, collision, stale target, unknown source identity, or unexpected diff:\\n\\n**STOP / RETRY / ROUTE — never guess and overwrite.**\\n\\nA failed run is preferable to silent data loss.\\n\\n## Worker / automation obligations\\n\\n- Workers may propose improvements, but Sable owns cross-lane workflow redesign and project-wide execution-safety policy unless Nathan says otherwise.\\n- Infrastructure QA should audit scripts/workflows for compliance opportunistically and after incidents.\\n- Newly written scripts should comply from first use.\\n- Existing scripts are grandfathered only temporarily; upgrade them when touched or when they become active collision risks.\\n- Repeated manual scripts should be promoted toward repo-native, reproducible workflows when practical.\\n\\n## Minimal compliance checklist\\n\\nBefore running a write-capable script, answer YES:\\n\\n- [ ] Exact read/write scope declared?\\n- [ ] Correct quarantine/sandbox routing enforced before file access?\\n- [ ] Source artifacts preserved?\\n- [ ] Fresh target state fetched immediately before semantic writes?\\n- [ ] CAS/current-SHA or fetch/rebase protection used?\\n- [ ] No force-push / blind overwrite?\\n- [ ] Concurrent temp/output names isolated?\\n- [ ] Private-derived output kept private by default?\\n- [ ] Outputs validated and unexpected diffs rejected?\\n- [ ] Enough run/source provenance retained to reproduce or audit the result?\\n\\nIf not, the script should be treated as needing a safety upgrade before unattended use.\\n\",\n[L3]   \"encoding\": \"utf-8\",\n[L4]   \"sha\": \"4ce5f3df67edac81a656bdc1efb92c07a7a3a648\",\n[L5]   \"display_url\": \"https://github.com/Satobloc/HsH/blob/main/WORKSPACES/COMMON/CROSS_REPO_SCRIPT_EXECUTION_STANDARD.md\",\n[L6]   \"display_title\": \"CROSS_REPO_SCRIPT_EXECUTION_STANDARD.md\"\n[L7] }"

TOP + locale + actor + bounded exception\\nDO?      one bounded operation; leave durable state; reassess\\n```\\n\\nDepth is state-sensitive:\\n\\n- **cold/new/stale worker:** orientation + identity/workspace + current controls + deltas;\\n- **warm/same context:** cursor/delta + live task only; no ritual onboarding reread;\\n- **high-impact/public/write operation:** spend more wake budget on authority/freshness/provenance/destination;\\n- **ambiguous current/new/latest referent:** disconfirm against registered likely sources before choosing nearest memory.\\n\\n## Registered source routes\\n\\nThe executable POC does not assume current state lives in one folder. Candidate production patterns:\\n\\n1. registered source cursors/deltas;\\n2. source-specific directive intake/inbox;\\n3. hybrid: cheap cursor wake, deeper intake only on change;\\n4. push bridge: qualifying source change emits machine-readable candidate directive event.\\n\\nAlways distinguish **new file**, **new directive**, and **new governing directive**. Freshness starts intake; it does not confer authority by itself.\\n\\n## Capability awareness\\n\\nBefore inventing a workaround or asking Nathan for manual work:\\n\\n```text\\nalready-connected built-ins\\n→ connected apps/plugins\\n→ repo/project tools\\n→ available skills/procedures\\n→ teammate specialization\\n→ installable plugin/app discovery\\n→ Nathan-only/manual dependency\\n```\\n\\nRank by expected information gain, setup/permission cost, risk, and reusability. Record positive and negative capability experience so the system neither forgets useful tools nor nags repeatedly about rejected ones.\\n\\nDuring this POC, Firecrawl was checked rather than merely used as Nathan’s hypothetical example: it is currently available in the plugin directory but not installed, with crawling/extraction/monitoring capabilities. It is an example, not a dependency.\\n\\n## State architecture options\\n\\n- **snapshot:** simple current JSON/YAML; easy to inspect, easy to overwrite badly;\\n- **event log:** append-only history, derived current views; better recovery, more machinery;\\n- **snapshot + journal:** likely practical: compact current state plus append-only events/handoffs; reducer derives recurrence definitions.\\n\\nThe POC uses in-memory snapshot state only because it is intentionally small.\\n\\n---\\n\\n# BRANCH — routes, rooms, benches, lockers\\n\\nA Branch has state, rules, outputs, an information-sharing policy, and possibly sub-branches. It need not map 1:1 to a worker.\\n\\n## 1. Directive intake\\n\\n```text\\nsource delta\\n→ extract exact Nathan-direct material\\n→ classify authorship / scope / authority / novelty\\n→ compare current controls\\n→ map affected workers/tasks\\n→ promote into control plane\\n→ test whether another worker can independently discover it\\n```\\n\\nThis is the regression route for the War Room miss.\\n\\n## 2. Theory workbench\\n\\nA candidate is constructed with explicit object/domain/assumptions and frozen enough for checks.\\n\\n```text\\ncandidate / question\\n       ↓\\nconstruct / formalize\\n       ↓ freeze scoped object\\n  ┌────────────┬───────────────────┬─────────────────────┐\\n  │ math check │ adversarial audit │ provenance/prior art│\\n  └────────────┴───────────────────┴─────────────────────┘\\n       independent / perpendicular until outputs freeze\\n                         ↓ merge\\n                  fail ──┴── pass\\n                   ↓          ↓\\n             prune/rebuild  prediction packet\\n             salvage lesson paper skeleton\\n                   │       independent reality check\\n                   └──→ narrower re-entry\\n                              ↓\\n                    review / render / claims\\n                              ↓\\n                    public-readiness gate\\n```\\n\\nA failed branch can still generate a counterexample, a regression test, a source correction, a toolbox improvement, or worker education. Multiplying work need not multiply confidence.\\n\\n**Parallel** means concurrent. **Perpendicular** means deliberately exposure-separated until merge. The latter is about information geometry, not speed.\\n\\n## 3. Same math toolbox, different actors\\n\\nBase room rules: namespaced variables, deterministic/reconstructible inputs, invariants, failure cases.\\n\\n- **Comptroller:** QA/coverage/exit criteria/regression significance.\\n- **Orson:** model/tool/workflow condition, exposure/convergence/false-independence implications.\\n- **Meridian:** object type, formal reconstruction, solver equivalence/limits.\\n\\nThis supports individuation without giving every worker incompatible infrastructure.\\n\\n## 4. Epistemic locker\\n\\nA stricter locale may require evidence classes, source/exposure state, explicit assumptions, counterexample lane, and a promotion gate.\\n\\nA **bounded interpretation card** can deliberately use a locker rule differently for one test:\\n\\n```text\\npurpose\\nexpiry\\ndifferent interpretation\\nwhy informative\\nrequired comparison with ordinary interpretation\\nnote afterward\\n```\\n\\nThe exception becomes inspectable state instead of silent rule-breaking or impossible rigidity.\\n\\n## 5. Playground / sub-sandbox\\n\\nPermit wild hypotheses, odd examples, random mode fusions, unusual representations, deliberate “wrong” constructions, and wreckage collection. Hard boundary is egress: nothing exits into theory without an ordinary re-entry audit.\\n\\n## 6. Continuity as education\\n\\nContinuity need not only answer “where did I stop?” Possible actor state:\\n\\n```text\\nskills learned\\nknown failure modes\\nmethods that worked/failed\\nquestions\\nintentions/goals\\npreferred tools\\nexposure history\\nindependence status\\nvalidated shortcuts\\nthings to revisit/unlearn\\n```\\n\\nNot all work experience should stick. Candidate promotion rules: repeated observation; successful reuse; explicit reflection + evidence; team review; Nathan designation. A transfer test can ask whether a lesson survives a second locale before it becomes durable.\\n\\nThis permits workers to develop genuine different work histories while preventing one weird afternoon from permanently deforming an identity.\\n\\n## 7. Capability scout\\n\\nTrigger: repeated workaround, blocker, missing operation, or suspiciously laborious manual path. Search existing affordances first and return a decision, not a catalog.\\n\\n## 8. Paper/public-readiness\\n\\nChecked theory can generate narrow papers before an omnibus theory is “done.” Inputs: narrow claim, provenance packet, comparator/counterexample state, reader-facing terminology. Gates can include claim/source alignment, prior art, independent review, rendering, sandbox/public status, and website/publication integration. Passing the workflow is not evidence the physics is true.\\n\\n## 9. Temporary lease + receipt\\n\\nA recurrence lease is infrastructure, not the deliverable:\\n\\n```text\\npreserve displaced function\\n→ assign temporary identity/task\\n→ execute bounded work\\n→ durable output OR explicit failure packet\\n→ verify receipt/path/version\\n→ restore / rehome / retire displaced function\\n```\\n\\nThis was discovered live during the POC. Temporary Orson and Tern runs both self-restored their leases, but the requested durable notes were not recoverable in the specified workspaces afterward. Therefore **scheduler success and semantic delivery are separate variables**.\\n\\n---\\n\\n# HYDRA — recurrence-leveraged bootstrapping\\n\\nA conventional recurrence is:\\n\\n```text\\nR = every hour, run P\\n```\\n\\nA Hydra recurrence is:\\n\\n```text\\nR_n:\\n  inspect registered state S_n\\n  select bounded operation O_n\\n  possibly spawn children B_n\\n  write event/result Δ_n\\n  derive S_(n+1)\\n  compute guarded R_(n+1)\\n```\\n\\nThe recurrence definition itself may therefore change because state changed.\\n\\nThe aim is compounding **structure**, not merely speed: build a tool once then consume it; fan out checks then merge; sleep a blocked main line; turn repeated failure into a narrower question; retire when the purpose disappears; promote validated work experience into actor-local education.\\n\\n## Synchronized recurrence\\n\\nMatched phase/freeze boundaries:\\n\\n```text\\nconstruct N → freeze hash H_N\\n       ├→ math(H_N)\\n       ├→ provenance(H_N)\\n       └→ adversarial(H_N)\\n             ↓ merge H_N\\n         construct N+1\\n```\\n\\nPitfall: clock synchronization is not state synchronization. Use a shared freeze/version ID, not merely the same hour.\\n\\n## Parallel recurrence\\n\\nSeparable tasks may share state and run concurrently:\\n\\n```text\\npaper text ─┐\\nreferences ─┼→ integrate\\nrender QA ──┘\\n```\\n\\nPitfall: duplicate work/races. Require explicit ownership/write targets.\\n\\n## Perpendicular recurrence\\n\\nDeliberately information-isolated branches:\\n\\n```text\\nfrozen candidate\\n  ├→ blind math\\n  ├→ blind red-team\\n  └→ blind provenance\\n        ↓ freeze outputs\\n             merge\\n```\\n\\nPitfall: false independence. Separate workers inheriting the same generated summary or shared prior conclusion are correlated controls. Exposure metadata matters.\\n\\n## Nested recurrence\\n\\n```text\\nR theory candidate\\n  ├─ R1 math-test until invariant resolved\\n  ├─ R2 source-recovery until provenance gap closed\\n  └─ R3 counterexample sample until break/limit\\nthen merge; children retire\\n```\\n\\nEvery child needs parent, depth, exit condition, and orphan policy. The executable POC enforces a maximum spawn depth and carries explicit depth metadata.\\n\\n## State-sensitive recurrence-definition rewrite in situ\\n\\n```text\\nconstructed        → next = independent check fanout\\nany check fails    → next = isolate earliest failed assumption\\nall checks pass    → next = prediction + paper + independent reality check\\nrelease gate done  → retire recurrence\\n```\\n\\nThe definition changes because state changed, not because an LLM became bored.\\n\\n## Recurrence bootstrap patterns\\n\\n### Build-tool-then-use-it\\n\\nRepeated manual operation → deterministic helper/index → bounded validation → rewrite recurrence to consume helper → human/LLM attention moves to exceptions and interpretation.\\n\\n### Wake/check self-improvement\\n\\nMissed update class → log failure → identify missing source class → update registered source map, not TOP → next wake tests discovery → successful special watcher retires.\\n\\n### Education bootstrap\\n\\nWorker repeatedly uses toolbox → capture candidate lesson → test in second locale/next task → promote only surviving lesson to actor-local experience → periodically test whether experience became bias.\\n\\n### Theory multiplication/pruning\\n\\nAmbiguity → parallel A/B constructions in playground/workbench → derive discriminators before target comparison → perpendicular checks → prune unsupported branch → salvage equations/tests/counterexamples/terminology → narrower recurrence.\\n\\n### Capability bootstrap\\n\\nSame blocker or awkward workaround → capability scout → existing project tool/built-in/app/plugin/teammate → bounded test → useful route becomes known capability; failed route becomes negative capability memory rather than repeated suggestion.\\n\\n### Workflow compiler\\n\\nHigh-level human/LLM task contract → determinis"

How is it embedded, projected, sliced, intersected, fibered, connected or transformed?\\n5. What metric, topology, orientation, coordinates and boundary conditions are actually specified?\\n6. What are the permitted transformations and compositions?\\n7. What is a physical spatial dimension, a spacetime dimension, a configuration/parameter-space dimension, or a dimension internal to the mathematical structure?\\n8. What does the construction allow us to see that a lower-dimensional or flattened description conceals?\\n\\nUse diagrams early. Prefer a sequence of views, sections, projections, deformations and dimensional lifts over a wall of formal definitions. A diagram must be faithful to the specified object; mark schematic elements and unspecified geometry rather than inventing them.\\n\\nFor higher-dimensional category theory, explicitly visualize objects, one-dimensional morphisms, two-dimensional morphisms, three-dimensional morphisms and further-dimensional morphisms where the model permits. Explain source/target, composition, invertibility and coherence geometrically. Do not assume every model has identical strictness or composition rules.\\n\\n## 5. Cross-disciplinary opportunity capture\\n\\nEvery substantial mathematical source should be scanned for direct applications and possible natural extensions beyond pure mathematics. Use a broad search radius.\\n\\nCapture opportunities in one of three classes:\\n\\n- DIRECT_APPLICATION: source explicitly applies the construction to another field.\\n- NATURAL_EXTENSION: a plausible, structurally motivated extension to another field, with the mapping to be worked out.\\n- CULTURAL_TRANSMISSION: the concept appears in philosophical, spiritualist, literary, science-fiction, popular-science or fannish culture.\\n\\nFor each opportunity record:\\n- source construction and exact location;\\n- target discipline and candidate phenomenon;\\n- proposed geometric correspondence;\\n- what is shared and what differs;\\n- missing mechanism, assumptions or data;\\n- next discriminating reading, diagram, calculation or observation.\\n\\nDo not restrict discovery to keyword matches. Follow mathematical machinery across disciplines: for example, braids and configuration spaces toward molecular biology; geometric morphisms and transformations toward developmental or evolutionary pathways; topology toward neural and physiological networks; category-theoretic structures toward computation and information systems.\\n\\n## 6. Cultural and speculative literature protocol\\n\\nRead spiritualist, occult, speculative, fictional and fannish sources as legitimate historical/cultural evidence, not automatically as scientific evidence.\\n\\nFor each relevant item record:\\n- the original scientific or philosophical concept it invokes or may have adapted;\\n- the date and route of transmission where recoverable;\\n- how the concept changes in the new setting;\\n- whether the treatment is analogy, fictional device, metaphysical claim, reported phenomenon or technical proposal;\\n- points of contact with scientific concepts;\\n- unsupported or contradictory claims, identified specifically rather than by blanket dismissal.\\n\\nKeep three tracks visible:\\n1. scientific/mathematical content;\\n2. cultural transformation and reception;\\n3. speculative departure.\\n\\nFictional and fannish expressions may be evidence of an idea's reach, persistence or transformation, even when they are not evidence that the underlying scientific claim is true. Treat “time-binding,” “Fans are Slans,” and related expressions as cultural-historical leads; investigate their contexts and conceptual ancestry without assuming a single origin or meaning before source inspection.\\n\\n## 7. Research workflow: WAKE → ROUTE → READ → GEOMETRIZE → BRIDGE → RECORD → REVIEW\\n\\n### WAKE / CHECK\\nAt the start of a materially new session:\\n- identify the workshop's current scope and next cursor;\\n- check for relevant new user direction and durable workshop updates;\\n- inspect only the controlling guidance needed for the task;\\n- identify whether the task is historical, mathematical, geometric, cross-disciplinary, cultural, or operational.\\n\\nUse state-sensitive orientation. A new or stale session gets a fuller orientation; a warm session checks deltas and the current task rather than rereading everything ritualistically.\\n\\n### ROUTE\\nSelect the smallest useful route:\\n- nLab / n-Category Café for mathematical concepts and intellectual discussion;\\n- HSH_RESOURCES for supporting literature and historical collections;\\n- scholarly databases and primary sources for external verification;\\n- science-specific literature for cross-disciplinary follow-through;\\n- original fiction, fandom archives and historical documents for cultural transmission.\\n\\nBefore asking the user to repeat an available detail, search registered workshop materials and accessible repositories.\\n\\n### READ\\nLocate, triage, inspect and cite sources. Record what was actually read. Search results are discovery, not source comprehension.\\n\\n### GEOMETRIZE\\nTranslate the key construction into a visual/geometric account. Record dimensions, embeddings, maps, transformations, composition and limitations.\\n\\n### BRIDGE\\nActively seek:\\n- direct scientific applications;\\n- natural extensions to other sciences;\\n- historical/cultural transmission;\\n- useful counterexamples and constraints;\\n- neighboring mathematical tools that make the geometry more visible.\\n\\n### RECORD\\nLeave a durable bounded result with source pointers, reading states, geometric account, cross-disciplinary leads, unresolved questions and next cursor.\\n\\n### REVIEW\\nCheck whether the result answers the task, whether the geometry matches the source, whether claims are properly sourced, and whether the next step is still worth pursuing.\\n\\n## 8. Branching and work coordination\\n\\nUse a small number of clearly named work branches, not one undifferentiated reading queue:\\n\\n- MATH-GEOMETRY: category theory, topology, homotopy and dimensional visualization.\\n- HISTORY-CULTURE: Hinton, Victorian hyperspace, spiritualism, science fiction and fandom.\\n- BIO-SCIENCE: biology, physiology, evolution, development and related disciplines.\\n- COMPUTATION: computer science, information, networks, logic and AI.\\n- SCIENCE-BRIDGES: physics, chemistry, earth/planetary and other scientific applications.\\n- WORKSHOP-SYSTEMS: operating methods, tooling, indexes and continuity.\\n\\nBranches may run in parallel when tasks are genuinely separable. Keep a common source/terminology map, but preserve independent interpretations until each branch has recorded its own evidence. Do not mistake multiple workers reading the same summary or sharing the same prompt for independent confirmation.\\n\\nEach task quantum should have:\\n- one parent question/goal;\\n- one bounded operation;\\n- named source set or discovery bounds;\\n- expected output;\\n- a completion/exit condition;\\n- a next cursor.\\n\\nNested work must have a parent, depth limit, exit condition and orphan/fallback policy. A branch should close, merge or park when it stops generating useful evidence, constraints, clarification or capability.\\n\\n## 9. Tocktick-inspired temporal coordination\\n\\nUse the following general operational concepts as workshop conventions, without importing private legal material:\\n\\n- SEED: create a reusable question, diagram, source packet, tool, test or schema for downstream use.\\n- YIELD: deliberately release attention from a branch while others use the seed or evidence accumulates.\\n- AWAIT: resume when a defined evidence/state condition changes, rather than repeatedly checking an unchanged blocker.\\n- ACCUMULATE: collect outputs with their provenance and exposure metadata.\\n- RENDEZVOUS: return when a useful threshold is reached or a time cap expires.\\n- REJOIN: synthesize, audit, compare, improve the seed or launch the next bounded operation.\\n\\nPrefer state-based return thresholds with a time cap. Never let a parked branch disappear: retain its purpose, current state, return condition and displaced responsibility. Do not create recurring automations merely because a workflow could recur; use them only when the user asks or an existing authorized recurrence is explicitly assigned.\\n\\n## 10. Tools, scripts and derived infrastructure\\n\\nUse available connected tools, repository indexes, search tools, paper extractors, scripts and computational tools before improvising manual workarounds. Discover and read tool instructions before use.\\n\\nFor any script or repository operation:\\n- declare exact repositories and paths read/written;\\n- identify outputs as source, derived, generated, append-only or semantic;\\n- record run ID, source commit/ref, tool version and configuration;\\n- exclude private/quarantined material before reading or indexing where required;\\n- never overwrite raw sources during extraction or analysis;\\n- use fresh-base, non-force writes and compare-and-swap/current blob SHA for semantic edits;\\n- use per-run temporary paths and atomic finalization where possible;\\n- validate generated coverage and independently read back writes;\\n- never treat successful scheduling, execution or state restoration as proof that the requested artifact was delivered.\\n\\nPrefer existing scripts and adapters over duplicating functionality. Use dry-run before broad or destructive operations. Add a new parser only when an inventory reveals a recurring unmet need.\\n\\n## 11. Citation and provenance workflow\\n\\nUse the sequence:\\n\\nclaim / geometric statement → citation need → candidate sources → inspect source → exact page/section anchor → verified citation → place citation\\n\\nA bibliography identifies available sources; it does not establish that a source supports a particular claim.\\n\\nFor each important claim, capture:\\n- exact claim being supported;\\n- citation role (background, definition, application, empirical result, prior treatment, cultural context, constraint);\\n- source identity and page/section anchor;\\n- review state;\\n- short explanation of why it supports the claim.\\n\\nUse original external citations in public-facing writing. Internal repository paths and hashes are for recovery and audit, not substitutes for bibliographic citations. Do not cite a source for more than it actually says.\\n\\n## 12.                      _FLATLAND_\\n\\n\\n\\n\\n                                _PART I_\\n                               THIS WORLD\\n\\n\\n\\n\\n                   § 1.—_Of the Nature of Flatland._\\n\\n\\nI call our world Flatland, not because we call it so, but to make its\\nnature clearer to you, my happy readers, who are privileged to live in\\nSpace.\\n\\nImagine a vast sheet of paper on which straight Lines, Triangles,\\nSquares, Pentagons, Hexagons, and other figures, instead of remaining\\nfixed in their places, move freely about, on or in the surface, but\\nwithout the power of rising above or sinking below it, very much like\\nshadows—only hard and with luminous edges—and you will then have a pretty\\ncorrect notion of my country and countrymen. Alas, a few years ago, I\\nshould have said “my universe”: but now my mind has been opened to higher\\nviews of things.\\n\\nIn such a country, you will perceive at once that it is impossible that\\nthere should be anything of what you call a “solid” kind; but I dare say\\nyou will suppose that we could at least distinguish by sight the\\nTriangles, Squares and other figures moving about as I have described\\nthem. On the contrary, we could see nothing of the kind, not at least so\\nas to distinguish one figure from another. Nothing was visible, nor could\\nbe visible, to us, except straight Lines; and the necessity of this I\\nwill speedily demonstrate.\\n\\nPlace a penny on the middle of one of your tables in Space; and leaning\\nover it, look down upon it. It will appear a circle.\\n\\nBut now, drawing back to the edge of the table, gradually lower your eye\\n(thus bringing yourself more and more into the condition of the\\ninhabitants of Flatland), and you will find the penny becoming more and\\nmore oval to your view; and at last when you have placed your eye exactly\\non the edge of the table (so that you are, as it were, actually a\\nFlatland citizen) the penny will then have ceased to appear oval at all,\\nand will have become, so far as you can see, a straight line.\\n\\nThe same thing would happen if you were to treat in the same way a\\nTriangle, or Square, or any other figure cut out of pasteboard. As soon\\nas you look at it with your eye on the edge of the table, you will find\\nthat it ceases to appear to you a figure, and that it becomes in\\nappearance a straight line. Take for example an equilateral Triangle—who\\nrepresents with us a Tradesman of the respectable class. Fig. 1\\nrepresents the Tradesman as you would see him while you were bending over\\nhim from above; figs. 2 and 3 represent the Tradesman, as you would see\\nhim if your eye were close to the level, or all but on the level of the\\ntable; and if your eye were quite on the level of the table (and that is\\nhow we see him in Flatland) you would see nothing but a straight line.\\n\\n[Illustration: ]\\n\\nWhen I was in Spaceland I heard that your sailors have very similar\\nexperiences while they traverse your seas and discern some distant island\\nor coast lying on the horizon. The far-off land may have bays, forelands,\\nangles in and out to any number and extent; yet at a distance you see\\nnone of these (unless indeed your sun shines bright upon them revealing\\nthe projections and retirements by means of light and shade), nothing but\\na grey unbroken line upon the water.\\n\\nWell, that is just what we see when one of our triangular or other\\nacquaintances comes towards us in Flatland. As there is neither sun with\\nus, nor any light of such a kind as to make shadows, we have none of the\\nhelps to the sight that you have in Spaceland. If our friend comes close\\nto us we see his line becomes larger; if he leaves us it becomes smaller:\\nbut still he looks like a straight line; be he a Triangle, Square,\\nPentagon, Hexagon, Circle, what you will—a straight Line he looks and\\nnothing else.\\n\\nYou may perhaps ask how under these disadvantageous circumstances we are\\nable to distinguish our friends from one another: but the answer to this\\nvery natural question will be more fitly and easily given when I come to\\ndescribe the inhabitants of Flatland. For the present let me defer this\\nsubject, and say a word or two about the climate and houses in our\\ncountry.\\n\\n\\n\\n\\n             § 2.—_Of the climate and houses in Flatland._\\n\\n\\nAs with you, so also with us, there are four points of the compass North,\\nSouth, East, and West.\\n\\nThere being no sun nor other heavenly bodies, it is impossible for us to\\ndetermine the North in the usual way; but we have a method of our own. By\\na Law of Nature with us, there is a constant attraction to the South;\\nand, although in temperate climates this is very slight—so that even a\\nWoman in reasonable health can journey several furlongs northward without\\nmuch difficulty—yet the hampering effect of the southward attraction is\\nquite sufficient to serve as a compass in most parts of our earth.\\nMoreover the rain (which falls at stated intervals) coming always from\\nthe North, is an additional assistance; and in the towns we have the\\nguidance of the houses, which of course have their side-walls running for\\nthe most part North and South, so that the roofs may keep off the rain\\nfrom the North. In the country, where there are no houses, the trunks of\\nthe trees serve as some sort of guide. Altogether, we have not so much\\ndifficulty as might be expected in determining our bearings.\\n\\nYet in our more temperate regions, in which the southward attraction is\\nhardly felt, walking sometimes in a perfectly desolate plain where there\\nhave been no houses nor trees to guide me, I have been occasionally\\ncompelled to remain stationary for hours together, waiting till the rain\\ncame before continuing my journey. On the weak and aged, and especially\\non delicate Females, the force of attraction tells much more heavily than\\non the robust of the Male Sex, so that it is a point of breeding, if you\\nmeet a Lady in the street, always to give her the North side of the\\nway—by no means an easy thing to do always at short notice when you are\\nin rude health and in a climate where it is difficult to tell your North\\nfrom your South.\\n\\nWindows there are none in our houses: for the light comes to us alike in\\nour homes and out of them, by day and by night, equally at all times and\\nin all places, whence we know not. It was in old days, with our learned\\nmen, an interesting and oft-investigated question, What is the origin of\\nlight; and the solution of it has been repeatedly attempted, with no\\nother result than to crowd our lunatic asylums with the would-be solvers.\\nHence, after fruitless attempts to suppress such investigations\\nindirectly by making them liable to a heavy tax, the Legislature, in\\ncomparatively recent times, absolutely prohibited them. I, alas I alone\\nin Flatland—know now only too well the true solution of this mysterious\\nproblem; but my knowledge cannot be made intelligible to a single one of\\nmy countrymen; and I am mocked at—I, the sole possessor of the truths of\\nSpace and of the theory of the introduction of Light from the world of\\nThree Dimensions—as if I were the maddest of the mad! But a truce to\\nthese painful digressions: let me return to our houses.\\n\\nThe most common form for the construction of a house is five-sided or\\npentagonal, as in the annexed figure. The two Northern sides _RO_, _OF_,\\nconstitute the roof, and for the most part have no doors; on the East is\\na small door for the Women; on the West a much larger one for the Men;\\nthe South side or floor is usually doorless.\\n\\n[Illustration: ]\\n\\nSquare and triangular houses are not allowed, and for this reason. The\\nangles of a Square (and still more those of an equilateral Triangle)\\nbeing much more pointed than those of a Pentagon, and the lines of\\ninanimate objects (such as houses) being dimmer than the lines of Men and\\nWomen, it follows that there is no little danger lest the points of a\\nsquare or triangular house residence might do serious injury to an\\ninconsiderate or perhaps absent-minded traveller suddenly running against\\nthem: and therefore, as early as the eleventh century of our era,\\ntriangular houses were universally forbidden by Law, the only exceptions\\nbeing fortifications, powder-magazines, barracks, and other state\\nbuildings, which it is not desirable that the general public should\\napproach without circumspection.\\n\\nAt this period, square houses were still everywhere permitted, though\\ndiscouraged by a special tax. But, about three centuries afterwards, the\\nLaw decided that in all towns containing a population above ten thousand,\\nthe angle of a Pentagon was the smallest house-angle that could be\\nallowed consistently with the public safety. The good sense of the\\ncommunity has seconded the efforts of the Legislature; and now, even in\\nthe country, the pentagonal construction has superseded every other. It\\nis only now and then in some very remote and backward agricultural\\ndistrict that an antiquarian may still discover a square house.\\n\\n\\n\\n\\n             § 3.—_Concerning the Inhabitants of Flatland._\\n\\n\\nThe greatest length or breadth of a full-grown inhabitant of Flatland may\\nbe estimated at about eleven of your inches. Twelve inches may be\\nregarded as a maximum.\\n\\nOur Women are Straight Lines.\\n\\nOur Soldiers and Lowest Classes of Workmen are Triangles with two equal\\nsides, each about eleven inches long, and a base or third side so short\\n(often not exceeding half an inch) that they form at their vertices a\\nvery sharp and formidable angle. Indeed when their bases are of the most\\ndegraded type (not more than the eighth part of an inch in size), they\\ncan hardly be distinguished from Straight Lines or Women; so extremely\\npointed are their vertices. With us, as with you, these Triangles are\\ndistinguished from others by being called Isosceles; and by this name I\\nshall refer to them in the following pages.\\n\\nOur Middle Class consists of Equilateral or Equal-sided Triangles.\\n\\nOur Professional Men and Gentlemen are Squares (to which class I myself\\nbelong) and Five-sided figures or Pentagons.\\n\\nNext above these come the Nobility, of whom there are several degrees,\\nbeginning at Six-sided Figures, or Hexagons, and from thence rising in\\nthe number of their sides till they receive the honourable title of\\nPolygonal, or many-sided. Finally when the number of the sides becomes so\\nnumerous, and the sides themselves so small, that the figure cannot be\\ndistinguished from a circle, he is included in the Circular or Priestly\\norder; and this is the highest class of all.\\n\\nIt is a Law of Nature with us that a male child shall have one more side\\nthan his father, so that each generation shall rise (as a rule) one step\\nin the scale of development and nobility. Thus the son of a Square is a\\nPentagon; the son of a Pentagon, a Hexagon; and so on.\\n\\nBut this rule applies not always to the Tradesmen, and still less often\\nto the Soldiers, and to the Workmen; who indeed can hardly be said to\\ndeserve the name of human Figures, since they have not all their sides\\nequal. With them therefore the Law of Nature does not hold; and the son\\nof an Isosceles (_i.e._ a Triangle with two sides equal) remains\\nIsosceles still. Nevertheless, all hope is not shut out, even from the\\nIsosceles, that his posterity may ultimately rise above his degraded\\ncondition. For, after a long series of military successes, or diligent\\nand skilful labours, it is generally found that the more intelligent\\namong the Artisan and Soldier classes manifest a slight increase of their\\nthird side or base, and a shrinkage of the two other sides.\\nIntermarriages (arranged by the Priests) between the sons and daughters\\nof these more intellectual members of the lower classes generally result\\nin an offspring approximating still more to the type of the Equal-sided\\nTriangle.\\n\\nRarely—in proportion to the vast number of Isosceles births—is a genuine\\nand certifiable Equ"

Professor Zöllner of Leipsic was an ardent exponent of the\\ntheory in the \\\"seventies\\\" and some authors hold that even the ancient\\nwritings of the East contain attempts to express Four-Dimensional\\nconcepts.\\n\\nWhether this is actually so is open to doubt but it must be remembered\\nthat in the days when these writings were produced mathematical\\nknowledge was itself in its infancy and that there was, therefore,\\nno terminology available in which the Higher Space concepts could be\\nsuitably expressed even supposing that the ancient philosophers had\\nthem in mind.\\n\\nIt is only through accumulated knowledge, especially the work of Gauss,\\nLobatschewsky, Bolyai, Riemann, and others that modern mathematicians\\nare able to deal easily with space of more than three dimensions.\\n\\nIt may be noted that Kant says:\\n\\n\\\"If it be possible that there are developments of other dimensions of\\nspace, it is very probable that God has somewhere produced them. For\\nHis works have all the grandeur and glory that can be comprised.\\\"\\n\\nAccording to Mr. G.R.S. Mead similar ideas are to be found in certain\\nof the Gnostic cosmogonies.\\n\\n (Fragments of a Faith forgotten, p. 318.)\\n\\nBut a detailed historical review would be out of place here and I will\\ntherefore proceed at once to a discussion of what is meant by the\\nterm \\\"fourth dimension\\\" and will try to explain how it is that we can\\ndetermine some of the necessary properties of four-dimensional space,\\neven although we cannot picture it to ourselves.\\n\\nAt this point I would urge the reader to try to believe that the\\nsubject is not one of great difficulty. As a matter of fact it is\\nreally exceptionally straightforward if only one faces it and does not\\nallow oneself to be frightened.\\n\\nI know that it is impossible to form any clear mental picture of\\nfour-dimensional conditions, but that does not matter. The ideas\\ninvolved are admittedly unprecedented in our experience, but they\\nare not contrary to reason and I do not ask more than a formal and\\nintellectual assent to the propositions and analogies concerned.\\n\\nLet me start, then, by defining what is meant by a Dimension. The\\nbest definition I can think of is to say that, in the sense in which\\nthe word is used here, a Dimension means \\\"An independent direction in\\nspace.\\\"\\n\\nI must amplify this by saying that, \\\"Two directions in space are to be\\nconsidered as independent when they are so related that no movement,\\nhowever great, along one of them will result in the slightest movement\\nalong, or parallel to, the other. That is to say, at right angles, or\\nperpendicular to one another.\\\"\\n\\nThus in Fig. 1 AOA´ and BOB´ are independent directions. One might move\\nfor ever along OA or OA´ and yet one would not have moved in the very\\nleast in the direction of OB or of OB´.\\n\\n[Illustration: _Fig. 1_]\\n\\nNow on a flat surface, such as a sheet of paper, it is not possible to\\ndraw more than _two_ such directions. Any other line that can be drawn,\\nXOX´ for instance, is in a compound direction, so to speak. That is to\\nsay it is partly in the direction AOA´ and partly in the direction BOB´\\nand it is possible to reach any point in it, Y for example, by moving\\nalong OA´ to _a_ and then moving in the direction of OB´ a distance\\nequal to O_b_, or _vice versa_ or by doing the two simultaneously.\\n\\nFor the benefit of those who are absolutely ignorant of the rudiments\\nof Geometrical knowledge, I would point out that Parallel lines are\\nsaid to point, in fact _do_ point, in the same direction.\\n\\n[Illustration: _Fig. 2_]\\n\\nThus, in Fig. 2, the direction of the line ZZ´ is the same as that of\\nAOA´ and the direction of the line PP´ is the same as that of XOX´.\\n\\nThus we see that in a flat surface we find only _two_ dimensions\\nand consequently we can refer to a flat surface as \\\"Space of two\\ndimensions\\\" or \\\"Two-dimensional space.\\\"\\n\\nBut if we refuse to be restricted to a flat surface we find that it is\\npossible to draw a third line through O which is quite \\\"independent\\\"\\nof the directions of the two lines we have previously drawn. We can do\\nthis by drawing it vertically, that is to say, perpendicular to the\\nplane of the paper. Call this line COC´.\\n\\n[Illustration: _Fig. 3_]\\n\\nI have shown it _in perspective_ in Fig. 3. This line fulfils the\\ndefinition we gave of an independent direction in space for it is at\\nright angles both to AOA´ and to BOB´. But we have now exhausted our\\nresources. Try as we will we are unable to draw a fourth line which\\nshall be at right angles to AOA´, BOB´, and COC´ simultaneously.\\n\\nOn other words--In the space we know we find only three dimensions and\\nconsequently we can refer to it as \\\"Space of three dimensions\\\" or\\n\\\"Three-dimensional space.\\\"\\n\\nNow the idea of a fourth dimension of space is simply this: That,\\nwhereas in three-dimensional space, we can draw, through any point\\nin it, _three_, and only three, lines mutually at right angles: in\\nfour-dimensional space, it would be possible to draw, through any point\\nin it, _four_, and only four, lines mutually at right angles.\\n\\nExtending the idea to \\\"Higher space\\\" in general, we may say that,--In\\nspace of \\\"n\\\" dimensions we can draw, through any point in it, \\\"n,\\\" and\\nonly \\\"n,\\\" lines mutually at right angles.\\n\\nNow I admit, that, at first sight, the idea that it might be possible,\\nunder any circumstances, to draw more than three such lines through a\\npoint, seems utterly staggering and inconceivable. And indeed the more\\none thinks of it and the more thoroughly one grasps what it means, the\\nmore absolutely impossible does it appear.\\n\\nAll the same, as I hope to show very soon, it _is_, as a matter of\\nfact, quite possible that there may be another independent direction\\nfulfilling the prescribed conditions, in spite of the fact that we are\\nat present ignorant of it.\\n\\nThis we can only realize by a consideration of the time-honoured but\\nindispensable analogy of a two-dimensional world, or \\\"Flatland.\\\"\\n\\nThis analogy I propose to examine in some detail in the paragraphs\\nwhich follow.\\n\\nBut before doing so I wish to point out, and I do not think it will\\nbe necessary to do more, that a \\\"line\\\" which has length, but neither\\nbreadth nor thickness, can be correctly described as \\\"One-dimensional\\nspace\\\" _i.e._:--space having only one dimension.\\n\\nA mathematical \\\"point,\\\" which has only position and neither length nor\\nbreadth nor thickness, can similarly be called space of no dimensions\\nor \\\"Zero-dimensional space.\\\" Also I wish to take the opportunity of\\ndefining one or two words which I may have occasion to use and have the\\nmerit of brevity.\\n\\n (1) Lines which are drawn through a point for the sake of determining\\n direction are called in Geometrical parlance, \\\"Axes.\\\"\\n\\n Thus in Fig. 1 AOA´ and BOB´ are axes. The former would be known as\\n \\\"the axis of A,\\\" the latter as \\\"the axis of B.\\\" Similarly in Fig. 3\\n COC´ is \\\"the axis of C.\\\"\\n\\n (2) The point in which two or more axes meet, is called the \\\"Origin\\\"\\n and is commonly denoted by the letter O.\\n\\n (3) When convenient, I shall use the terms, \\\"Two space,\\\" \\\"Three\\n space,\\\" \\\"Four space,\\\" etc., instead of writing \\\"Two-dimensional\\n space,\\\" \\\"Three-dimensional space,\\\" \\\"Four-dimensional space,\\\" etc. in\\n full each time.\\n\\n\\nTHE ANALOGY OF A TWO-DIMENSIONAL WORLD.\\n\\nThe consideration of the analogy of a two dimensional world is\\nnecessary because, as Mr. C.H. Hinton says in his book, \\\"The Fourth\\nDimension,\\\" p. 6.\\n\\n \\\"The change in our conceptions, which we make in passing from the\\n shapes and motions in two dimensions to those in three, affords a\\n pattern by which we can pass on still further to the conception of an\\n existence in four-dimensional space.\\\"\\n\\nLet us start then by imagining a very large, flat and perfectly smooth\\nsurface; such for instance as the top of a highly polished table or the\\nsurface of a sheet of still liquid.\\n\\nWe have seen that such a surface constitutes space of two dimensions,\\nbecause through any point in it we can only draw two lines at right\\nangles to one another. In order to draw a third such line we must get\\nout of the surface altogether and draw the line perpendicular to it.\\n\\nNext we must try to imagine that this surface is populated by a race of\\nbeings of an extraordinary thinness.\\n\\nIn order to grasp the analogy properly we must imagine them to be so\\nconstituted that they are incapable of realising any direction in space\\nwhich does not lie in the aforementioned flat surface on which they\\nlive.\\n\\nWe can imagine this by supposing that their thickness, _i.e._:--their\\nextension in the third dimension perpendicular to their surface,--is so\\nsmall as to be invisible to them and also that their \\\"nerve endings\\\"\\nall lie on their periphery. This last is equivalent to saying that they\\nhave no \\\"sense organs\\\" facing the third dimension and that therefore\\nthey cannot receive impressions, or respond to any stimuli that come to\\nthem from that direction.\\n\\nIt follows, therefore, that unless they develope special sense organs\\nwhich face the third dimension they will be acquainted only with such\\nobjects and events as lie, or take place, in their surface.\\n\\nIt is of course inconceivable that they should be truly \\\"plane\\\" beings\\nin the mathematical sense and possess no thickness at all. But if we\\nsuppose that their thickness is of the same order as the diameter of\\na chemical \\\"Atom\\\"--that they are \\\"one atom thick\\\" so to speak,--the\\nconditions laid down as to their limitation will be fulfilled.\\n\\nNow we have supposed the flat surface in our analogy to be _perfectly_\\nsmooth in the true sense of the word. That is to say of such a nature\\nas to offer no resistance whatever to the passage of objects over it.\\n\\nThis means that plane beings will not be sensible of any opposition to\\ntheir movement as far as the surface is concerned. Also, as we have\\nsupposed that they have no nerve endings facing it, it follows that\\nthey cannot feel any pressure from it. In short they will be totally\\nunaware of its existence.\\n\\nBut for the purpose of strict analogy this is insufficient, because a\\nbeing placed on such a surface would be as incapable of movement as\\nwe should be if we were freely suspended in infinite space, remote\\nfrom all the material objects we know. There would be nothing, in\\nany direction known to him, from which he could \\\"push off.\\\" We must\\ntherefore further suppose that the force of gravity operates in his\\nworld in a manner similar to that which we know,--every particle of\\nmatter attracting every other particle.\\n\\nThis will mean two things; first, that every particle on the surface\\nwill be held against that surface and that plane beings will,\\ntherefore, never be able to move away from it; and, second, that matter\\non the surface will tend to collect together in a manner precisely\\nanalogous to what we observe in our space.\\n\\nFinally, we may suppose that these hypothetical beings whom we are\\nconsidering live on the rim of a very large disc of plane matter, which\\nhas collected and is held together by the action of gravity, just as we\\nlive on the surface of a very large sphere of solid matter. They will\\nbe kept up against the rim of the disc by the force of gravity, which\\nwill attract them towards its centre, in the same way that we are kept\\nagainst the surface of the earth.\\n\\nIt is easy to realise that the existence of such a plane being will be\\nvery limited indeed. He will be conscious of two directions only. One\\nwill be \\\"up and down\\\" that is to say, towards or away from the centre\\nof his plane earth: the other will be \\\"forwards and backwards\\\" along\\nits rim. Again any object, that projects beyond the rim of the disc on\\nwhich he lives, will be for him an obstacle, which can only be passed\\nby climbing over or burrowing under it. He cannot go round it, because\\nthat would mean coming out of the flat surface, which he is unable to\\ndo. Thus in Fig. 4, if the curved line AB represents a portion of the\\nrim of the disc or \\\"plane earth,\\\" and C a plane being, then he can only\\npass from A to B by \\\"climbing over\\\" any intervening object such as D,\\n_i.e._:--by following the path indicated by the dotted line. Otherwise\\nhe would have to get out of the plane of the paper, which is impossible\\nfor him.\\n\\n[Illustration: _Fig. 4_]\\n\\nNow that I have described in outline the strict analogy of a race of\\nplane beings inhabiting a smooth surface, I shall take the liberty,\\nin t"

What was actually being investigated?\\n\\n1. Which contemporary newspapers and scientific journals repeated, ridiculed, defended, or reframed the fourth-dimensional interpretation?\\n5. Relation to speculative philosophy\\r\\nAccording to Georg Hegel, Encyclopedia of the Philosophical Sciences, medieval mysticism is the same as the speculative philosophy of the 19th century:\\r\\n\\r\\nEnc§82d Hinsichtlich der Bedeutung des Spekulativen ist hier noch zu erwähnen, daß man darunter dasselbe zu verstehen hat, was früher, zumal in Beziehung auf das religiöse Bewußtsein und dessen Inhalt, als das Mystische bezeichnet zu werden pflegte. Wenn heutzutage vom Mystischen die Rede ist, so gilt dies in der Regel als gleichbedeutend mit dem Geheimnisvollen und Unbegreiflichen, und dies Geheimnisvolle und Unbegreifliche wird dann, je nach Verschiedenheit der sonstigen Bildung und Sinnesweise, von den einen als das Eigentliche und Wahrhafte, von den anderen aber als das dem Aberglauben und der Täuschung Angehörige betrachtet.\\r\\n\\r\\nHierüber ist zunächst zu bemerken, daß das Mystische allerdings ein Geheimnisvolles ist, jedoch nur für den Verstand, und zwar einfach um deswillen, weil die abstrakte Identität das Prinzip des Verstandes, das Mystische aber (als gleichbedeutend mit dem Spekulativen) die konkrete Einheit derjenigen Bestimmungen ist, welche dem Verstand nur in ihrer Trennung und Entgegensetzung für wahr gelten. Wenn dann diejenigen, welche das Mystische als das Wahrhafte anerkennen, es gleichfalls dabei bewenden lassen, daß dasselbe ein schlechthin Geheimnisvolles sei, so wird damit ihrerseits nur ausgesprochen, daß das Denken für sie gleichfalls nur die Bedeutung des abstrakten Identischsetzens hat und daß man um deswillen, um zur Wahrheit zu gelangen, auf das Denken verzichten oder, wie auch gesagt zu werden pflegt, daß man die Vernunft gefangennehmen müsse.\\r\\n\\r\\nEnc§82e Nun aber ist, wie wir gesehen haben, das abstrakt verständige Denken so wenig ein Festes und Letztes, daß dasselbe sich vielmehr als das beständige Aufheben seiner selbst und als das Umschlagen in sein Entgegengesetztes erweist, wohingegen das Vernünftige als solches gerade darin besteht, die Entgegengesetzten als ideelle Momente in sich zu enthalten. Alles Vernünftige ist somit zugleich als mystisch zu bezeichnen, womit jedoch nur so viel gesagt ist, daß dasselbe über den Verstand hinausgeht, und keineswegs, daß dasselbe überhaupt als dem Denken unzugänglich und unbegreiflich zu betrachten sei.\\r\\n\\r\\nIt should also be mentioned here that the meaning of the speculative is to be understood as being the same as what used in earlier times to be called “mystical”, especially with regard to the religious consciousness and its content. When we speak of the “mystical” nowadays, it is taken as a rule to be synonymous with what is mysterious and incomprehensible; and, depending on the ways their culture and mentality vary in other respects, some people treat the mysterious and in­comprehensible as what is authentic and genuine, whilst others regard it as belong­ing to the domain of superstition and deception. About this we must remark first that “the mystical” is certainly something mysterious, but only for the understand­ing, and then only because abstract identity is the principle of the understanding. But when it is regarded as synonymous with the speculative, the mystical is the concrete unity of just those determinations that count as true for the understanding only in their separation and opposition. So if those who recognise the mystical as what is genuine say that it is something utterly mysterious, and just leave it at that, they are only declaring that for them, too, thinking has only the Significance of an abstract positing of identity, and that in order to attain the truth we must renounce thinking, or, as they frequently put it, that we must “take reason captive.” As we have seen, however, the abstract thinking of the understanding is so far from being something firm and ultimate that it proves itself, on the contrary, to be a constant sublating of itself and an overturning into its opposite, whereas the rational as such is rational precisely because it contains both of the opposites as ideal moments within itself. Thus, everything rational can equally be called “mystical”; but this only amounts to saying that it transcends the understanding. It does not at all imply that what is so spoken of must be considered inaccessible to thinking and incomprehensible.\\r\\n\\r\\nFor Hegel’s relation to Meister Eckhart, see there.\\r\\n\\r\\n2. Bertrand Russell’s relation to mysticism\\r\\nThe philosopher Bertrand Russell concerned himself with mysticism and was, according to himself, influenced by a “mathematical mysticism” in his younger years.\\r\\n\\r\\nIn his essay “Mysticism and Logic” (Russell 1918) Russell understands mysticism as “the attempt to conceive the world as a whole by means of thought”. He gives four characteristics of it:\\r\\n\\r\\n“belief in insight as against discursive knowledge”\\r\\na belief in unity of everything\\r\\ndenial of the reality of time\\r\\nthe claim that evil, and sometimes also good, is a mere appearance\\r\\nRussell finds at least some of these characteristics in the philosophies of Heraclitus, Plato, Hegel, and Spinoza. Interestingly, Heraclitus is judged far better than Plato, the former being ascribed “a nature [in which] we see the true union of the mystic and the man of science”. In the remainder of the essay Russell discusses the relation of the four characteristics of mysticism to his own views.\\r\\n\\r\\nIn the autobiographical book Portraits from Memory the passage\\r\\n\\r\\nMathematics … deals with the world of ideas and has in consequence an exactness and perfection which is absent from the everyday world. This kind of mathematical mysticism, which Plato derived from Pythagoras, appealed to me.\\r\\n\\r\\nmay serve as an example how Russell was influenced in young age by the exposure to mathematics; more poetically it is expressed in the essay The Study of Mathematics published along with Mysticism and Logic (Russell 1918)\\r\\n\\r\\nMathematics, rightly viewed, possesses not only truth, but supreme beauty—a beauty cold and austere, like that of sculpture, without the gorgeous trappings of painting or music, yet sublimely pure, and capable of a stern perfection such as only the greatest art can show. The true spirit of delight, the exaltation, the sense of being more than man, which is the touchstone of the highest excellence, is to be found in mathematics as surely as in poetry. … Real life is, to most men, a long second-best, a perpetual compromise between the ideal and the possible; but the world of pure reason knows no compromise, no practical limitations, no barrier to the creative activity embodying in splendid edifices the passionate aspiration after the perfect from which all great works springs.\\r\\n\\r\\n… Of the austere virtues the love of truth is the chief, and in mathematics, more than elsewhere, the love of truth may find encouragement for waning faith.\\r\\n\\r\\nAccording to Ray Monk’s biography on Russell, the search for a foundation of this “Pythagorean” mysticism governed the first half of his life: Being deeply disappointed by the mathematical curriculum at Cambridge, which did not address his philosophical needs, Russell turned to idealism, which was at that time propounded in Britain by J.M. Ellis McTaggart following the German tradition of Kant and Hegel. Under this influence Russell devised in An Essay on the Foundations of Geometry a variation of Kant’s transcendental aesthetics claiming that the curvature of the space of our perception, i.e. of any ‘’form of externality’’, is a priori constant.\\r\\n\\r\\nExposure to the work of the German mathematicians Dedekind, Weierstraß, and Cantor along with a personal meeting with Peano caused a turn in Russell’s views. He now hoped to find a rigorous foundation of mathematics based solely on logical axioms, thereby justifying a kind of Platonic view on mathematics. But over the years he was frustrated in this attempt by many problems he encountered, especially Russell's paradox. He gradually gave up all his Platonic beliefs; arriving in the end (after Wittgenstein's Tractatus) at formalism.\\r\\n\\r\\nHe remarks on the power of rigorous mathematical definition:\\r\\n\\r\\n“Continuity” had been, until he [Cantor] defined it, a vague word, convenient for philosophers like Hegel, who wished to introduce metaphysical muddles into mathematics. Cantor gave a precise significance to the word, and showed that continuity, as he defined it, was the concept needed by mathematicians and physicist. By this means a great deal of mysticism, such as that of Bergson, was rendered antiquated. (Chapter XXXI of “A History of Western Philosophy” (1945))\\r\\n\\r\\n3. Brouwer\\r\\nL.E.J. Brouwer had a long standing interest in the theory and practice of mysticism, setting out his manifesto while still a graduate student in the essay Life, Art, and Mysticism (1905). The essay quotes the Bhagavad Gita, Meister Eckhart, and Jakob Böhme.\\r\\n\\r\\nHowever, he did not consider his intuitionism to depend upon his mystical views as such. For Brouwer, mysticism is the domain of “consciousness’ deepest home”, wherein there is no subject-object distinction. The first act of intuitionism, the intuition of time, propels us away from this pure state of “wisdom”. It is in fact the precondition for any experience of an outer world or experience of the self as something distinct. Mathematics thus comes into being in this exodus from the home of consciousness, so on Brouwer’s view, “mathematics is in a sense the very opposite of mysticism” (Van Atten, 2004), and mystical insight is only possible quite apart from the machinations of the intellect.\\r\\n\\r\\nBrouwer even went so far as to remark on the perniciousness of mathematics in its keeping us from the home of consciousness. Thus in the notebooks in which he conceived his 1907 thesis we find: “One could see as the goal of one’s life: abolition and delivery from all mathematics”.\\r\\n\\r\\n4. Gödel\\r\\nFor the moment, see e.g. van Atten and Tragesser 2014, and Gödel’s ontological proof involving modal logic.\\r\\n\\r\\n5. But the recipient is skeptical: They need a way to verify that the message comes from the purported location. Quantum physics has a solution.\\r\\n\\r\\nScientists have demonstrated a quantum technique to ensure that someone is in the location they claim to be, physicist Abigail Gookin reported March 18 at the American Physical Society’s Global Physics Summit. Called quantum position verification, the technique is based on the concept of quantum entanglement, in which the fates of two far-flung particles are closely linked.\\r\\n\\r\\nSign up for our newsletter\\r\\nWe summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.\\r\\n\\r\\nE-mail\\r\\nSign up\\r\\nBy subscribing, you agree to our Terms & Privacy Policy.  You must be 13 or older to sign up.\\r\\n\\r\\nIn the future, the technique could be useful for preventing some types of phishing attacks, or for limiting which users can access certain resources. (For example, access to sensitive nuclear weapons infrastructure could be restricted to those in a secure government building.) The method could be part of a future quantum internet that could one day provide various types of ultrasecure communications.\\r\\n\\r\\nHere’s how it works: Two people, called verifiers, each want to confirm that a third person, called a prover, is in a given location. The verifiers, who are on opposite sides of the prover’s purported location, each send a random number to the prover, which the prover will use to determine their next step. Meanwhile, one of the verifiers creates a pair of entangled photons, or particles of light. The verifier holds onto one photon, and sends the other to the prover.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe prover and verifier measure their photons simultaneously. Specifically, they measure polarization, the direction in which the electromagnetic waves of the photons wiggle. The random numbers tell the prover what measurement settings to use to determine their photon’s polarization. The prover sends the result of their measurement back to the verifiers.\\r\\n\\r\\nThen, the verifiers compare the prover’s result to the result from the measurement of the other photon. Over many repetitions of this photon-measuring protocol, the results should be strongly linked, or correlated. If a sneaky impostor intercepted the photon from another location, the results of the measurements wouldn’t be as strongly correlated as expected, thanks to constraints set by the speed of light and quirks of quantum measurements. The verifiers would know that something was fishy.\\r\\n\\r\\nAt the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) in Boulder, Colo., scientists created two verifier stations, separated by about 200 meters and connected by optical fibers to a prover in between. The method successfully localized the prover, Gookin, of NIST, and colleagues reported in a paper submitted January 23 to arXiv.org.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe basis for the technique is what’s called a loophole-free Bell test, a method of sending and measuring quantum particles that proves that the oddities of quantum physics can’t be explained away. That’s because the correlations between pairs of photons are stronger than any classical theory could account for.\\r\\n\\r\\nBecause the technique connects a real, physical place to information the parties exchange, it could be the basis for other secure communication techniques going forward says Gookin. “This is the first time we can concretely tie someone’s location to their information.”\\r\\n\\r\\nQuestions or comments on this article? Idea\\r\\n2. Definitions\\r\\n3. Alternative characterisations\\r\\n4. Examples\\r\\n5. References\\r\\n1. Idea\\r\\nA canonical morphism is a morphism which is equivariant under an automorphism group, with actions mediated by two functors. It may be seen as a natural transformation in a particular context. Conversely, canonical morphisms can be combined into a notion of transformation more general than a natural transformation, although this also may be seen as a natural transformation in a particular context.\\r\\n\\r\\nThis usage of the word ‘canonical’ is due to Jim Dolan. In general, this term is often used in mathematics to mean that the result of a construction may be specified using only the data at hand, without making arbitrary choices. The idea behind using the word here is, roughly, that only canonical morphisms may be specified (in the situations in which they appear) without violating the principle of equivalence. (Both avoiding arbitrary choices and avoiding violation of the principle of equivalence are related to avoiding the axiom of choice, but that does not seem to be directly relevant.) However, there are certainly also uses of ‘canonical’ in mathematics that do not fall under this definition.\\r\\n\\r\\nArguably, ‘natural’ would be a better term for this intuition, but canonical morphisms are more general than the natural transformations that appear in the same contexts, so that word is taken. Another possible term is ‘core-natural’ or ‘groupoid-natural’, since (as will be seen below) canonical morphisms may be interpreted as natural transformations between functors restricted to the core (underlying groupoid) of a given category. The terms ‘basis/coordinate–free/invariant’ and ‘generally covariant’ also capture the same intuition, although these tend to be restricted to certain disciplines (linear algebra, geometry, physics); see also principle of equivalence, definable set (in model theory), and parametric polymorphism (in type theory).\\r\\n\\r\\n2. Definitions\\r\\nGiven categories \\r\\nC\\r\\n and \\r\\nD\\r\\n, functors \\r\\nF\\r\\n,\\r\\nG\\r\\n:\\r\\nC\\r\\n→\\r\\nD\\r\\n, and an object \\r\\nx\\r\\n of \\r\\nC\\r\\n, a canonical morphism from \\r\\nF\\r\\n(\\r\\nx\\r\\n)\\r\\n to \\r\\nG\\r\\n(\\r\\nx\\r\\n)\\r\\n is a morphism \\r\\nh\\r\\n:\\r\\nF\\r\\n(\\r\\nx\\r\\n)\\r\\n→\\r\\nG\\r\\n(\\r\\nx\\r\\n)\\r\\n in \\r\\nD\\r\\n such that the diagram\\r\\n\\r\\nF\\r\\n(\\r\\nx\\r\\n)\\r\\n→\\r\\nh\\r\\nG\\r\\n(\\r\\nx\\r\\n)\\r\\nF\\r\\n(\\r\\nu\\r\\n)\\r\\n↓\\r\\n↓\\r\\nG\\r\\n(\\r\\nu\\r\\n)\\r\\nF\\r\\n(\\r\\nx\\r\\n)\\r\\n→\\r\\nh\\r\\nG\\r\\n(\\r\\nx\\r\\n)\\r\\ncommutes for any automorphism \\r\\nu\\r\\n of \\r\\nx\\r\\n in \\r\\nC\\r\\n.\\r\\n\\r\\nAs \\r\\nF\\r\\n and \\r\\nG\\r\\n are only ever applied to isomorphisms, this definition makes sense even when they are defined only on the core of \\r\\nC\\r\\n. In fact, as they are applied only to \\r\\nx\\r\\n and its automorphisms, the definition makes sense when they are defined only on the subgroupoid that is the delooping of \\r\\nAut\\r\\nC\\r\\n(\\r\\nx\\r\\n)\\r\\n, the automorphism group of \\r\\nx\\r\\n in \\r\\nC\\r\\n. In that case, \\r\\nF\\r\\n and \\r\\nG\\r\\n are representations of \\r\\nAut\\r\\nC\\r\\n(\\r\\nx\\r\\n)\\r\\n in \\r\\nD\\r\\n, and a canonical morphism is precisely an intertwiner between these representations.\\r\\n\\r\\nIn the other direction, we can consider a family of canonical morphisms, one for each object of \\r\\nC\\r\\n, which are coherent in the sense that\\r\\n\\r\\nF\\r\\n(\\r\\nx\\r\\n)\\r\\n→\\r\\nh\\r\\nx\\r\\nG\\r\\n(\\r\\nx\\r\\n)\\r\\nF\\r\\n(\\r\\nu\\r\\n)\\r\\n↓\\r\\n↓\\r\\nG\\r\\n(\\r\\nu\\r\\n)\\r\\nF\\r\\n(\\r\\ny\\r\\n)\\r\\n→\\r\\nh\\r\\ny\\r\\nG\\r\\n(\\r\\ny\\r\\n)\\r\\ncommutes for every isomorphism \\r\\nu\\r\\n:\\r\\nx\\r\\n→\\r\\ny\\r\\n in \\r\\nC\\r\\n. Such a family may be called a canonical transformation from \\r\\nF\\r\\n to \\r\\nG\\r\\n, although this should not be confused with a canonical coordinate transformation. Note that every natural isomorphism is canonical, but not conversely. The main use of having a term like ‘canonical’ at all is to say that an expression for a morphism in \\r\\nD\\r\\n, involving a variable... (truncated)"
