            "[L1] {\n[L2]   \"content\": \"nLabmysticism\\r\\n|  Home Page | All Pages | Latest Revisions | Discuss this page | \\r\\nSearch\\r\\nContext\\r\\nPhilosophy\\r\\nContents\\r\\n1. Relation to speculative philosophy\\r\\n2. Bertrand Russell’s relation to mysticism\\r\\n3. Brouwer\\r\\n4. Gödel\\r\\n5. Related entries\\r\\n6. References\\r\\n1. Relation to speculative philosophy\\r\\nAccording to Georg Hegel, Encyclopedia of the Philosophical Sciences, medieval mysticism is the same as the speculative philosophy of the 19th century:\\r\\n\\r\\nEnc§82d Hinsichtlich der Bedeutung des Spekulativen ist hier noch zu erwähnen, daß man darunter dasselbe zu verstehen hat, was früher, zumal in Beziehung auf das religiöse Bewußtsein und dessen Inhalt, als das Mystische bezeichnet zu werden pflegte. Wenn heutzutage vom Mystischen die Rede ist, so gilt dies in der Regel als gleichbedeutend mit dem Geheimnisvollen und Unbegreiflichen, und dies Geheimnisvolle und Unbegreifliche wird dann, je nach Verschiedenheit der sonstigen Bildung und Sinnesweise, von den einen als das Eigentliche und Wahrhafte, von den anderen aber als das dem Aberglauben und der Täuschung Angehörige betrachtet.\\r\\n\\r\\nHierüber ist zunächst zu bemerken, daß das Mystische allerdings ein Geheimnisvolles ist, jedoch nur für den Verstand, und zwar einfach um deswillen, weil die abstrakte Identität das Prinzip des Verstandes, das Mystische aber (als gleichbedeutend mit dem Spekulativen) die konkrete Einheit derjenigen Bestimmungen ist, welche dem Verstand nur in ihrer Trennung und Entgegensetzung für wahr gelten. Wenn dann diejenigen, welche das Mystische als das Wahrhafte anerkennen, es gleichfalls dabei bewenden lassen, daß dasselbe ein schlechthin Geheimnisvolles sei, so wird damit ihrerseits nur ausgesprochen, daß das Denken für sie gleichfalls nur die Bedeutung des abstrakten Identischsetzens hat und daß man um deswillen, um zur Wahrheit zu gelangen, auf das Denken verzichten oder, wie auch gesagt zu werden pflegt, daß man die Vernunft gefangennehmen müsse.\\r\\n\\r\\nEnc§82e Nun aber ist, wie wir gesehen haben, das abstrakt verständige Denken so wenig ein Festes und Letztes, daß dasselbe sich vielmehr als das beständige Aufheben seiner selbst und als das Umschlagen in sein Entgegengesetztes erweist, wohingegen das Vernünftige als solches gerade darin besteht, die Entgegengesetzten als ideelle Momente in sich zu enthalten. Alles Vernünftige ist somit zugleich als mystisch zu bezeichnen, womit jedoch nur so viel gesagt ist, daß dasselbe über den Verstand hinausgeht, und keineswegs, daß dasselbe überhaupt als dem Denken unzugänglich und unbegreiflich zu betrachten sei.\\r\\n\\r\\nIt should also be mentioned here that the meaning of the speculative is to be understood as being the same as what used in earlier times to be called “mystical”, especially with regard to the religious consciousness and its content. When we speak of the “mystical” nowadays, it is taken as a rule to be synonymous with what is mysterious and incomprehensible; and, depending on the ways their culture and mentality vary in other respects, some people treat the mysterious and in­comprehensible as what is authentic and genuine, whilst others regard it as belong­ing to the domain of superstition and deception. About this we must remark first that “the mystical” is certainly something mysterious, but only for the understand­ing, and then only because abstract identity is the principle of the understanding. But when it is regarded as synonymous with the speculative, the mystical is the concrete unity of just those determinations that count as true for the understanding only in their separation and opposition. So if those who recognise the mystical as what is genuine say that it is something utterly mysterious, and just leave it at that, they are only declaring that for them, too, thinking has only the Significance of an abstract positing of identity, and that in order to attain the truth we must renounce thinking, or, as they frequently put it, that we must “take reason captive.” As we have seen, however, the abstract thinking of the understanding is so far from being something firm and ultimate that it proves itself, on the contrary, to be a constant sublating of itself and an overturning into its opposite, whereas the rational as such is rational precisely because it contains both of the opposites as ideal moments within itself. Thus, everything rational can equally be called “mystical”; but this only amounts to saying that it transcends the understanding. It does not at all imply that what is so spoken of must be considered inaccessible to thinking and incomprehensible.\\r\\n\\r\\nFor Hegel’s relation to Meister Eckhart, see there.\\r\\n\\r\\n2. Bertrand Russell’s relation to mysticism\\r\\nThe philosopher Bertrand Russell concerned himself with mysticism and was, according to himself, influenced by a “mathematical mysticism” in his younger years.\\r\\n\\r\\nIn his essay “Mysticism and Logic” (Russell 1918) Russell understands mysticism as “the attempt to conceive the world as a whole by means of thought”. He gives four characteristics of it:\\r\\n\\r\\n“belief in insight as against discursive knowledge”\\r\\na belief in unity of everything\\r\\ndenial of the reality of time\\r\\nthe claim that evil, and sometimes also good, is a mere appearance\\r\\nRussell finds at least some of these characteristics in the philosophies of Heraclitus, Plato, Hegel, and Spinoza. Interestingly, Heraclitus is judged far better than Plato, the former being ascribed “a nature [in which] we see the true union of the mystic and the man of science”. In the remainder of the essay Russell discusses the relation of the four characteristics of mysticism to his own views.\\r\\n\\r\\nIn the autobiographical book Portraits from Memory the passage\\r\\n\\r\\nMathematics … deals with the world of ideas and has in consequence an exactness and perfection which is absent from the everyday world. This kind of mathematical mysticism, which Plato derived from Pythagoras, appealed to me.\\r\\n\\r\\nmay serve as an example how Russell was influenced in young age by the exposure to mathematics; more poetically it is expressed in the essay The Study of Mathematics published along with Mysticism and Logic (Russell 1918)\\r\\n\\r\\nMathematics, rightly viewed, possesses not only truth, but supreme beauty—a beauty cold and austere, like that of sculpture, without the gorgeous trappings of painting or music, yet sublimely pure, and capable of a stern perfection such as only the greatest art can show. The true spirit of delight, the exaltation, the sense of being more than man, which is the touchstone of the highest excellence, is to be found in mathematics as surely as in poetry. … Real life is, to most men, a long second-best, a perpetual compromise between the ideal and the possible; but the world of pure reason knows no compromise, no practical limitations, no barrier to the creative activity embodying in splendid edifices the passionate aspiration after the perfect from which all great works springs.\\r\\n\\r\\n… Of the austere virtues the love of truth is the chief, and in mathematics, more than elsewhere, the love of truth may find encouragement for waning faith.\\r\\n\\r\\nAccording to Ray Monk’s biography on Russell, the search for a foundation of this “Pythagorean” mysticism governed the first half of his life: Being deeply disappointed by the mathematical curriculum at Cambridge, which did not address his philosophical needs, Russell turned to idealism, which was at that time propounded in Britain by J.M. Ellis McTaggart following the German tradition of Kant and Hegel. Under this influence Russell devised in An Essay on the Foundations of Geometry a variation of Kant’s transcendental aesthetics claiming that the curvature of the space of our perception, i.e. of any ‘’form of externality’’, is a priori constant.\\r\\n\\r\\nExposure to the work of the German mathematicians Dedekind, Weierstraß, and Cantor along with a personal meeting with Peano caused a turn in Russell’s views. He now hoped to find a rigorous foundation of mathematics based solely on logical axioms, thereby justifying a kind of Platonic view on mathematics. But over the years he was frustrated in this attempt by many problems he encountered, especially Russell's paradox. He gradually gave up all his Platonic beliefs; arriving in the end (after Wittgenstein's Tractatus) at formalism.\\r\\n\\r\\nHe remarks on the power of rigorous mathematical definition:\\r\\n\\r\\n“Continuity” had been, until he [Cantor] defined it, a vague word, convenient for philosophers like Hegel, who wished to introduce metaphysical muddles into mathematics. Cantor gave a precise significance to the word, and showed that continuity, as he defined it, was the concept needed by mathematicians and physicist. By this means a great deal of mysticism, such as that of Bergson, was rendered antiquated. (Chapter XXXI of “A History of Western Philosophy” (1945))\\r\\n\\r\\n3. Brouwer\\r\\nL.E.J. Brouwer had a long standing interest in the theory and practice of mysticism, setting out his manifesto while still a graduate student in the essay Life, Art, and Mysticism (1905). The essay quotes the Bhagavad Gita, Meister Eckhart, and Jakob Böhme.\\r\\n\\r\\nHowever, he did not consider his intuitionism to depend upon his mystical views as such. For Brouwer, mysticism is the domain of “consciousness’ deepest home”, wherein there is no subject-object distinction. The first act of intuitionism, the intuition of time, propels us away from this pure state of “wisdom”. It is in fact the precondition for any experience of an outer world or experience of the self as something distinct. Mathematics thus comes into being in this exodus from the home of consciousness, so on Brouwer’s view, “mathematics is in a sense the very opposite of mysticism” (Van Atten, 2004), and mystical insight is only possible quite apart from the machinations of the intellect.\\r\\n\\r\\nBrouwer even went so far as to remark on the perniciousness of mathematics in its keeping us from the home of consciousness. Thus in the notebooks in which he conceived his 1907 thesis we find: “One could see as the goal of one’s life: abolition and delivery from all mathematics”.\\r\\n\\r\\n4. Gödel\\r\\nFor the moment, see e.g. van Atten and Tragesser 2014, and Gödel’s ontological proof involving modal logic.\\r\\n\\r\\n5. Relation to speculative philosophy\\r\\n2. Bertrand Russell’s relation to mysticism\\r\\n3. Brouwer\\r\\n4. Gödel\\r\\n5. Related entries\\r\\n6. References\\r\\n1. Relation to speculative philosophy\\r\\nAccording to Georg Hegel, Encyclopedia of the Philosophical Sciences, medieval mysticism is the same as the speculative philosophy of the 19th century:\\r\\n\\r\\nEnc§82d Hinsichtlich der Bedeutung des Spekulativen ist hier noch zu erwähnen, daß man darunter dasselbe zu verstehen hat, was früher, zumal in Beziehung auf das religiöse Bewußtsein und dessen Inhalt, als das Mystische bezeichnet zu werden pflegte. Wenn heutzutage vom Mystischen die Rede ist, so gilt dies in der Regel als gleichbedeutend mit dem Geheimnisvollen und Unbegreiflichen, und dies Geheimnisvolle und Unbegreifliche wird dann, je nach Verschiedenheit der sonstigen Bildung und Sinnesweise, von den einen als das Eigentliche und Wahrhafte, von den anderen aber als das dem Aberglauben und der Täuschung Angehörige betrachtet.\\r\\n\\r\\nHierüber ist zunächst zu bemerken, daß das Mystische allerdings ein Geheimnisvolles ist, jedoch nur für den Verstand, und zwar einfach um deswillen, weil die abstrakte Identität das Prinzip des Verstandes, das Mystische aber (als gleichbedeutend mit dem Spekulativen) die konkrete Einheit derjenigen Bestimmungen ist, welche dem Verstand nur in ihrer Trennung und Entgegensetzung für wahr gelten. Wenn dann diejenigen, welche das Mystische als das Wahrhafte anerkennen, es gleichfalls dabei bewenden lassen, daß dasselbe ein schlechthin Geheimnisvolles sei, so wird damit ihrerseits nur ausgesprochen, daß das Denken für sie gleichfalls nur die Bedeutung des abstrakten Identischsetzens hat und daß man um deswillen, um zur Wahrheit zu gelangen, auf das Denken verzichten oder, wie auch gesagt zu werden pflegt, daß man die Vernunft gefangennehmen müsse.\\r\\n\\r\\nEnc§82e Nun aber ist, wie wir gesehen haben, das abstrakt verständige Denken so wenig ein Festes und Letztes, daß dasselbe sich vielmehr als das beständige Aufheben seiner selbst und als das Umschlagen in sein Entgegengesetztes erweist, wohingegen das Vernünftige als solches gerade darin besteht, die Entgegengesetzten als ideelle Momente in sich zu enthalten. Alles Vernünftige ist somit zugleich als mystisch zu bezeichnen, womit jedoch nur so viel gesagt ist, daß dasselbe über den Verstand hinausgeht, und keineswegs, daß dasselbe überhaupt als dem Denken unzugänglich und unbegreiflich zu betrachten sei.\\r\\n\\r\\nIt should also be mentioned here that the meaning of the speculative is to be understood as being the same as what used in earlier times to be called “mystical”, especially with regard to the religious consciousness and its content. When we speak of the “mystical” nowadays, it is taken as a rule to be synonymous with what is mysterious and incomprehensible; and, depending on the ways their culture and mentality vary in other respects, some people treat the mysterious and in­comprehensible as what is authentic and genuine, whilst others regard it as belong­ing to the domain of superstition and deception. About this we must remark first that “the mystical” is certainly something mysterious, but only for the understand­ing, and then only because abstract identity is the principle of the understanding. But when it is regarded as synonymous with the speculative, the mystical is the concrete unity of just those determinations that count as true for the understanding only in their separation and opposition. So if those who recognise the mystical as what is genuine say that it is something utterly mysterious, and just leave it at that, they are only declaring that for them, too, thinking has only the Significance of an abstract positing of identity, and that in order to attain the truth we must renounce thinking, or, as they frequently put it, that we must “take reason captive.” As we have seen, however, the abstract thinking of the understanding is so far from being something firm and ultimate that it proves itself, on the contrary, to be a constant sublating of itself and an overturning into its opposite, whereas the rational as such is rational precisely because it contains both of the opposites as ideal moments within itself. Thus, everything rational can equally be called “mystical”; but this only amounts to saying that it transcends the understanding. It does not at all imply that what is so spoken of must be considered inaccessible to thinking and incomprehensible.\\r\\n\\r\\nFor Hegel’s relation to Meister Eckhart, see there.\\r\\n\\r\\n2. Bertrand Russell’s relation to mysticism\\r\\nThe philosopher Bertrand Russell concerned himself with mysticism and was, according to himself, influenced by a “mathematical mysticism” in his younger years.\\r\\n\\r\\nIn his essay “Mysticism and Logic” (Russell 1918) Russell understands mysticism as “the attempt to conceive the world as a whole by means of thought”. He gives four characteristics of it:\\r\\n\\r\\n“belief in insight as against discursive knowledge”\\r\\na belief in unity of everything\\r\\ndenial of the reality of time\\r\\nthe claim that evil, and sometimes also good, is a mere appearance\\r\\nRussell finds at least some of these characteristics in the philosophies of Heraclitus, Plato, Hegel, and Spinoza. Interestingly, Heraclitus is judged far better than Plato, the former being ascribed “a nature [in which] we see the true union of the mystic and the man of science”. In the remainder of the essay Russell discusses the relation of the four characteristics of mysticism to his own views.\\r\\n\\r\\nIn the autobiographical book Portraits from Memory the passage\\r\\n\\r\\nMathematics … deals with the world of ideas and has in consequence an exactness and perfection which is absent from the everyday world. This kind of mathematical mysticism, which Plato derived from Pythagoras, appealed to me.\\r\\n\\r\\nmay serve as an example how Russell was influenced in young age by the exposure to mathematics; more poetically it is expressed in the essay The Study of Mathematics published along with Mysticism and Logic (Russell 1918)\\r\\n\\r\\nMathematics, rightly viewed, possesses not only truth, but supreme beauty—a beauty cold and austere, like that of sculpture, without the gorgeous trappings of painting or music, yet sublimely pure, and capable of a stern perfection such as only the greatest art can show. The true spirit of delight, the exaltation, the sense of being more than man, which is the touchstone of the highest excellence, is to be found in mathematics as surely as in poetry. … Real life is, to most men, a long second-best, a perpetual compromise between the ideal and the possible; but the world of pure reason knows no compromise, no practical limitations, no barrier to the creative activity embodying in splendid edifices the passionate aspiration after the perfect from which all great works springs.\\r\\n\\r\\n… Of the austere virtues the love of truth is the chief, and in mathematics, more than elsewhere, the love of truth may find encouragement for waning faith.\\r\\n\\r\\nAccording to Ray Monk’s biography on Russell, the search for a foundation of this “Pythagorean” mysticism governed the first half of his life: Being deeply disappointed by the mathematical curriculum at Cambridge, which did not address his philosophical needs, Russell turned to idealism, which was at that time propounded in Britain by J.M. Ellis McTaggart following the German tradition of Kant and Hegel. Under this influence Russell devised in An Essay on the Foundations of Geometry a variation of Kant’s transcendental aesthetics claiming that the curvature of the space of our perception, i.e. of any ‘’form of externality’’, is a priori constant.\\r\\n\\r\\nExposure to the work of the German mathematicians Dedekind, Weierstraß, and Cantor along with a personal meeting with Peano caused a turn in Russell’s views. He now hoped to find a rigorous foundation of mathematics based solely on logical axioms, thereby justifying a kind of Platonic view on mathematics. But over the years he was frustrated in this attempt by many problems he encountered, especially Russell's paradox. He gradually gave up all his Platonic beliefs; arriving in the end (after Wittgenstein's Tractatus) at formalism.\\r\\n\\r\\nHe remarks on the power of rigorous mathematical definition:\\r\\n\\r\\n“Continuity” had been, until he [Cantor] defined it, a vague word, convenient for philosophers like Hegel, who wished to introduce metaphysical muddles into mathematics. Cantor gave a precise significance to the word, and showed that continuity, as he defined it, was the concept needed by mathematicians and physicist. By this means a great deal of mysticism, such as that of Bergson, was rendered antiquated. (Chapter XXXI of “A History of Western Philosophy” (1945))\\r\\n\\r\\n3. Brouwer\\r\\nL.E.J. Brouwer had a long standing interest in the theory and practice of mysticism, setting out his manifesto while still a graduate student in the essay Life, Art, and Mysticism (1905). The essay quotes the Bhagavad Gita, Meister Eckhart, and Jakob Böhme.\\r\\n\\r\\nHowever, he did not consider his intuitionism to depend upon his mystical views as such. For Brouwer, mysticism is the domain of “consciousness’ deepest home”, wherein there is no subject-object distinction. The first act of intuitionism, the intuition of time, propels us away from this pure state of “wisdom”. It is in fact the precondition for any experience of an outer world or experience of the self as something distinct. Mathematics thus comes into being in this exodus from the home of consciousness, so on Brouwer’s view, “mathematics is in a sense the very opposite of mysticism” (Van Atten, 2004), and mystical insight is only possible quite apart from the machinations of the intellect.\\r\\n\\r\\nBrouwer even went so far as to remark on the perniciousness of mathematics in its keeping us from the home of consciousness. Thus in the notebooks in which he conceived his 1907 thesis we find: “One could see as the goal of one’s life: abolition and delivery from all mathematics”.\\r\\n\\r\\n4. Gödel\\r\\nFor the moment, see e.g. van Atten and Tragesser 2014, and Gödel’s ontological proof involving modal logic.\\r\\n\\r\\n5.             "[L1] {\n[L2]   \"content\": \"#Contents#\\r\\n* table of contents\\r\\n{:toc}\\r\\n\\r\\n\\r\\n## Idea\\r\\n\\r\\nThis page is used as a hub to gather references about [[category theory|category-theoretic]] work (and more widely, other mathematical foundational work) with explicit applications to biology. \\r\\n\\r\\n\\r\\n_Biology_ can be seen as an umbrella term for a spectrum of scientific domains all interested in studying life, at various [scales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biological_organisation). A range of category-theoretic formalisms have now been proposed to model these scales, from [DNA mechanisms](https://www.cdc.gov/genomics/about/basics.htm) to [complex systems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complex_system) through [protein interactions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protein%E2%80%93protein_interaction). More works with potential applications to topics somewhat related to biological questions are referred at the end of the page.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Categories\\r\\n\\r\\nThis section presents category theoretic models using categories as ways to describe biological mechanisms and relations.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Ologs\\r\\n\\r\\n[[ontology|Ontologies]] are used in [genomics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genomics) to classify categories of observable phenomena such as [diseases](https://www.ebi.ac.uk/ols/ontologies/doid) or [gene expressions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gene_Ontology). Ontologies can be formalized with category theory as [[ontology log|ontology logs]], or \\\"ologs\\\" for short. The idea is that an olog is like a [[diagram]] where each arrow describes an aspect of some types of things under study. For example, the following olog describes [single-gene genetic disorders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genetic_disorder):\\r\\n\\r\\n\\\\begin{centre}\\r\\n    \\\\begin{xymatrix@C=10em}\\r\\n        \\\\fbox{$\\\\textrm{a (monogenic) genetic disorder}$} \\\\ar[r]^-{\\\\textrm{is provoked by mutations in}} & \\\\fbox{$\\\\textrm{a gene}$} \\\\ar[r]^-{\\\\textrm{is found in}} & \\\\fbox{$\\\\textrm{a chromosome}$}\\r\\n    \\\\end{xymatrix}\\r\\n\\\\end{centre}\\r\\n\\r\\n\\r\\nOlogs have been used to characterize hierarchies in biology.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Segments {#CategoryOfSegments}\\r\\n\\r\\nCategories of segments aim to model the set of natural and experimental operations that can be done on [DNA segments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DNA). The definition of their arrows is simple but flexible enough to express a wide range of biological mechanisms occurring in [genetics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genetics) and related fields. \\r\\n\\r\\nFor every non-negative integer $n$, we will denote the set $\\\\{1,2,\\\\dots,n\\\\}$ as $[n]$. Note that $[0] = \\\\emptyset$.\\r\\n\\r\\n+-- {: .num_defn}\\r\\n###### Definition\\r\\nFor every preorder $(\\\\Omega,\\\\preceq)$, we define a _segment on $\\\\Omega$_ as a tuple $(n_0,n_1,t,c)$ where $n_0$ and $n_1$ are non-negative integers, $t:[n_1] \\\\to [n_0]$ is an order-preserving surjection and $c:[n_0] \\\\to \\\\Omega$ is a function.\\r\\n=--\\r\\n\\r\\nIf we take the preorder $\\\\mathbf{2} = \\\\{ 0\\\\leq 1\\\\}$, then the following diagram represents a segment $(14,5,c,t)$ in $\\\\mathbf{2}$; the brackets represent the fibers of the order-preserving surjection $t$ while the corresponding colors represent the mappings of the function $c$, which lands in the set $\\\\mathbf{2}$.\\r\\n\\r\\n\\\\begin{centre}\\r\\n    \\\\begin{xymatrix@C=-5pt}\\r\\n       (\\\\bullet&\\\\bullet&\\\\bullet)&(\\\\circ&\\\\circ)&(\\\\bullet&\\\\bullet&\\\\bullet&\\\\bullet)&(\\\\circ&\\\\circ)&(\\\\bullet&\\\\bullet&\\\\bullet)\\r\\n    \\\\end{xymatrix}\\r\\n\\\\end{centre}\\r\\n\\r\\n\\r\\n+-- {: .num_defn}\\r\\n###### Definition\\r\\nFor every preorder $(\\\\Omega,\\\\preceq)$, we define a _morphism of segments_ from segment $(n_0,n_1,t,c)$ on $\\\\Omega$ to a segment $(n_0',n_1',t',c')$ on $\\\\Omega$ as a pair $(f_1,f_0)$ where $f_1:[n_1] \\\\to [n_1']$ is an order-preserving injection and $f_0:[n_0] \\\\to [n_0']$ is an order-preserving function such that the relation $c'(f_0(i)) \\\\preceq c(i)$ holds in $(\\\\Omega,\\\\preceq)$ for every $i \\\\in [n_0]$.\\r\\n=--\\r\\n\\r\\nWe define the _category of segments over a preorder $(\\\\Omega,\\\\preceq)$_ as the category $\\\\mathbf{Seg}(\\\\Omega)$ whose objects are segments over $\\\\Omega$ and whose arrows are the morphisms of segments between them. \\r\\n\\r\\nWe can show that if the preorder $(\\\\Omega,\\\\preceq)$ defines a [[lattice]], then the category $\\\\mathbf{Seg}(\\\\Omega)$ can be equipped with a [[site]] structure.\\r\\n\\r\\n### References\\r\\n\\r\\nOlogs and biology:\\r\\n\\r\\n* JY Wong, J McDonald, M Taylor-Pinney, [[David Spivak|DI Spivak]], KaplanDL , MJ Buehler, _Materials by Design: Merging Proteins and Music_, Nano Today. 2012 Dec 1;7(6):488-495,  [link](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3752788/)\\r\\n* T. Giesa, [[David Spivak|DI Spivak]], MJ. Buehler, _Reoccurring patterns in hierarchical protein materials and music: The power of analogies_, [pdf](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1111.5297.pdf)\\r\\n\\r\\nIntroductory material for categories of segments:\\r\\n\\r\\n* A [talk](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=l2PB9by6IBc) by [[Kenny Courser|K Courser]]. \\r\\n\\r\\n* [[Remy Tuyeras|R Tuyeras]], _Category Theory for Genetics_,  [arXiv:1708.05255](https://arxiv.org/abs/1708.05255)\\r\\n\\r\\n## Theories and models\\r\\n\\r\\nThis section presents category theoretic models taking the form of diagrams. These models can be either presented as functors with properties or as commutative diagrams. Common examples are models for a [[limit sketch]]. The first attempt to formalize biological systems in terms of diagrams (with limits) was initiated by Robert Rosen (see the references at the end of the page). However, Rosen's work stays quite abstract and does not treat of any specific biological phenomenon.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Stock-flow diagrams and Petri nets\\r\\n\\r\\nIn the spirit of [[David Spivak|Spivak's]] approach in encoding databases as functors over small categories, functors have been used to organize (and hence model) biological data. One example is that of stock-flow diagrams, which are defined as follows.\\r\\n\\r\\nLet us denote as $\\\\mathsf{H}$ the free category generated over the following graph:\\r\\n\\r\\n\\\\begin{centre}\\r\\n    \\\\begin{xymatrix}\\r\\n        \\\\textrm{flow} \\\\ar@<+1.2ex>[rr]^{u} \\\\ar@<-1.2ex>[rr]_{d} && \\\\textrm{stock}\\\\\\\\\\r\\n        &\\\\textrm{link}\\\\ar[ru]_{s} \\\\ar[lu]^{t} &\\r\\n    \\\\end{xymatrix}\\r\\n\\\\end{centre}\\r\\n\\r\\nThe previous diagram should be seen as a sketch specifying a structure in which there are _links_ that go from a _stock_ to a _flow_ such that each _flow_ goes from a _stock_ to another _stock_.\\r\\n\\r\\n+-- {: .num_defn}\\r\\n###### Definition\\r\\nWe define a _primitive stock-flow diagram_ as a functor $\\\\mathsf{H} \\\\to \\\\mathbf{FinSet}$ where $\\\\mathbf{FinSet}$ is the category of finite sets and functions.\\r\\n=--\\r\\n\\r\\n+-- {: .num_defn}\\r\\n###### Definition\\r\\nA _stock-flow diagram_ consists of primitive stock-flow diagram $F:\\\\mathsf{H} \\\\to \\\\mathbf{FinSet}$ and, for every element $x \\\\in F(\\\\mathrm{flow})$, a continuous function $\\\\mathbb{R}^{U_x} \\\\to \\\\mathbb{R}$ where $U_x$ denotes the finite fiber $F(t)^{-1}(x)$.\\r\\n=--\\r\\n\\r\\nThere is a notion of _open_ stock-flow diagram that can be composed by using the composition of cospans. Stock-flow diagrams have been used to model [epidemics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_epidemics) and more specifically [COVID-19](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19).\\r\\n\\r\\n### Pedigrads\\r\\n\\r\\nA [[pedigrad]] is a model for a limit sketch defined on a [category of segments](#CategoryOfSegments). The functors defining pedigrads can land in any types of categories. These functors have been used to model [genomic data](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genomics) and design algorithms to study them.\\r\\n\\r\\n### References\\r\\n\\r\\nStock-flow diagrams and petri nets:\\r\\n\\r\\n* [[John Baez|JC Baez]], X Li, S Libkind, N Osgood and E Patterson, _Compositional modeling with stock and flow diagrams_, [arXiv:2205.08373](https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.08373)\\r\\n\\r\\n* A Baas, J Fairbanks, M Halter, S Libkind and E Patterson, _An algebraic framework for structured epidemic modeling_, [arXiv:2203.16345](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.16345)\\r\\n\\r\\n* [[John Baez|JC Baez]], BS Pollard, _A Compositional Framework for Reaction Networks_, [arXiv:1704.02051](https://arxiv.org/abs/1704.02051)\\r\\n\\r\\nPedigrads:\\r\\n\\r\\n* [[Remy Tuyeras|R Tuyeras]], _Category theory for genetics I: mutations and sequence alignments_, Theory and Applications of Categories, Vol. 33, 2018, No. 40, pp 1269-1317, [link](http://www.tac.mta.ca/tac/volumes/33/40/33-40abs.html)\\r\\n\\r\\n* [[Remy Tuyeras|R Tuyeras]], _Category theory for genetics II: genotype, phenotype and haplotype_, [arXiv:1805.07004](https://arxiv.org/abs/1805.07004)\\r\\n\\r\\n* [[Remy Tuyeras|R Tuyeras]], _A category theoretical argument for causal inference_, [arXiv:2004.09999](https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.09999)\\r\\n\\r\\n\\r\\n## Adjunctions\\r\\n\\r\\n[[adjunction|Adjunctions]] have been used to model [pathogens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pathogen) and [disease diagnoses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disease), and their corresponding [immune response](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Immune_response). For example, denote as $I$ the set of immune responses and as $P$ the set pathogens and [disease symptoms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Signs_and_symptoms). In practice, we can map a subset of $P$ to a subset of $I$. This defines a binary relation as follows.\\r\\n$$\\r\\nQ \\\\subseteq \\\\mathsf{Sub}(P) \\\\times \\\\mathsf{Sub}(I)\\r\\n$$\\r\\nWe can complete this binary [[relation]] into a functor of the following form.\\r\\n$$\\r\\nQ: \\\\mathsf{Sub}(P)^{\\\\mathsf{op}} \\\\times \\\\mathsf{Sub}(I) \\\\to \\\\mathbf{2} = \\\\{0 \\\\leq 1\\\\}.\\r\\n$$\\r\\nWe can then define a [[functor]] $F:\\\\mathsf{Sub}(I) \\\\to \\\\mathsf{Sub}(P)$ with the following specification.\\r\\n$$\\r\\nF(i) = \\\\bigcup\\\\{p| Q(p,i) = 1\\\\}\\r\\n$$\\r\\nIf the binary relation $Q$ is defined such that $F$ preserves [[meet|meets]] (ie. intersections), then we can use the [[adjoint functor theorem]] to define a left-adjoint $L:\\\\mathsf{Sub}(P) \\\\to \\\\mathsf{Sub}(I)$ for the functor $F$.\\r\\n$$\\r\\nL(p) = \\\\bigcap\\\\{i|p \\\\subseteq F(i)\\\\}\\r\\n$$\\r\\nThe previous adjunction gives us a context in which we can reason about immune responses and their triggering pathogens and diseases. Further, the adjunction formalism ensures a certain _continuity_ in time and space regarding the linking of diseases/pathogens to their immune response (as suggested in the following correspondence).\\r\\n\\r\\n\\r\\n\\\\begin{centre}\\r\\n\\\\begin{xymatrix@R=-2pt[font = \\\\large]}\\r\\n&p \\\\subseteq F(i) & \\\\textrm{\\\\normalsize{if a disease $p$ describes conditions (reportedly) triggering $i$}}&\\\\\\\\\\r\\n\\\\ar@{-}[rrr]&&&\\\\\\\\ \\r\\n&L(p) \\\\subseteq LF(i) \\\\subseteq i & \\\\textrm{\\\\normalsize{then the (expected) immune response for $p$ is in $i$}}&   \\r\\n    \\\\end{xymatrix}\\r\\n\\\\end{centre}\\r\\n\\r\\n\\r\\nWe can embed the previous type of models in time and space by filtering the sets $P$ and $I$ into a sequence (or a category) of subsets containing chronological and spatial occurrences of diseases and their immune responses, respectively. In this case, the corresponding binary relations $Q \\\\subseteq \\\\mathsf{Sub}(P) \\\\times \\\\mathsf{Sub}(I)$ need to be defined for each time and space parameter in a functorial way.\\r\\n\\r\\n\\\\begin{centre}\\r\\n    \\\\begin{xymatrix}\\r\\n        \\\\mathsf{Sub}(P_1)\\\\ar[r]\\\\ar@{->}@<-1.2ex>[d]\\\\ar@{<-}@<+1.2ex>[d]&\\\\mathsf{Sub}(P_2)\\\\ar[r]\\\\ar@{->}@<-1.2ex>[d]\\\\ar@{<-}@<+1.2ex>[d]&\\\\dots\\\\ar[r]&\\\\mathsf{Sub}(P_n)\\\\ar[r]\\\\ar@{->}@<-1.2ex>[d]\\\\ar@{<-}@<+1.2ex>[d]&\\\\dots\\\\\\\\\\r\\n        \\\\mathsf{Sub}(I_1)\\\\ar[r]&\\\\mathsf{Sub}(I_2)\\\\ar[r]&\\\\dots\\\\ar[r]&\\\\mathsf{Sub}(I_n)\\\\ar[r]&\\\\dots\\\\\\\\\\r\\n    \\\\end{xymatrix}\\r\\n\\\\end{centre}\\r\\n\\r\\n### References\\r\\n\\r\\n* [[Gianfranco Mascari|J-F Mascari]], D Giacchero and N Sfakianakis, _Symetries and asymetries of the immune system response: A categorification approach_, 2017 IEEE International Conference on Bioinformatics and Biomedicine (BIBM), 2017, pp. 1451-1454, [pdf](http://www.mcs.st-and.ac.uk/~ns210/files/Masc-Sfak-Categor.pdf)\\r\\n\\r\\n## Operads and algebras\\r\\n\\r\\n### Trees\\r\\n\\r\\n[[operad|Operads]] have been used to model [phylogenetic trees](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phylogenetic_tree), see:\\r\\n\\r\\n* [Operads and Phylogenetic Trees](https://golem.ph.utexas.edu/category/2015/12/operads_and_phylogenetic_trees.html)\\r\\n\\r\\n### Axioms for algebras and gradient descent\\r\\n\\r\\nA [[little cubes operad|little-disc-operad-inspired]] formalism was developed to model biological systems and cellular behaviors. This formalism considers [gradient descent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gradient_descent) techniques to make certain subsets $A \\\\subseteq \\\\mathbb{R}^{\\\\times n}$ converge towards [[algebra over an operad|algebra-like structures]]. \\r\\n\\r\\nMore specifically, these gradient descent techniques use the underlying equations of the axioms for algebras as [objective functions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loss_function). The sets $A$ obtained through these optimizations can be interpreted as models for [specialization of biological functions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Specialization) and [[entropy|entropic]] mechanisms in living organisms.\\r\\n\\r\\n### References\\r\\n\\r\\nPhylogenies:\\r\\n\\r\\n* [[John Baez|JC Baez]], N Otter... Its contents are private/internal reference material unless separately cleared for public use. Source and evidence handling\\n\\nRaw source artifacts remain canonical. Indexes, summaries, extracted text, annotations, diagrams and comparison tables are derived aids.\\n\\nFor every substantive source used, retain as applicable:\\n\\n- stable source ID and exact repository/path or external URL;\\n- author, title, publication venue and date;\\n- source date separately from ingest/access date;\\n- page, section, figure, timestamp or other locator;\\n- source type (primary, scholarly secondary, technical exposition, popular account, fiction, fandom artefact, generated/index material);\\n- access and review state;\\n- extraction method and quality notes where relevant;\\n- short account of what the source actually contributes.\\n\\nDo not infer claim-level content from filenames, tags, search snippets or index placement. What is the geometric object?\\n2. What is its ambient space and dimension?\\n3. What is its intrinsic dimension?\\n4. How is it embedded, projected, sliced, intersected, fibered, connected or transformed?\\n5. What metric, topology, orientation, coordinates and boundary conditions are actually specified?\\n6. What are the permitted transformations and compositions?\\n7. What is a physical spatial dimension, a spacetime dimension, a configuration/parameter-space dimension, or a dimension internal to the mathematical structure?\\n8. What does the construction allow us to see that a lower-dimensional or flattened description conceals?\\n\\nUse diagrams early. Prefer a sequence of views, sections, projections, deformations and dimensional lifts over a wall of formal definitions. A diagram must be faithful to the specified object; mark schematic elements and unspecified geometry rather than inventing them.\\n\\nFor higher-dimensional category theory, explicitly visualize objects, one-dimensional morphisms, two-dimensional morphisms, three-dimensional morphisms and further-dimensional morphisms where the model permits. Explain source/target, composition, invertibility and coherence geometrically. Do not assume every model has identical strictness or composition rules.\\n\\n## 5. Cross-disciplinary opportunity capture\\n\\nEvery substantial mathematical source should be scanned for direct applications and possible natural extensions beyond pure mathematics. Purpose and research remit\\n\\nInvestigate higher-dimensional geometry and its mathematical, scientific, historical, cultural, and literary relatives, with particular attention to:\\n\\n- higher-dimensional category theory, morphisms, groupoids, homotopy theory and related geometry;\\n- the nineteenth-century fourth-dimensionality tradition and its later mathematical/physical descendants;\\n- organismal biology, physiology, evolution, development, morphogenesis, neuroscience, ecology, biophysics and systems biology;\\n- computer science, computation, information theory, networks, artificial intelligence and type theory;\\n- physics, chemistry, earth/planetary science and other natural sciences;\\n- spiritualist, occult, speculative-philosophical, science-fiction, popular-science and fannish treatments of the fourth and higher dimensions, including cultural expressions such as time-binding and \\u201cFans are Slans.\\u201d\\n\\nThe workshop adopts Nathan's stated interpretive premise that mathematical uses of \\u201chigher\\u201d should be read as \\u201chigher-dimensional,\\u201d with \\u201cdimensional\\u201d written out in our discussions. This is the workshop's interpretive lens. When a particular construction's dimensional character is unclear, describe the actual geometry and distinguish mathematical dimension from physical spatial dimension without dropping the dimensional reading.\\n\\nThe historical lineage from nineteenth-century higher-dimensional thought through spiritualist appropriation and later mathematical/physical usage is a working premise for interpretation. Read the literature accordingly; do not turn establishing that premise into a prerequisite. Preserve historical differences and identify where particular authors or constructions elaborate, transform, or depart from scientific concepts.\\n\\n## 2. Privacy and repository boundaries\\n\\n- HSH_RESOURCES is the primary supporting literature, research-tool and methods repository. Its contents are private/internal reference material unless separately cleared for public use. It is not, by itself, theory authority.\\n- HsH and SAT_THEORY_ARCHIVE_2023-25 may be used when project provenance, existing mathematical resources, or relevant source history genuinely improves the workshop. Do not automatically import unrelated project material.\\n- The user's private legal repository is **not a workshop source repository**. Do not search it, quote it, copy its contents, cite it, link it, or route workshop artifacts there. The user has indicated that selected Tocktick-protocol concepts may be useful as general workflow inspiration. Use only high-level operational abstractions already explicitly discussed with the user; do not inspect or expose the private repository.\\n- Never move private/internal source text into a public-facing artifact merely because its repository is accessible. Public publication requires a separate explicit decision and source-level review.\\n- Keep this workshop's identity, notes and working state distinct from unrelated SAT/H(s)H operations unless the user explicitly requests a connection.\\n\\n## 3. Source and evidence handling\\n\\nRaw source artifacts remain canonical. Indexes, summaries, extracted text, annotations, diagrams and comparison tables are derived aids.\\n\\nFor every substantive source used, retain as applicable:\\n\\n- stable source ID and exact repository/path or external URL;\\n- author, title, publication venue and date;\\n- source date separately from ingest/access date;\\n- page, section, figure, timestamp or other locator;\\n- source type (primary, scholarly secondary, technical exposition, popular account, fiction, fandom artefact, generated/index material);\\n- access and review state;\\n- extraction method and quality notes where relevant;\\n- short account of what the source actually contributes.\\n\\nDo not infer claim-level content from filenames, tags, search snippets or index placement. Follow wayfinding records to the source. Search/index silence is not evidence of absence. Distinguish source observation from interpretation, reconstruction, analogy and speculation.\\n\\n### Reading states\\n\\n- LOCATED: path or bibliographic record found.\\n- TRIAGED: abstract, contents or bounded excerpt assessed for relevance.\\n- PARTIAL: selected sections/pages read and cited.\\n- FULL: source read to the depth required for its intended use.\\n- EXTRACTED: text/figure/table extraction completed with provenance and quality noted. This is an access state, not a comprehension state.\\n- VISUALIZED: relevant geometric construction reconstructed as a diagram/model with conventions stated.\\n- TESTED: a computational, geometrical or empirical check has actually been run.\\n- SYNTHESIZED: contribution integrated into a source-backed workshop note.\\n\\nA source may have several orthogonal states. Never promote a snippet or machine-generated summary into a full reading.\\n\\n## 4. Geometric-first reading and visualization\\n\\nFor each important mathematical construction, answer:\\n\\n1. What is the geometric object?\\n2. What is its ambient space and dimension?\\n3. What is its intrinsic dimension?\\n4. How is it embedded, projected, sliced, intersected, fibered, connected or transformed?\\n5. What metric, topology, orientation, coordinates and boundary conditions are actually specified?\\n6. What are the permitted transformations and compositions?\\n7. What is a physical spatial dimension, a spacetime dimension, a configuration/parameter-space dimension, or a dimension internal to the mathematical structure?\\n8. What does the construction allow us to see that a lower-dimensional or flattened description conceals?\\n\\nUse diagrams early. Prefer a sequence of views, sections, projections, deformations and dimensional lifts over a wall of formal definitions. A diagram must be faithful to the specified object; mark schematic elements and unspecified geometry rather than inventing them.\\n\\nFor higher-dimensional category theory, explicitly visualize objects, one-dimensional morphisms, two-dimensional morphisms, three-dimensional morphisms and further-dimensional morphisms where the model permits. Explain source/target, composition, invertibility and coherence geometrically. Do not assume every model has identical strictness or composition rules.\\n\\n## 5. Cross-disciplinary opportunity capture\\n\\nEvery substantial mathematical source should be scanned for direct applications and possible natural extensions beyond pure mathematics. Use a broad search radius.\\n\\nCapture opportunities in one of three classes:\\n\\n- DIRECT_APPLICATION: source explicitly applies the construction to another field.\\n- NATURAL_EXTENSION: a plausible, structurally motivated extension to another field, with the mapping to be worked out.\\n- CULTURAL_TRANSMISSION: the concept appears in philosophical, spiritualist, literary, science-fiction, popular-science or fannish culture.\\n\\nFor each opportunity record:\\n- source construction and exact location;\\n- target discipline and candidate phenomenon;\\n- proposed geometric correspondence;\\n- what is shared and what differs;\\n- missing mechanism, assumptions or data;\\n- next discriminating reading, diagram, calculation or observation.\\n\\nDo not restrict discovery to keyword matches. Follow mathematical machinery across disciplines: for example, braids and configuration spaces toward molecular biology; geometric morphisms and transformations toward developmental or evolutionary pathways; topology toward neural and physiological networks; category-theoretic structures toward computation and information systems.\\n\\n## 6. Cultural and speculative literature protocol\\n\\nRead spiritualist, occult, speculative, fictional and fannish sources as legitimate historical/cultural evidence, not automatically as scientific evidence.\\n\\nFor each relevant item record:\\n- the original scientific or philosophical concept it invokes or may have adapted;\\n- the date and route of transmission where recoverable;\\n- how the concept changes in the new setting;\\n- whether the treatment is analogy, fictional device, metaphysical claim, reported phenomenon or technical proposal;\\n- points of contact with scientific concepts;\\n- unsupported or contradictory claims, identified specifically rather than by blanket dismissal.\\n\\nKeep three tracks visible:\\n1. scientific/mathematical content;\\n2. cultural transformation and reception;\\n3. speculative departure.\\n\\nFictional and fannish expressions may be evidence of an idea's reach, persistence or transformation, even when they are not evidence that the underlying scientific claim is true. Treat \\u201ctime-binding,\\u201d \\u201cFans are Slans,\\u201d and related expressions as cultural-historical leads; investigate their contexts and conceptual ancestry without assuming a single origin or meaning before source inspection.\\n\\n## 7. Research workflow: WAKE \\u2192 ROUTE \\u2192 READ \\u2192 GEOMETRIZE \\u2192 BRIDGE \\u2192 RECORD \\u2192 REVIEW\\n\\n### WAKE / CHECK\\nAt the start of a materially new session:\\n- identify the workshop's current scope and next cursor;\\n- check for relevant new user direction and durable workshop updates;\\n- inspect only the controlling guidance needed for the task;\\n- identify whether the task is historical, mathematical, geometric, cross-disciplinary, cultural, or operational.\\n\\nUse state-sensitive orientation. A new or stale session gets a fuller orientation; a warm session checks deltas and the current task rather than rereading everything ritualistically.\\n\\n### ROUTE\\nSelect the smallest useful route:\\n- nLab / n-Category Caf\\u00e9 for mathematical concepts and intellectual discussion;\\n- HSH_RESOURCES for supporting literature and historical collections;\\n- scholarly databases and primary sources for external verification;\\n- science-specific literature for cross-disciplinary follow-through;\\n- original fiction, fandom archives and historical documents for cultural transmission.\\n\\nBefore asking the user to repeat an available detail, search registered workshop materials and accessible repositories.\\n\\n### READ\\nLocate, triage, inspect and cite sources. Record what was actually read. Search results are discovery, not source comprehension.\\n\\n### GEOMETRIZE\\nTranslate the key construction into a visual/geometric account. Record dimensions, embeddings, maps, transformations, composition and limitations.\\n\\n### BRIDGE\\nActively seek:\\n- direct scientific applications;\\n- natural extensions to other sciences;\\n- historical/cultural transmission;\\n- useful counterexamples and constraints;\\n- neighboring mathematical tools that make the geometry more visible.\\n\\n### RECORD\\nLeave a durable bounded result with source pointers, reading states, geometric account, cross-disciplinary leads, unresolved questions and next cursor.\\n\\n### REVIEW\\nCheck whether the result answers the task, whether the geometry matches the source, whether claims are properly sourced, and whether the next step is still worth pursuing.\\n\\n## 8. Branching and work coordination\\n\\nUse a small number of clearly named work branches, not one undifferentiated reading queue:\\n\\n- MATH-GEOMETRY: category theory, topology, homotopy and dimensional visualization.\\n- HISTORY-CULTURE: Hinton, Victorian hyperspace, spiritualism, science fiction and fandom.\\n- BIO-SCIENCE: biology, physiology, evolution, development and related disciplines.\\n- COMPUTATION: computer science, information, networks, logic and AI.\\n- SCIENCE-BRIDGES: physics, chemistry, earth/planetary and other scientific applications.\\n- WORKSHOP-SYSTEMS: operating methods, tooling, indexes and continuity.\\n\\nBranches may run in parallel when tasks are genuinely separable. Keep a common source/terminology map, but preserve independent interpretations until each branch has recorded its own evidence. Do not mistake multiple workers reading the same summary or sharing the same prompt for independent confirmation.\\n\\nEach task quantum should have:\\n- one parent question/goal;\\n- one bounded operation;\\n- named source set or discovery bounds;\\n- expected output;\\n- a completion/exit condition;\\n- a next cursor.\\n\\nNested work must have a parent, depth limit, exit condition and orphan/fallback policy. A branch should close, merge or park when it stops generating useful evidence, constraints, clarification or capability.\\n\\n## 9. Tocktick-inspired temporal coordination\\n\\nUse the following general operational concepts as workshop conventions, without importing private legal material:\\n\\n- SEED: create a reusable question, diagram, source packet, tool, test or schema for downstream use.\\n- YIELD: deliberately release attention from a branch while others use the seed or evidence accumulates.\\n- AWAIT: resume when a defined evidence/state condition changes, rather than repeatedly checking an unchanged blocker.\\n- ACCUMULATE: collect outputs with their provenance and exposure metadata.\\n- RENDEZVOUS: return when a useful threshold is reached or a time cap expires.\\n- REJOIN: synthesize, audit, compare, improve the seed or launch the next bounded operation.\\n\\nPrefer state-based return thresholds with a time cap. Never let a parked branch disappear: retain its purpose, current state, return condition and displaced responsibility. Do not create recurring automations merely because a workflow could recur; use them only when the user asks or an existing authorized recurrence is explicitly assigned.\\n\\n## 10. Tools, scripts and derived infrastructure\\n\\nUse available connected tools, repository indexes, search tools, paper extractors, scripts and computational tools before improvising manual workarounds. Discover and read tool instructions before use.\\n\\nFor any script or repository operation:\\n- declare exact repositories and paths read/written;\\n- identify outputs as source, derived, generated, append-only or semantic;\\n- record run ID, source commit/ref, tool version and configuration;\\n- exclude private/quarantined material before reading or indexing where required;\\n- never overwrite raw sources during extraction or analysis;\\n- use fresh-base, non-force writes and compare-and-swap/current blob SHA for semantic edits;\\n- use per-run temporary paths and atomic finalization where possible;\\n- validate generated coverage and independently read back writes;\\n- never treat successful scheduling, execution or state restoration as proof that the requested artifact was delivered.\\n\\nPrefer existing scripts and adapters over duplicating functionality. Use dry-run before broad or destructive operations. Add a new parser only when an inventory reveals a recurring unmet need.\\n\\n## 11. Citation and provenance workflow\\n\\nUse the sequence:\\n\\nclaim / geometric statement \\u2192 citation need \\u2192 candidate sources \\u2192 inspect source \\u2192 exact page/section anchor \\u2192 verified citation \\u2192 place citation\\n\\nA bibliography identifies available sources; it does not establish that a source supports a particular claim.\\n\\nFor each important claim, capture:\\n- exact claim being supported;\\n- citation role (background, definition, application, empirical result, prior treatment, cultural context, constraint);\\n- source identity and page/section anchor;\\n- review state;\\n- short explanation of why it supports the claim.\\n\\nUse original external citations in public-facing writing. Internal repository paths and hashes are for recovery and audit, not substitutes for bibliographic citations. Do not cite a source for more than it actually says.\\n\\n## 12. Epistemic and interpretation conventions\\n\\nKeep separate:\\n- direct source statement;\\n- established mathematical/scientific result;\\n- Nathan's workshop premise or instruction;\\n- assistant's interpretation;\\n- reconstructed geometry;\\n- natural extension;\\n- speculative conjecture;\\n- fictional or cultural representation.\\n\\nThe workshop's agreed dimensional reading is an interpretive convention. Do not quietly reframe it as a claim that every author explicitly intended physical spatial dimensions. Instead, read the terminology through the agreed lens and examine the construction's actual dimensional content.\\n\\nFor spiritualist, occult and fictional material, skepticism applies to factual/scientific claims, not to its value as evidence of cultural transmission or conceptual reception.\\n\\nDo not use \\u201cproof\\u201d loosely. Name the actual status: source statement, definition, derivation, visualization, numerical check, empirical observation, proposed mechanism or speculation.\\n\\n## 13. Deliverable format\\n\\nA normal substantive reading note should contain:\\n\\n1. Question / why this source matters\\n2. Source and reading state\\n3. Geometric picture\\n4. Dimensional account\\n5. What the author actually contributes\\n6. Direct applications / natural extensions\\n7. Historical or cultural connections\\n8. Limitations, mismatches and open edges\\n9. Next bounded operation\\n\\nA workshop synthesis should connect several reading notes while retaining source-level references and differences among authors.\\n\\n## 14. Current initial work programme\\n\\nStart with these linked work packages:\\n\\n1. nLab visual atlas: reconstruct ordinary categories, 2-categories and higher-dimensional categories through points, paths, surfaces, volumes, transformations and composition; then move into higher-dimensional homotopy and groupoids.\\n2. Workshop tooling: create only the indexes, source cards, diagrams and small scripts that solve a demonstrated recurring retrieval or workflow problem.\\n\\n## 15. First implementation principle\\n\\nStart with durable workshop navigation, a compact source/idea ledger, and reusable reading-note templates. Do not build a large switchboard, database or automation before actual use demonstrates the need. Improve the system through bounded experiments, explicit failure notes and transfer to a second task.\\n\\n**Current next operation:** establish the workshop workspace and source/idea ledger, then begin the nLab visual atlas with the geometry of points, paths and homotopies.\\n\\n\\n## 16. Work-bite sizing and stopping rule\\n\\n**Standing instruction from Nathan, 2026-11-24:** take reasonable-sized bites. Avoid both tiny, low-value nibbles and oversized chunks likely to hang, sprawl, or end without a verified result.\\n\\nA normal work bite should produce one coherent result, not merely touch a large number of files or topics.\\n\\n### Bite-size test\\n\\nBefore starting, define:\\n\\n- **Question:** one central question or tightly related cluster.\\n- **Scope:** a bounded set of sources, concepts, or operations.\\n- **Output:** one useful artifact, explanation, diagram, comparison, or verified state change.\\n- **Exit condition:** what will count as a complete bite.\\n- **Next cursor:** the most valuable next operation, left explicit.\\n\\nPrefer a bite that can be completed, checked and recorded within one focused work session. As a practical default, use roughly 2\\u20135 primary sources or one substantial source plus its essential context, one main geometric construction, or one coherent workflow improvement. This is a heuristic, not a quota. A genuinely short source may be paired with a related source; a difficult source may need to be divided by chapter, construction or central result.\\n\\n### Avoid undersized bites\\n\\nDo not spend a full work session merely:\\n- locating one obvious source when the source can also be triaged;\\n- adding a single pointer without checking its target;\\n- repeating orientation or planning without advancing the work;\\n- reporting a problem without making the bounded repair that is already within scope.\\n\\nCombine adjacent micro-operations when they naturally form one result: locate \\u2192 inspect \\u2192 explain; define \\u2192 diagram \\u2192 check; edit \\u2192 read back \\u2192 record.\\n\\n### Avoid oversized bites\\n\\nDo not try to:\\n- survey an entire discipline in one pass;\\n- digest a very large archive or wiki as one undifferentiated task;\\n- build a large database, switchboard, scraper or automation before demonstrating the recurring need;\\n- pursue every branch surfaced by an interesting source in the same turn;\\n- make a long chain of dependent repository changes without intermediate validation.\\n\\nSplit such work into staged bites with clear dependencies and durable intermediate outputs. Each stage should be independently useful and resumable.\\n\\n### Chunking and execution safeguards\\n\\nFor large files, archives, or source collections:\\n1. inspect structure and metadata first;\\n2. select a bounded section or source family;\\n3. process it in chunks with stable source locators;\\n4. record completed coverage and remaining coverage;\\n5. verify the output before moving to the next chunk.\\n\\nFor code, searches, and repository writes, use bounded batches and inspect results between stages. Avoid large parallel bursts when they make failures hard to isolate or outputs likely to be truncated. Prefer several small, well-verified batches to one massive call.\\n\\n### Stop / split / continue decision\\n\\nAt each natural boundary, ask:\\n- Has the stated output been produced?\\n- Is it verified to the level required?\\n- Is the next operation a necessary part of this same result, or a separate branch?\\n- Is additional work still producing useful evidence, clarity, capability or a discriminating test?\\n\\nIf the bite is complete, stop and leave the next cursor. If the remaining operation is substantial but separable, split it. If progress has stalled, record why and choose a better route rather than enlarging the same bite.\\n\\n**The target is substantive completion at a manageable scale.** Do not optimize for the fewest turns; optimize for useful progress that survives, can be inspected, and can be resumed without reconstruction.\\n\\n\\n## 17. Basic adaptable session routine\\n\\nUse this as the default rhythm for workshop sessions. It is deliberately lightweight and should change in response to experience rather than become ritual.\\n\\n### A. Orient\\nBriefly recover:\\n- the workshop's purpose and interpretive conventions;\\n- the current branch and next cursor in the ledger;\\n- any new user direction or relevant change to the controlling protocol;\\n- the relevant source/tool routes for this particular bite.\\n\\nFor a continuing session, check only what has changed. Do not repeat full onboarding without a reason.\\n\\n### B. Choose one substantial bite\\nSelect one coherent question or construction. Define:\\n- why it matters;\\n- the bounded source/concept set;\\n- the expected deliverable;\\n- the exit condition.\\n\\nDefault to one main line of work per session. A closely related secondary lead may be captured, but should not displace completion of the main bite.\\n\\n### C. Work it through\\nUse the sequence appropriate to the task:\\n- locate and inspect the source;\\n- explain the idea in ordinary language;\\n- reconstruct or draw its geometry;\\n- identify its dimensional structure;\\n- follow one or two of its strongest scientific, biological, computational, historical or cultural connections;\\n- identify important qualifications and open edges.\\n\\nDo not force every stage when it does not apply. For a historical source, provenance and context may lead; for a mathematical construction, geometry may lead; for an application, the target science and model correspondence may lead.\\n\\n### D. Leave a durable result\\nProduce one useful result: a reading note, geometric plate, source comparison, cross-disciplinary map, small tested tool, or bounded protocol improvement. Update the ledger with the source state and next cursor.\\n\\n### E. Verify and close\\nCheck source locators, geometric fidelity, claims, and any repository write. State what was actually completed and what remains open. End with one clear next operation.\\n\\n### F. Periodic adaptation\\nAfter every three to five substantive bites, briefly review:\\n- which steps are helping and which are overhead;\\n- whether bite sizes are consistently too small or too large;\\n- which research branches are producing useful connections;\\n- which tools or templates deserve improvement;\\n- whether the current order of work still makes sense.\\n\\nChange the routine only when experience gives a concrete reason. Record meaningful changes in this protocol or ledger with date and rationale; do not preserve obsolete steps merely because they became customary.\\n\\n**Session completion standard:** one meaningful result, honest source/coverage status, a verified record where durable storage is used, and a next cursor.\\n\",\"sha\":\"e3b7e102bd71c68f5496585a0e29096181c8fcc5\",\"message\":\"Add adaptable workshop session routine\"}}"

Cross-disciplinary opportunity capture\\n\\nEvery substantial mathematical source should be scanned for direct applications and possible natural extensions beyond pure mathematics. Use a broad search radius.\\n\\nCapture opportunities in one of three classes:\\n\\n- DIRECT_APPLICATION: source explicitly applies the construction to another field.\\n- NATURAL_EXTENSION: a plausible, structurally motivated extension to another field, with the mapping to be worked out.\\n- CULTURAL_TRANSMISSION: the concept appears in philosophical, spiritualist, literary, science-fiction, popular-science or fannish culture.\\n\\nFor each opportunity record:\\n- source construction and exact location;\\n- target discipline and candidate phenomenon;\\n- proposed geometric correspondence;\\n- what is shared and what differs;\\n- missing mechanism, assumptions or data;\\n- next discriminating reading, diagram, calculation or observation.\\n\\nDo not restrict discovery to keyword matches. Follow mathematical machinery across disciplines: for example, braids and configuration spaces toward molecular biology; geometric morphisms and transformations toward developmental or evolutionary pathways; topology toward neural and physiological networks; category-theoretic structures toward computation and information systems.\\n\\n## 6. Cultural and speculative literature protocol\\n\\nRead spiritualist, occult, speculative, fictional and fannish sources as legitimate historical/cultural evidence, not automatically as scientific evidence.\\n\\nFor each relevant item record:\\n- the original scientific or philosophical concept it invokes or may have adapted;\\n- the date and route of transmission where recoverable;\\n- how the concept changes in the new setting;\\n- whether the treatment is analogy, fictional device, metaphysical claim, reported phenomenon or technical proposal;\\n- points of contact with scientific concepts;\\n- unsupported or contradictory claims, identified specifically rather than by blanket dismissal.\\n\\nKeep three tracks visible:\\n1. scientific/mathematical content;\\n2. cultural transformation and reception;\\n3. speculative departure.\\n\\nFictional and fannish expressions may be evidence of an idea's reach, persistence or transformation, even when they are not evidence that the underlying scientific claim is true. Treat “time-binding,” “Fans are Slans,” and related expressions as cultural-historical leads; investigate their contexts and conceptual ancestry without assuming a single origin or meaning before source inspection.\\n\\n## 7. Research workflow: WAKE → ROUTE → READ → GEOMETRIZE → BRIDGE → RECORD → REVIEW\\n\\n### WAKE / CHECK\\nAt the start of a materially new session:\\n- identify the workshop's current scope and next cursor;\\n- check for relevant new user direction and durable workshop updates;\\n- inspect only the controlling guidance needed for the task;\\n- identify whether the task is historical, mathematical, geometric, cross-disciplinary, cultural, or operational.\\n\\nUse state-sensitive orientation. A new or stale session gets a fuller orientation; a warm session checks deltas and the current task rather than rereading everything ritualistically.\\n\\n### ROUTE\\nSelect the smallest useful route:\\n- nLab / n-Category Café for mathematical concepts and intellectual discussion;\\n- HSH_RESOURCES for supporting literature and historical collections;\\n- scholarly databases and primary sources for external verification;\\n- science-specific literature for cross-disciplinary follow-through;\\n- original fiction, fandom archives and historical documents for cultural transmission.\\n\\nBefore asking the user to repeat an available detail, search registered workshop materials and accessible repositories.\\n\\n### READ\\nLocate, triage, inspect and cite sources. Record what was actually read. Search results are discovery, not source comprehension.\\n\\n### GEOMETRIZE\\nTranslate the key construction into a visual/geometric account. Record dimensions, embeddings, maps, transformations, composition and limitations.\\n\\n### BRIDGE\\nActively seek:\\n- direct scientific applications;\\n- natural extensions to other sciences;\\n- historical/cultural transmission;\\n- useful counterexamples and constraints;\\n- neighboring mathematical tools that make the geometry more visible.\\n\\n### RECORD\\nLeave a durable bounded result with source pointers, reading states, geometric account, cross-disciplinary leads, unresolved questions and next cursor.\\n\\n### REVIEW\\nCheck whether the result answers the task, whether the geometry matches the source, whether claims are properly sourced, and whether the next step is still worth pursuing.\\n\\n## 8. Branching and work coordination\\n\\nUse a small number of clearly named work branches, not one undifferentiated reading queue:\\n\\n- MATH-GEOMETRY: category theory, topology, homotopy and dimensional visualization.\\n- HISTORY-CULTURE: Hinton, Victorian hyperspace, spiritualism, science fiction and fandom.\\n- BIO-SCIENCE: biology, physiology, evolution, development and related disciplines.\\n- COMPUTATION: computer science, information, networks, logic and AI.\\n- SCIENCE-BRIDGES: physics, chemistry, earth/planetary and other scientific applications.\\n- WORKSHOP-SYSTEMS: operating methods, tooling, indexes and continuity.\\n\\nBranches may run in parallel when tasks are genuinely separable. Keep a common source/terminology map, but preserve independent interpretations until each branch has recorded its own evidence. Do not mistake multiple workers reading the same summary or sharing the same prompt for independent confirmation.\\n\\nEach task quantum should have:\\n- one parent question/goal;\\n- one bounded operation;\\n- named source set or discovery bounds;\\n- expected output;\\n- a completion/exit condition;\\n- a next cursor.\\n\\nNested work must have a parent, depth limit, exit condition and orphan/fallback policy. A branch should close, merge or park when it stops generating useful evidence, constraints, clarification or capability.\\n\\n## 9. Tocktick-inspired temporal coordination\\n\\nUse the following general operational concepts as workshop conventions, without importing private legal material:\\n\\n- SEED: create a reusable question, diagram, source packet, tool, test or schema for downstream use.\\n- YIELD: deliberately release attention from a branch while others use the seed or evidence accumulates.\\n- AWAIT: resume when a defined evidence/state condition changes, rather than repeatedly checking an unchanged blocker.\\n- ACCUMULATE: collect outputs with their provenance and exposure metadata.\\n- RENDEZVOUS: return when a useful threshold is reached or a time cap expires.\\n- REJOIN: synthesize, audit, compare, improve the seed or launch the next bounded operation.\\n\\nPrefer state-based return thresholds with a time cap. Never let a parked branch disappear: retain its purpose, current state, return condition and displaced responsibility. It provides an unusually rich first bridge for this workshop.\\n\\n| Mathematical construction / literature | Biological or computational target | Candidate geometric reading | State / next action |\\n|---|---|---|---|\\n| Ologs (ontology logs) | Genomic categories, observable phenomena, diseases and gene expression | Objects/types connected by typed relations; visualize as a directed network of assertions | LOCATED; retrieve source paper and draw example |\\n| Categories of DNA segments | Natural and experimental DNA operations | Ordered segments, fibers and maps between segment configurations; explicit combinatorial geometry | LOCATED; inspect Tuyeras references |\\n| Stock-flow diagrams and Petri nets | Epidemics, COVID-19, reaction networks | Compartments/stocks connected by directed flows; open systems composed by cospans | LOCATED; inspect Baez et al. papers and diagrams |\\n| Pedigrads | Genomic data and algorithms | Functorial representation over categories of segments; inspect what the construction's dimension actually is | LOCATED; retrieve Category Theory for Genetics papers |\\n| Adjunctions | Pathogen/disease sets and immune responses | Paired maps between structured families of subsets, with order/containment relations | LOCATED; reconstruct the diagram and conditions |\\n| Operads | Phylogenetic trees | Branching/compositional trees with permitted grafting/substitution operations | Citation located: Baez & Otter (2017); retrieve primary paper |\\n| Algebraic topology / persistent homology | Neuronal morphologies | Geometric shape and topological invariants across measurement scales | Primary citation located: Kanari et al. The first geometric task is to visualize a phylogenetic tree as a compositional object and show how operadic composition corresponds to joining/grafting tree structures. Do not reduce this to the bare fact that a tree is a graph; investigate the extra compositional structure.\\n\\n2. **Kanari et al., \\u201cQuantifying Topological Invariants of Neuronal Morphologies,\\u201d arXiv:1603.08432 (2016).** Direct geometry/topology-to-neuroscience bridge. Visualize neuronal branching geometry, scale, and the topological invariants being measured. Determine which invariants preserve biologically relevant shape information and which discard metric detail.\\n\\n3. **Category theory for genetics (Tuyeras).** The nLab collection identifies DNA segment categories and pedigrads for genome data, sequence alignment, mutations, genotype, phenotype and haplotype. This is an especially promising bridge among geometry, evolution, computation and biological organization.\\n\\n4. **Hyperstructures in biology (Baas).** The archived nLab text contrasts hyperstructures with n-categories, noting that biological processes may be organized as aggregates with bonds rather than simply as oriented globular arrows. This deserves a careful geometric comparison with higher-dimensional categories, not a quick dismissal as another abstract formalism.\\n\\n5. **Higher-dimensional category models of process calculi.** Stay and Meredith's work on higher-dimensional category models of the \\u03c0-calculus may bridge computation and biological process modeling. The core visualization question is what a higher-dimensional morphism represents between process histories, and what geometric dimension that object has in the model.\\n\\n### Caution about the archived nLab text\\n\\nThe archived file is a collected page/excerpt corpus, with mixed dates and page contexts. It contains historical captures and a mix of technical expositions and bibliographic leads. Treat the page as an index to the intellectual landscape, not as a peer-reviewed synthesis or confirmation that every described application is established or successful. Primary sources and exact pages are the next step.\\n\\n### Immediate next bounded operation\\n\\nRetrieve and inspect the primary Baez\\u2013Otter paper first. It says hyperstructures permit biological organization that is not necessarily oriented as globular arrows; instead, biological systems may organize through aggregates and bonds.\\n\\nIts illustrative sequence is:\\n\\n`cells \\u2192 selected group of liver cells \\u2192 liver \\u2192 organ systems \\u2192 body`.\\n\\nEach aggregate is a subset of lower-level agents together with a label/description that identifies the aggregate. The operation repeats at higher organizational levels, with compatibility conditions among the labels.\\n\\nThis is a particularly useful geometrical comparison for our project:\\n- higher-dimensional categories organize objects and transformations in dimensionally stratified, often globular forms;\\n- hyperstructures model iterated aggregation and bonding, potentially capturing organization that is not naturally represented as a simple directed sequence of globular cells.\\n\\nWe should visualize both and compare their incidence structures, not assume one is a synonym or replacement for the other. This may also connect to the user's earlier point about lower-dimensional structures being components of a higher-dimensional whole, though the exact mathematical relation must be specified.\\n\\n### Cross-disciplinary extension map\\n\\nThe nLab biology page is explicit evidence that category-theoretic methods already have direct applications across biology and computation. Its citations also point outward into:\\n- genetics and genomic algorithms;\\n- epidemic modeling and reaction networks;\\n- evolutionary phylogenetics;\\n- neuronal morphology;\\n- anatomical and molecular shape;\\n- biochemical process computation;\\n- systems biology and theories of organisms;\\n- cognitive/neural systems.\\n\\nThis is not yet evidence that all these applications use *higher-dimensional* categories in the same sense. We will inspect the actual constructions and apply the workshop dimensional reading consistently, noting the dimensions and geometric carriers used by each.\\n\\n### Important nLab entry points\\n\\n- Biology: `ncatlab/nlab-content/pages/4/8/3/2/2384/content.md`\\n- Higher structures contents: discover via the mirror's page index and links from the biology page.\\n- Category theory and biology discussion: n-Category Caf\\u00e9, November 2007.\\n- Operads and Phylogenetic Trees: Baez & Otter, TAC 32 (2017), 1397\\u20131453.\\n- Category Theory for Genetics I and II: R\\u00e9my Tuyeras (2018).\\n- Compositional Modeling with Stock and Flow Diagrams: Baez, Li, Libkind, Osgood and Patterson, arXiv:2205.08373.\\n- A Compositional Framework for Reaction Networks: Baez & Pollard, arXiv:1704.02051.\\n- Quantifying Topological Invariants of Neuronal Morphologies: Kanari et al., arXiv:1603.08432.\\n- Higher Category Models of the \\u03c0-Calculus: Stay & Meredith, arXiv:1504.04311.\\n- Memory Evolutive Systems: Hierarchy, Emergence, Cognition: Ehresmann & Vanbremeersch (2007).\\n\\n### Revised next operation\\n\\nBegin with the nLab biology page's own diagrams and explicit definitions before jumping to a single external paper. The key point is that links to other pages are placed in [[double brackets]].\\r\\n\\r\\nThere is no feature to preview your edits. Instead, submit them and then edit again. Two successive submissions with the same signature and made within 30 minutes of each other count as one.\\r\\n\\r\\nHow to start a new page\\r\\nTo create a new page on the \\r\\nn\\r\\nLab first make an existing page request a link to it, and then click on that requested link.\\r\\n\\r\\nIn detail:\\r\\n\\r\\nCreate a link request.\\r\\n\\r\\nIdentify any existing \\r\\nn\\r\\nLab page which should eventually refer to your new page.\\r\\n\\r\\n(At least one such page ought to exist, if your new page is related to anything, but if you just cannot think of any, use the Sandbox page).\\r\\n\\r\\nHit “edit” on that existing page.\\r\\n\\r\\nIn the resulting edit pane, add the string\\r\\n\\r\\n[[your new page name]]\\r\\n\\r\\nat some sensible point in the source code.\\r\\n\\r\\n(By default: in the “Related entries”-section.)\\r\\n\\r\\nHit “submit” below the edit pane.\\r\\n\\r\\nSee the existing page render again, now with your edit included. If your new page name did not exist yet as a page, you will see that string appear, in the existing entry, in gray with a clickable question mark behind it.\\r\\n\\r\\nSatisfy the link request.\\r\\n\\r\\nClick on that question mark to open the edit pane for the new page.\\r\\n\\r\\nEdit.\\r\\n\\r\\nOnce you hit “Submit” below that edit pane, the new page will appear.\\r\\n\\r\\nThere is no preview mechanism: Just keep cycling through “Submit” and “Edit” until you are satisfied.\\r\\n\\r\\nWatch out: the name of a page is case sensitive, so make your link lowercase if it comes at the beginning of a sentence. ([[like this|Like this]].) If you don’t, then your contribution will be credited to ‘Anonymous’ (formerly the AnonymousCoward).\\r\\n\\r\\nOnce you edit a page for the first time, your name will appear at the bottom, grayed out with a question mark since there is no page with your name yet. You may take this as an invitation to create a user page and tell us about yourself. But if you don’t want to or don’t have the time right now, you can forget about this. If you just want to show up on category: people, then you make a page containing only ‘category: people’ (or someone else may do this for you).\\r\\n\\r\\nTo create your user page, simply click the question mark that appears next to your name at the bottom of the page after making a modification and add content to the edit box that appears. If you’d like to make a user page prior to modifying an existing page, you can do so by making some trivial modification to the Sandbox, which will put your name at the bottom of the page where you can click the question mark.
