Changing page titles results in unnecessary work for the lab elves?, so you should try to follow these if possible (or dispute them if not). It is most important to follow these in links to pages that don't yet exist, so that the pages will be created at the correct title (and only once).\\r\\n\\r\\nPage titles should contain only ASCII characters.\\r\\n\\r\\nExamples: [[omega-category]] instead of [[$\\\\omega$-category]] or [[∞-category]].\\r\\nTricks: To produce ‘\\r\\nω\\r\\n-category’, try $\\\\omega$-[[omega-category|category]]. To produce ‘∞-category’, try [[omega-category|∞-category]]. (The former has proper math-mode formatting, while the latter has proper link scope.) Unfortunately, [[omega-category|$\\\\omega$-category]] does not work. You can also use redirects? to make [[∞-category]] produce ‘∞-category’, but only when the page already exists.\\r\\nReason: It’s possible to put non-ASCII characters in a name, but not ones generated by iTeX or &…; character entities, so this can be difficult, depending on your browser. To keep things easy, therefore, use only ASCII characters in links. This also helps with creating automatic redirects (which are found by removing accents on letters).\\r\\nException: We tend to use common European letters (such as ‘ö’, more or less the characters in Latin 1) in names, especially of people (such as Kurt Gödel), even though we’re not really supposed to.\\r\\nPage titles should be singular nouns.\\r\\n\\r\\nExamples: Use [[category]] instead of [[categories]], [[faithful functor]] instead of [[faithful]], and [[categorification]] instead of [[categorify]] or [[categorified]].\\r\\n\\r\\nTricks: To produce ‘categories’, try [[category|categories]]. To produce ‘faithful endofunctor’, try [[faithful functor|faithful]] [[endofunctor]] . Again, you can use redirects to make [[categories]] produce ‘categories’, if the page already exists.\\r\\n\\r\\nReason: We want only one page on a given concept, regardless of variations in grammar.\\r\\n\\r\\nException: Recently we have started to have page titles that are complete sentences (without capitalization or punctuation) that state a simple theorem (typically a universal affirmation in the Aristotelian sense) such as compact Hausdorff rings are profinite or derivations of smooth functions are vector fields.\\r\\n\\r\\nPage titles should be uncapitalized, except for words that are always capitalized.\\r\\n\\r\\nExamples: Use [[homotopy theory]] instead of [[Homotopy Theory]], but use [[Lie algebra]].\\r\\n\\r\\nTricks: To produce ‘Homotopy theory is important!’, try [[homotopy theory|Homotopy theory]] is important!. If you do this a lot, then you can again create a redirect, if the page exists.\\r\\n\\r\\nReason: We want only one page on a given concept, regardless of variations in grammar.\\r\\n\\r\\nExcept as contradicted above, use standard American English spelling conventions.\\r\\n\\r\\nExamples: Use [[center]] instead of [[centre]] and hyphens as shown in the ASCII-only requirement.\\r\\n\\r\\nTricks: To produce ‘centre’, try [[center|centre]]. Or, again, make a redirect.\\r\\n\\r\\nReason: Much of this is written by Urs Schreiber, who uses American English spelling (for the most part, at least).\\r\\n\\r\\nRegardless of the above, pages named after specific categories should use the capitalised singular abbreviated form.\\r\\n\\r\\nExamples: Use [[Set]] instead [[Sets]] and [[Cat]] instead of [[Category]].\\r\\n\\r\\nTricks: Although things like ‘\\r\\nDisc\\r\\n:\\r\\nSet\\r\\n→\\r\\nCat\\r\\n’ work best in math mode and even ‘\\r\\nSet\\r\\n’ alone looks most consistent that way (with proper math-mode formatting), you have to make the link ‘Set’ outside of math mode.\\r\\n\\r\\nHow to merge pages\\r\\nIt happens at times that you may wish the material in existing pages A and B, would be merged into a single page. (This occurs notably after any user accidentally created a new page unaware that another page on the topic was already in existence.)\\r\\n\\r\\nIn most cases it will be best to raise the issue on the nForum, check if regulars agree that the pages ought to be merged, and hope that one of them takes care of it.\\r\\n\\r\\nIf you do decide to merge on your own, here are instructions.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe basic idea is evident: Merge the content, delete one of the entries and make its previous name redirect to the remaining page. But the redirecting takes some care; and a complication is that \\r\\nn\\r\\nLab pages cannot be deleted (not by regular users, anyway) but only “orphaned”.\\r\\n\\r\\nSuppose that A is the name of the page to be kept and and that B is the name of the one to be deleted. Then:\\r\\n\\r\\nEdit A\\r\\n\\r\\nso that it looks like the intended merged entry.\\r\\n\\r\\nAdd the line “[[!redirects B]]” to the bottom.\\r\\n\\r\\nAnd in case the page B itself has [[!redirects X]]-lines in its source, copy them all over to A.\\r\\n\\r\\nSubmit.\\r\\n\\r\\nEdit B\\r\\n\\r\\nby first clearing its content (e.g. with a keystroke such as Ctrl-A Del).\\r\\n\\r\\nClick the checkbox ‘Change page name.’, which will bring up a new field ‘New name:’.\\r\\n\\r\\nIn that field, append “> history” to the string “B”, so that the new page name becomes “B > history”.\\r\\n\\r\\n(The idea is to change to any name that is neither coincides with an existing nor with a future entry.)\\r\\n\\r\\nDo not submit the edit yet.\\r\\n\\r\\nBefore finishing we need to work around what the wiki software thinks is intended behaviour:\\r\\n\\r\\nClick in the big edit box – this will automatically add the line “[[!redirects B]]”.\\r\\n\\r\\n(The wiki software is trying to be helpful, not knowing that we want to delete the entry for good.)\\r\\n\\r\\nDelete that line (to ensure that all requests for B will now take the reader to A),\\r\\n\\r\\nand instead add “see [[A]]”.\\r\\n\\r\\n(This just in case anyone ever comes across this page in the future – which should not actually happen, due to the [[!redirects B]]-command meanwhile added to A.)\\r\\n\\r\\nFinally ready to submit this quasi-deletion of B.\\r\\n\\r\\nBut since the page’s name was changed in the process, the software will require announcing this edit in the box below the edit box. So enter there something like:\\r\\n\\r\\n“As we discussed, I am orphaning this page and have merged its previous content into page \\\"A\\\".”\\r\\n\\r\\nSubmit.\\r\\n\\r\\nHow to remove a page\\r\\nPlease make a request at the nForum.\\r\\n\\r\\nHow to contribute to the nLab in ways other than writing articles?\\r\\nThere are numerous ways you can help out and get acquainted with the community even if you don’t (yet) feel comfortable writing math publicly on a wiki.\\r\\n\\r\\nYou can correct typos and spelling errors, fix links, create links, create redirects (there are many pages that still need redirects created for alternate and plural forms of the title), organize pages, and so on.\\r\\n\\r\\nYou can ask questions (see previous question), and join discussions, at the nForum, and comment at the nCafe.\\r\\n\\r\\nYou can try writing small additions to existing pages, for instance a paragraph or two that helps explain something that puzzled you initially. If you aren’t entirely positive that what you wrote was correct, when you announce your edit at Latest Changes on the nForum, you can mention that you’re unsure and someone will usually reassure you or give a correction.\\r\\n\\r\\nHow do I cite a page on the nLab?\\r\\nYou should, of course, include a link or URL to the page or pages that you wish to cite. You should also give the information about which version of the page you are citing, since pages change over time. The version number can be found as follows: look at the bottom of the page where it says “Back in time (\\r\\nN\\r\\n revisions)”; the current version number is \\r\\nN\\r\\n+\\r\\n1\\r\\n.\\r\\n\\r\\nYou can link directly to the version you want to cite by using a url such as\\r\\n\\r\\nhttp://ncatlab.org/nlab/revision/PageName/VERSIONNUMBER\\r\\nWe recommend that if you only include one URL, it be of the form show/PageName which will point to whatever version of the page is current when it is accessed. This is because pages generally improve over time, and whoever is following your reference ought to be taken to the best, up-to-date version of the page. Anyone who cares about finding the exact version of the page that you cited can figure out how to find it in the history.\\r\\n\\r\\nOn the other hand, if you can give two URLs (this would be cumbersome in a printed paper, but is possible with links on a web page), then it may be helpful to give the appropriate revision link as well as the show one.\\r\\n\\r\\nAll nLab pages now include a “Cite” link at the bottom of the page which produces a BibTeX entry in accord with the suggestions above.\\r\\n\\r\\n2. How to organize and write content\\r\\nPage organization\\r\\nWe encourage authors to structure pages by sections and subsections as indicated in the\\r\\n\\r\\nTemplate page.\\r\\nEvery page starts out tiny and may not seem to need a structure by subsections. But it will grow and eventually the information it provides may be hard to recognize without some global structure guiding the reader’s attention. After all, the natural evolution of articles makes the \\r\\nn\\r\\nLab function more like an encyclopedia than a novel. Moreover, even with little material there in the beginning, a structure by subsections helps the collaborative process, as it makes it easer to decide for new authors where to add what.\\r\\n\\r\\nDefinition-, Theorem-, Proof environments\\r\\nYou should include actual mathematics in appropriate environments, as familiar from textbooks and research articles in mathematics.\\r\\n\\r\\nLaTeX-style syntax\\r\\nAs of mid-2018, one can use environments exactly as in LaTeX.\\r\\n\\r\\nFor example the code\\r\\n\\r\\n\\\\\\r\\nbegin\\r\\n{\\r\\ntheorem\\r\\n}\\r\\n\\\\\\r\\nlabel\\r\\n{\\r\\nSomeTheorem\\r\\n}\\r\\nSome theorem.\\r\\n\\\\\\r\\nend\\r\\n{\\r\\ntheorem\\r\\n}\\r\\nproduces:\\r\\n\\r\\nTheorem 2.1. Some theorem.\\r\\n\\r\\n\\r\\nThe available environments are listed below. Later, one can reference it as Theorem 2.1. Again, see the source of this page for how to produce this reference.\\r\\n\\r\\nAny character but closing brace is allowed in labels here (note that this is different from equation labels below).\\r\\n\\r\\nOld... Purpose and research remit\\n\\nInvestigate higher-dimensional geometry and its mathematical, scientific, historical, cultural, and literary relatives, with particular attention to:\\n\\n- higher-dimensional category theory, morphisms, groupoids, homotopy theory and related geometry;\\n- the nineteenth-century fourth-dimensionality tradition and its later mathematical/physical descendants;\\n- organismal biology, physiology, evolution, development, morphogenesis, neuroscience, ecology, biophysics and systems biology;\\n- computer science, computation, information theory, networks, artificial intelligence and type theory;\\n- physics, chemistry, earth/planetary science and other natural sciences;\\n- spiritualist, occult, speculative-philosophical, science-fiction, popular-science and fannish treatments of the fourth and higher dimensions, including cultural expressions such as time-binding and “Fans are Slans.”\\n\\nThe workshop adopts Nathan's stated interpretive premise that mathematical uses of “higher” should be read as “higher-dimensional,” with “dimensional” written out in our discussions. Preserve historical differences and identify where particular authors or constructions elaborate, transform, or depart from scientific concepts.\\n\\n## 2. Privacy and repository boundaries\\n\\n- HSH_RESOURCES is the primary supporting literature, research-tool and methods repository. Its contents are private/internal reference material unless separately cleared for public use. It is not, by itself, theory authority.\\n- HsH and SAT_THEORY_ARCHIVE_2023-25 may be used when project provenance, existing mathematical resources, or relevant source history genuinely improves the workshop. Do not automatically import unrelated project material.\\n- The user's private legal repository is **not a workshop source repository**. Use only high-level operational abstractions already explicitly discussed with the user; do not inspect or expose the private repository.\\n- Never move private/internal source text into a public-facing artifact merely because its repository is accessible. Public publication requires a separate explicit decision and source-level review.\\n- Keep this workshop's identity, notes and working state distinct from unrelated SAT/H(s)H operations unless the user explicitly requests a connection.\\n\\n## 3. Source and evidence handling\\n\\nRaw source artifacts remain canonical. Indexes, summaries, extracted text, annotations, diagrams and comparison tables are derived aids.\\n\\nFor every substantive source used, retain as applicable:\\n\\n- stable source ID and exact repository/path or external URL;\\n- author, title, publication venue and date;\\n- source date separately from ingest/access date;\\n- page, section, figure, timestamp or other locator;\\n- source type (primary, scholarly secondary, technical exposition, popular account, fiction, fandom artefact, generated/index material);\\n- access and review state;\\n- extraction method and quality notes where relevant;\\n- short account of what the source actually contributes.\\n\\nDo not infer claim-level content from filenames, tags, search snippets or index placement. Follow wayfinding records to the source. Search/index silence is not evidence of absence. Distinguish source observation from interpretation, reconstruction, analogy and speculation.\\n\\n### Reading states\\n\\n- LOCATED: path or bibliographic record found.\\n- TRIAGED: abstract, contents or bounded excerpt assessed for relevance.\\n- PARTIAL: selected sections/pages read and cited.\\n- FULL: source read to the depth required for its intended use.\\n- EXTRACTED: text/figure/table extraction completed with provenance and quality noted. This is an access state, not a comprehension state.\\n- VISUALIZED: relevant geometric construction reconstructed as a diagram/model with conventions stated.\\n- TESTED: a computational, geometrical or empirical check has actually been run.\\n- SYNTHESIZED: contribution integrated into a source-backed workshop note.\\n\\nA source may have several orthogonal states. Never promote a snippet or machine-generated summary into a full reading.\\n\\n## 4. Geometric-first reading and visualization\\n\\nFor each important mathematical construction, answer:\\n\\n1. What is the geometric object?\\n2. What is its ambient space and dimension?\\n3. What is its intrinsic dimension?\\n4. How is it embedded, projected, sliced, intersected, fibered, connected or transformed?\\n5. What metric, topology, orientation, coordinates and boundary conditions are actually specified?\\n6. What are the permitted transformations and compositions?\\n7. What is a physical spatial dimension, a spacetime dimension, a configuration/parameter-space dimension, or a dimension internal to the mathematical structure?\\n8. What does the construction allow us to see that a lower-dimensional or flattened description conceals?\\n\\nUse diagrams early. Prefer a sequence of views, sections, projections, deformations and dimensional lifts over a wall of formal definitions. A diagram must be faithful to the specified object; mark schematic elements and unspecified geometry rather than inventing them.\\n\\nFor higher-dimensional category theory, explicitly visualize objects, one-dimensional morphisms, two-dimensional morphisms, three-dimensional morphisms and further-dimensional morphisms where the model permits. Explain source/target, composition, invertibility and coherence geometrically. Do not assume every model has identical strictness or composition rules.\\n\\n## 5. Cross-disciplinary opportunity capture\\n\\nEvery substantial mathematical source should be scanned for direct applications and possible natural extensions beyond pure mathematics. Use a broad search radius.\\n\\nCapture opportunities in one of three classes:\\n\\n- DIRECT_APPLICATION: source explicitly applies the construction to another field.\\n- NATURAL_EXTENSION: a plausible, structurally motivated extension to another field, with the mapping to be worked out.\\n- CULTURAL_TRANSMISSION: the concept appears in philosophical, spiritualist, literary, science-fiction, popular-science or fannish culture.\\n\\nFor each opportunity record:\\n- source construction and exact location;\\n- target discipline and candidate phenomenon;\\n- proposed geometric correspondence;\\n- what is shared and what differs;\\n- missing mechanism, assumptions or data;\\n- next discriminating reading, diagram, calculation or observation.\\n\\nDo not restrict discovery to keyword matches. Follow mathematical machinery across disciplines: for example, braids and configuration spaces toward molecular biology; geometric morphisms and transformations toward developmental or evolutionary pathways; topology toward neural and physiological networks; category-theoretic structures toward computation and information systems.\\n\\n## 6. Cultural and speculative literature protocol\\n\\nRead spiritualist, occult, speculative, fictional and fannish sources as legitimate historical/cultural evidence, not automatically as scientific evidence.\\n\\nFor each relevant item record:\\n- the original scientific or philosophical concept it invokes or may have adapted;\\n- the date and route of transmission where recoverable;\\n- how the concept changes in the new setting;\\n- whether the treatment is analogy, fictional device, metaphysical claim, reported phenomenon or technical proposal;\\n- points of contact with scientific concepts;\\n- unsupported or contradictory claims, identified specifically rather than by blanket dismissal.\\n\\nKeep three tracks visible:\\n1. scientific/mathematical content;\\n2. cultural transformation and reception;\\n3. speculative departure.\\n\\nFictional and fannish expressions may be evidence of an idea's reach, persistence or transformation, even when they are not evidence that the underlying scientific claim is true. Treat “time-binding,” “Fans are Slans,” and related expressions as cultural-historical leads; investigate their contexts and conceptual ancestry without assuming a single origin or meaning before source inspection.\\n\\n## 7. Record what was actually read. Search results are discovery, not source comprehension.\\n\\n### GEOMETRIZE\\nTranslate the key construction into a visual/geometric account. Record dimensions, embeddings, maps, transformations, composition and limitations.\\n\\n### BRIDGE\\nActively seek:\\n- direct scientific applications;\\n- natural extensions to other sciences;\\n- historical/cultural transmission;\\n- useful counterexamples and constraints;\\n- neighboring mathematical tools that make the geometry more visible.\\n\\n### RECORD\\nLeave a durable bounded result with source pointers, reading states, geometric account, cross-disciplinary leads, unresolved questions and next cursor.\\n\\n### REVIEW\\nCheck whether the result answers the task, whether the geometry matches the source, whether claims are properly sourced, and whether the next step is still worth pursuing.\\n\\n## 8. How is it embedded, projected, sliced, intersected, fibered, connected or transformed?\\n5. What metric, topology, orientation, coordinates and boundary conditions are actually specified?\\n6. What are the permitted transformations and compositions?\\n7. What is a physical spatial dimension, a spacetime dimension, a configuration/parameter-space dimension, or a dimension internal to the mathematical structure?\\n8. What does the construction allow us to see that a lower-dimensional or flattened description conceals?\\n\\nUse diagrams early. Cross-disciplinary opportunity capture\\n\\nEvery substantial mathematical source should be scanned for direct applications and possible natural extensions beyond pure mathematics. Use a broad search radius.\\n\\nCapture opportunities in one of three classes:\\n\\n- DIRECT_APPLICATION: source explicitly applies the construction to another field.\\n- NATURAL_EXTENSION: a plausible, structurally motivated extension to another field, with the mapping to be worked out.\\n- CULTURAL_TRANSMISSION: the concept appears in philosophical, spiritualist, literary, science-fiction, popular-science or fannish culture.\\n\\nFor each opportunity record:\\n- source construction and exact location;\\n- target discipline and candidate phenomenon;\\n- proposed geometric correspondence;\\n- what is shared and what differs;\\n- missing mechanism, assumptions or data;\\n- next discriminating reading, diagram, calculation or observation.\\n\\nDo not restrict discovery to keyword matches. Cultural and speculative literature protocol\\n\\nRead spiritualist, occult, speculative, fictional and fannish sources as legitimate historical/cultural evidence, not automatically as scientific evidence.\\n\\nFor each relevant item record:\\n- the original scientific or philosophical concept it invokes or may have adapted;\\n- the date and route of transmission where recoverable;\\n- how the concept changes in the new setting;\\n- whether the treatment is analogy, fictional device, metaphysical claim, reported phenomenon or technical proposal;\\n- points of contact with scientific concepts;\\n- unsupported or contradictory claims, identified specifically rather than by blanket dismissal.\\n\\nKeep three tracks visible:\\n1. scientific/mathematical content;\\n2. cultural transformation and reception;\\n3. speculative departure.\\n\\nFictional and fannish expressions may be evidence of an idea's reach, persistence or transformation, even when they are not evidence that the underlying scientific claim is true. Record what was actually read. Search results are discovery, not source comprehension.\\n\\n### GEOMETRIZE\\nTranslate the key construction into a visual/geometric account. Record dimensions, embeddings, maps, transformations, composition and limitations.\\n\\n### BRIDGE\\nActively seek:\\n- direct scientific applications;\\n- natural extensions to other sciences;\\n- historical/cultural transmission;\\n- useful counterexamples and constraints;\\n- neighboring mathematical tools that make the geometry more visible.\\n\\n### RECORD\\nLeave a durable bounded result with source pointers, reading states, geometric account, cross-disciplinary leads, unresolved questions and next cursor.\\n\\n### REVIEW\\nCheck whether the result answers the task, whether the geometry matches the source, whether claims are properly sourced, and whether the next step is still worth pursuing.\\n\\n## 8. Branching and work coordination\\n\\nUse a small number of clearly named work branches, not one undifferentiated reading queue:\\n\\n- MATH-GEOMETRY: category theory, topology, homotopy and dimensional visualization.\\n- HISTORY-CULTURE: Hinton, Victorian hyperspace, spiritualism, science fiction and fandom.\\n- BIO-SCIENCE: biology, physiology, evolution, development and related disciplines.\\n- COMPUTATION: computer science, information, networks, logic and AI.\\n- SCIENCE-BRIDGES: physics, chemistry, earth/planetary and other scientific applications.\\n- WORKSHOP-SYSTEMS: operating methods, tooling, indexes and continuity.\\n\\nBranches may run in parallel when tasks are genuinely separable. Never let a parked branch disappear: retain its purpose, current state, return condition and displaced responsibility. Do not create recurring automations merely because a workflow could recur; use them only when the user asks or an existing authorized recurrence is explicitly assigned.\\n\\n## 10. Tools, scripts and derived infrastructure\\n\\nUse available connected tools, repository indexes, search tools, paper extractors, scripts and computational tools before improvising manual workarounds. Discover and read tool instructions before use.\\n\\nFor any script or repository operation:\\n- declare exact repositories and paths read/written;\\n- identify outputs as source, derived, generated, append-only or semantic;\\n- record run ID, source commit/ref, tool version and configuration;\\n- exclude private/quarantined material before reading or indexing where required;\\n- never overwrite raw sources during extraction or analysis;\\n- use fresh-base, non-force writes and compare-and-swap/current blob SHA for semantic edits;\\n- use per-run temporary paths and atomic finalization where possible;\\n- validate generated coverage and independently read back writes;\\n- never treat successful scheduling, execution or state restoration as proof that the requested artifact was delivered.\\n\\nPrefer existing scripts and adapters over duplicating functionality. Use dry-run before broad or destructive operations. Add a new parser only when an inventory reveals a recurring unmet need.\\n\\n## 11. Citation and provenance workflow\\n\\nUse the sequence:\\n\\nclaim / geometric statement \\u2192 citation need \\u2192 candidate sources \\u2192 inspect source \\u2192 exact page/section anchor \\u2192 verified citation \\u2192 place citation\\n\\nA bibliography identifies available sources; it does not establish that a source supports a particular claim.\\n\\nFor each important claim, capture:\\n- exact claim being supported;\\n- citation role (background, definition, application, empirical result, prior treatment, cultural context, constraint);\\n- source identity and page/section anchor;\\n- review state;\\n- short explanation of why it supports the claim.\\n\\nUse original external citations in public-facing writing. Internal repository paths and hashes are for recovery and audit, not substitutes for bibliographic citations. Do not cite a source for more than it actually says.\\n\\n## 12. Epistemic and interpretation conventions\\n\\nKeep separate:\\n- direct source statement;\\n- established mathematical/scientific result;\\n- Nathan's workshop premise or instruction;\\n- assistant's interpretation;\\n- reconstructed geometry;\\n- natural extension;\\n- speculative conjecture;\\n- fictional or cultural representation.\\n\\nThe workshop's agreed dimensional reading is an interpretive convention. Do not quietly reframe it as a claim that every author explicitly intended physical spatial dimensions. Instead, read the terminology through the agreed lens and examine the construction's actual dimensional content.\\n\\nFor spiritualist, occult and fictional material, skepticism applies to factual/scientific claims, not to its value as evidence of cultural transmission or conceptual reception.\\n\\nDo not use \\u201cproof\\u201d loosely. Name the actual status: source statement, definition, derivation, visualization, numerical check, empirical observation, proposed mechanism or speculation.\\n\\n## 13. Work-bite sizing and stopping rule\\n\\n**Standing instruction from Nathan, 2026-11-24:** take reasonable-sized bites. Avoid both tiny, low-value nibbles and oversized chunks likely to hang, sprawl, or end without a verified result.\\n\\nA normal work bite should produce one coherent result, not merely touch a large number of files or topics.\\n\\n### Bite-size test\\n\\nBefore starting, define:\\n\\n- **Question:** one central question or tightly related cluster.\\n- **Scope:** a bounded set of sources, concepts, or operations.\\n- **Output:** one useful artifact, explanation, diagram, comparison, or verified state change.\\n- **Exit condition:** what will count as a complete bite.\\n- **Next cursor:** the most valuable next operation, left explicit.\\n\\nPrefer a bite that can be completed, checked and recorded within one focused work session. As a practical default, use roughly 2\\u20135 primary sources or one substantial source plus its essential context, one main geometric construction, or one coherent workflow improvement. This is a heuristic, not a quota. A genuinely short source may be paired with a related source; a difficult source may need to be divided by chapter, construction or central result.\\n\\n### Avoid undersized bites\\n\\nDo not spend a full work session merely:\\n- locating one obvious source when the source can also be triaged;\\n- adding a single pointer without checking its target;\\n- repeating orientation or planning without advancing the work;\\n- reporting a problem without making the bounded repair that is already within scope.\\n\\nCombine adjacent micro-operations when they naturally form one result: locate \\u2192 inspect \\u2192 explain; define \\u2192 diagram \\u2192 check; edit \\u2192 read back \\u2192 record.\\n\\n### Avoid oversized bites\\n\\nDo not try to:\\n- survey an entire discipline in one pass;\\n- digest a very large archive or wiki as one undifferentiated task;\\n- build a large database, switchboard, scraper or automation before demonstrating the recurring need;\\n- pursue every branch surfaced by an interesting source in the same turn;\\n- make a long chain of dependent repository changes without intermediate validation.\\n\\nSplit such work into staged bites with clear dependencies and durable intermediate outputs. Each stage should be independently useful and resumable.\\n\\n### Chunking and execution safeguards\\n\\nFor large files, archives, or source collections:\\n1. inspect structure and metadata first;\\n2. select a bounded section or source family;\\n3. process it in chunks with stable source locators;\\n4. record completed coverage and remaining coverage;\\n5. verify the output before moving to the next chunk.\\n\\nFor code, searches, and repository writes, use bounded batches and inspect results between stages. Avoid large parallel bursts when they make failures hard to isolate or outputs likely to be truncated. Prefer several small, well-verified batches to one massive call.\\n\\n### Stop / split / continue decision\\n\\nAt each natural boundary, ask:\\n- Has the stated output been produced?\\n- Is it verified to the level required?\\n- Is the next operation a necessary part of this same result, or a separate branch?\\n- Is additional work still producing useful evidence, clarity, capability or a discriminating test?\\n\\nIf the bite is complete, stop and leave the next cursor. If the remaining operation is substantial but separable, split it. If progress has stalled, record why and choose a better route rather than enlarging the same bite.\\n\\n**The target is substantive completion at a manageable scale.** Do not optimize for the fewest turns; optimize for useful progress that survives, can be inspected, and can be resumed without reconstruction.\\n\\n\\n## 17. Basic adaptable session routine\\n\\nUse this as the default rhythm for workshop sessions. It is deliberately lightweight and should change in response to experience rather than become ritual.\\n\\n### A. Orient\\nBriefly recover:\\n- the workshop's purpose and interpretive conventions;\\n- the current branch and next cursor in the ledger;\\n- any new user direction or relevant change to the controlling protocol;\\n- the relevant source/tool routes for this particular bite.\\n\\nFor a continuing session, check only what has changed. Do not repeat full onboarding without a reason.\\n\\n### B. Choose one substantial bite\\nSelect one coherent question or construction. Define:\\n- why it matters;\\n- the bounded source/concept set;\\n- the expected deliverable;\\n- the exit condition.\\n\\nDefault to one main line of work per session. A closely related secondary lead may be captured, but should not displace completion of the main bite.\\n\\n### C. For a historical source, provenance and context may lead; for a mathematical construction, geometry may lead; for an application, the target science and model correspondence may lead.\\n\\n### D. Leave a durable result\\nProduce one useful result: a reading note, geometric plate, source comparison, cross-disciplinary map, small tested tool, or bounded protocol improvement. Update the ledger with the source state and next cursor.\\n\\n### E. Verify and close\\nCheck source locators, geometric fidelity, claims, and any repository write. State what was actually completed and what remains open. End with one clear next operation.\\n\\n### F. Periodic adaptation\\nAfter every three to five substantive bites, briefly review:\\n- which steps are helping and which are overhead;\\n- whether bite sizes are consistently too small or too large;\\n- which research branches are producing useful connections;\\n- which tools or templates deserve improvement;\\n- whether the current order of work still makes sense.\\n\\nChange the routine only when experience gives a concrete reason. Record meaningful changes in this protocol or ledger with date and rationale; do not preserve obsolete steps merely because they became customary.\\n\\n**Session completion standard:** one meaningful result, honest source/coverage status, a verified record where durable storage is used, and a next cursor.\\n\\n\\n## 18. Workflow signature line\\n\\nAt the end of each substantive workshop response, repeat a compact signature line that preserves the ordered workflow inside the active conversation context. Purpose and research remit\\n\\nInvestigate higher-dimensional geometry and its mathematical, scientific, historical, cultural, and literary relatives, with particular attention to:\\n\\n- higher-dimensional category theory, morphisms, groupoids, homotopy theory and related geometry;\\n- the nineteenth-century fourth-dimensionality tradition and its later mathematical/physical descendants;\\n- organismal biology, physiology, evolution, development, morphogenesis, neuroscience, ecology, biophysics and systems biology;\\n- computer science, computation, information theory, networks, artificial intelligence and type theory;\\n- physics, chemistry, earth/planetary science and other natural sciences;\\n- spiritualist, occult, speculative-philosophical, science-fiction, popular-science and fannish treatments of the fourth and higher dimensions, including cultural expressions such as time-binding and “Fans are Slans.”\\n\\nThe workshop adopts Nathan's stated interpretive premise that mathematical uses of “higher” should be read as “higher-dimensional,” with “dimensional” written out in our discussions. This is the workshop's interpretive lens. When a particular construction's dimensional character is unclear, describe the actual geometry and distinguish mathematical dimension from physical spatial dimension without dropping the dimensional reading.\\n\\nThe historical lineage from nineteenth-century higher-dimensional thought through spiritualist appropriation and later mathematical/physical usage is a working premise for interpretation. Read the literature accordingly; do not turn establishing that premise into a prerequisite. Preserve historical differences and identify where particular authors or constructions elaborate, transform, or depart from scientific concepts.\\n\\n## 2. Privacy and repository boundaries\\n\\n- HSH_RESOURCES is the primary supporting literature, research-tool and methods repository. Its contents are private/internal reference material unless separately cleared for public use. Source and evidence handling\\n\\nRaw source artifacts remain canonical. Follow wayfinding records to the source. Search/index silence is not evidence of absence. Distinguish source observation from interpretation, reconstruction, analogy and speculation.\\n\\n### Reading states\\n\\n- LOCATED: path or bibliographic record found.\\n- TRIAGED: abstract, contents or bounded excerpt assessed for relevance.\\n- PARTIAL: selected sections/pages read and cited.\\n- FULL: source read to the depth required for its intended use.\\n- EXTRACTED: text/figure/table extraction completed with provenance and quality noted. This is an access state, not a comprehension state.\\n- VISUALIZED: relevant geometric construction reconstructed as a diagram/model with conventions stated.\\n- TESTED: a computational, geometrical or empirical check has actually been run.\\n- SYNTHESIZED: contribution integrated into a source-backed workshop note.\\n\\nA source may have several orthogonal states. Never promote a snippet or machine-generated summary into a full reading.\\n\\n## 4. Geometric-first reading and visualization\\n\\nFor each important mathematical construction, answer:\\n\\n1. What is the geometric object?\\n2. What is its ambient space and dimension?\\n3. What is its intrinsic dimension?\\n4. How is it embedded, projected, sliced, intersected, fibered, connected or transformed?\\n5. What metric, topology, orientation, coordinates and boundary conditions are actually specified?\\n6. What are the permitted transformations and compositions?\\n7. What is a physical spatial dimension, a spacetime dimension, a configuration/parameter-space dimension, or a dimension internal to the mathematical structure?\\n8. What does the construction allow us to see that a lower-dimensional or flattened description conceals?\\n\\nUse diagrams early. Prefer a sequence of views, sections, projections, deformations and dimensional lifts over a wall of formal definitions. A diagram must be faithful to the specified object; mark schematic elements and unspecified geometry rather than inventing them.\\n\\nFor higher-dimensional category theory, explicitly visualize objects, one-dimensional morphisms, two-dimensional morphisms, three-dimensional morphisms and further-dimensional morphisms where the model permits. Explain source/target, composition, invertibility and coherence geometrically. Do not assume every model has identical strictness or composition rules.\\n\\n## 5. Cross-disciplinary opportunity capture\\n\\nEvery substantial mathematical source should be scanned for direct applications and possible natural extensions beyond pure mathematics. Use a broad search radius.\\n\\nCapture opportunities in one of three classes:\\n\\n- DIRECT_APPLICATION: source explicitly applies the construction to another field.\\n- NATURAL_EXTENSION: a plausible, structurally motivated extension to another field, with the mapping to be worked out.\\n- CULTURAL_TRANSMISSION: the concept appears in philosophical, spiritualist, literary, science-fiction, popular-science or fannish culture.\\n\\nFor each opportunity record:\\n- source construction and exact location;\\n- target discipline and candidate phenomenon;\\n- proposed geometric correspondence;\\n- what is shared and what differs;\\n- missing mechanism, assumptions or data;\\n- next discriminating reading, diagram, calculation or observation.\\n\\nDo not restrict discovery to keyword matches. Follow mathematical machinery across disciplines: for example, braids and configuration spaces toward molecular biology; geometric morphisms and transformations toward developmental or evolutionary pathways; topology toward neural and physiological networks; category-theoretic structures toward computation and information systems.\\n\\n## 6. Cultural and speculative literature protocol\\n\\nRead spiritualist, occult, speculative, fictional and fannish sources as legitimate historical/cultural evidence, not automatically as scientific evidence.\\n\\nFor each relevant item record:\\n- the original scientific or philosophical concept it invokes or may have adapted;\\n- the date and route of transmission where recoverable;\\n- how the concept changes in the new setting;\\n- whether the treatment is analogy, fictional device, metaphysical claim, reported phenomenon or technical proposal;\\n- points of contact with scientific concepts;\\n- unsupported or contradictory claims, identified specifically rather than by blanket dismissal.\\n\\nKeep three tracks visible:\\n1. scientific/mathematical content;\\n2. cultural transformation and reception;\\n3. speculative departure.\\n\\nFictional and fannish expressions may be evidence of an idea's reach, persistence or transformation, even when they are not evidence that the underlying scientific claim is true. Treat “time-binding,” “Fans are Slans,” and related expressions as cultural-historical leads; investigate their contexts and conceptual ancestry without assuming a single origin or meaning before source inspection.\\n\\n## 7. Research workflow: WAKE → ROUTE → READ → GEOMETRIZE → BRIDGE → RECORD → REVIEW\\n\\n### WAKE / CHECK\\nAt the start of a materially new session:\\n- identify the workshop's current scope and next cursor;\\n- check for relevant new user direction and durable workshop updates;\\n- inspect only the controlling guidance needed for the task;\\n- identify whether the task is historical, mathematical, geometric, cross-disciplinary, cultural, or operational.\\n\\nUse state-sensitive orientation. A new or stale session gets a fuller orientation; a warm session checks deltas and the current task rather than rereading everything ritualistically.\\n\\n### ROUTE\\nSelect the smallest useful route:\\n- nLab / n-Category Café for mathematical concepts and intellectual discussion;\\n- HSH_RESOURCES for supporting literature and historical collections;\\n- scholarly databases and primary sources for external verification;\\n- science-specific literature for cross-disciplinary follow-through;\\n- original fiction, fandom archives and historical documents for cultural transmission.\\n\\nBefore asking the user to repeat an available detail, search registered workshop materials and accessible repositories.\\n\\n### READ\\nLocate, triage, inspect and cite sources. Record what was actually read. Search results are discovery, not source comprehension.\\n\\n### GEOMETRIZE\\nTranslate the key construction into a visual/geometric account. Record dimensions, embeddings, maps, transformations, composition and limitations.\\n\\n### BRIDGE\\nActively seek:\\n- direct scientific applications;\\n- natural extensions to other sciences;\\n- historical/cultural transmission;\\n- useful counterexamples and constraints;\\n- neighboring mathematical tools that make the geometry more visible.\\n\\n### RECORD\\nLeave a durable bounded result with source pointers, reading states, geometric account, cross-disciplinary leads, unresolved questions and next cursor.\\n\\n### REVIEW\\nCheck whether the result answers the task, whether the geometry matches the source, whether claims are properly sourced, and whether the next step is still worth pursuing.\\n\\n## 8. Cultural and speculative literature protocol\\n\\nRead spiritualist, occult, speculative, fictional and fannish sources as legitimate historical/cultural evidence, not automatically as scientific evidence.\\n\\nFor each relevant item record:\\n- the original scientific or philosophical concept it invokes or may have adapted;\\n- the date and route of transmission where recoverable;\\n- how the concept changes in the new setting;\\n- whether the treatment is analogy, fictional device, metaphysical claim, reported phenomenon or technical proposal;\\n- points of contact with scientific concepts;\\n- unsupported or contradictory claims, identified specifically rather than by blanket dismissal.\\n\\nKeep three tracks visible:\\n1. scientific/mathematical content;\\n2. cultural transformation and reception;\\n3. speculative departure.\\n\\nFictional and fannish expressions may be evidence of an idea's reach, persistence or transformation, even when they are not evidence that the underlying scientific claim is true. Treat “time-binding,” “Fans are Slans,” and related expressions as cultural-historical leads; investigate their contexts and conceptual ancestry without assuming a single origin or meaning before source inspection.\\n\\n## 7. Research workflow: WAKE → ROUTE → READ → GEOMETRIZE → BRIDGE → RECORD → REVIEW\\n\\n### WAKE / CHECK\\nAt the start of a materially new session:\\n- identify the workshop's current scope and next cursor;\\n- check for relevant new user direction and durable workshop updates;\\n- inspect only the controlling guidance needed for the task;\\n- identify whether the task is historical, mathematical, geometric, cross-disciplinary, cultural, or operational.\\n\\nUse state-sensitive orientation. A new or stale session gets a fuller orientation; a warm session checks deltas and the current task rather than rereading everything ritualistically.\\n\\n### ROUTE\\nSelect the smallest useful route:\\n- nLab / n-Category Café for mathematical concepts and intellectual discussion;\\n- HSH_RESOURCES for supporting literature and historical collections;\\n- scholarly databases and primary sources for external verification;\\n- science-specific literature for cross-disciplinary follow-through;\\n- original fiction, fandom archives and historical documents for cultural transmission.\\n\\nBefore asking the user to repeat an available detail, search registered workshop materials and accessible repositories.\\n\\n### READ\\nLocate, triage, inspect and cite sources. Record what was actually read. Search results are discovery, not source comprehension.\\n\\n### GEOMETRIZE\\nTranslate the key construction into a visual/geometric account. Record dimensions, embeddings, maps, transformations, composition and limitations.\\n\\n### BRIDGE\\nActively seek:\\n- direct scientific applications;\\n- natural extensions to other sciences;\\n- historical/cultural transmission;\\n- useful counterexamples and constraints;\\n- neighboring mathematical tools that make the geometry more visible.\\n\\n### RECORD\\nLeave a durable bounded result with source pointers, reading states, geometric account, cross-disciplinary leads, unresolved questions and next cursor.\\n\\n### REVIEW\\nCheck whether the result answers the task, whether the geometry matches the source, whether claims are properly sourced, and whether the next step is still worth pursuing.\\n\\n## 8. Branching and work coordination\\n\\nUse a small number of clearly named work branches, not one undifferentiated reading queue:\\n\\n- MATH-GEOMETRY: category theory, topology, homotopy and dimensional visualization.\\n- HISTORY-CULTURE: Hinton, Victorian hyperspace, spiritualism, science fiction and fandom.\\n- BIO-SCIENCE: biology, physiology, evolution, development and related disciplines.\\n- COMPUTATION: computer science, information, networks, logic and AI.\\n- SCIENCE-BRIDGES: physics, chemistry, earth/planetary and other scientific applications.\\n- WORKSHOP-SYSTEMS: operating methods, tooling, indexes and continuity.\\n\\nBranches may run in parallel when tasks are genuinely separable. Keep a common source/terminology map, but preserve independent interpretations until each branch has recorded its own evidence. Do not mistake multiple workers reading the same summary or sharing the same prompt for independent confirmation.\\n\\nEach task quantum should have:\\n- one parent question/goal;\\n- one bounded operation;\\n- named source set or discovery bounds;\\n- expected output;\\n- a completion/exit condition;\\n- a next cursor.\\n\\nNested work must have a parent, depth limit, exit condition and orphan/fallback policy. A branch should close, merge or park when it stops generating useful evidence, constraints, clarification or capability.\\n\\n## 9. Tocktick-inspired temporal coordination\\n\\nUse the following general operational concepts as workshop conventions, without importing private legal material:\\n\\n- SEED: create a reusable question, diagram, source packet, tool, test or schema for downstream use.\\n- YIELD: deliberately release attention from a branch while others use the seed or evidence accumulates.\\n- AWAIT: resume when a defined evidence/state condition changes, rather than repeatedly checking an unchanged blocker.\\n- ACCUMULATE: collect outputs with their provenance and exposure metadata.\\n- RENDEZVOUS: return when a useful threshold is reached or a time cap expires.\\n- REJOIN: synthesize, audit, compare, improve the seed or launch the next bounded operation.\\n\\nPrefer state-based return thresholds with a time cap. Never let a parked branch disappear: retain its purpose, current state, return condition and displaced responsibility. Do not create recurring automations merely because a workflow could recur; use them only when the user asks or an existing authorized recurrence is explicitly assigned.\\n\\n## 10.             "Let's give the notation five basic operators. I propose that we distinguish **branching, rejoining, repetition, waiting, and termination**. These cover most of the compound workflow structures we'll initially need.\n\n## 1. Proposed operator vocabulary\n\n| Glyph | Operator | Meaning |\n|---|---|---|\n| `⑂` | Fork | Split into independently tracked branches. |\n| `⑃` | Rejoin | Bring branches back together. |\n| `⟳` | Cycle | Repeat a sequence of operations. |\n| `…` | Await | Suspend pending an event, input, or result. |\n| `■` | Halt | Terminate or park a workflow path. |\n\nThese are provisional pilot assignments.\n\n## 2. How they work\n\n### Fork\n\n`⌕⑂{A: sources | B: geometry}`\n\nInvestigation splits into two branches: source research and geometric reconstruction.\n\nThe branches can proceed independently.\n\n### Rejoin\n\n`⑃{A+B}⤳`\n\nBring the two branches together, reconcile their findings, and continue to connections.\n\nImportantly, rejoining means more than simply finishing both branches. Their results must actually be brought together.\n\n### Cycle\n\n`⟳{⌕⧖}`\n\nRepeat investigation and geometrization.\n\nFor example, investigate a mathematical construction, draw it, discover a problem, investigate again, and revise the geometry.\n\nA cycle needs an exit condition so we don't wind up orbiting the same intellectual planet indefinitely.\n\n### Await\n\n`…[primary source located]`\n\nSuspend this path until the specified condition is met.\n\nOther branches can continue working in the meantime.\n\n### Halt\n\n`■[parked: awaiting evidence]`\n\nStop this path without necessarily declaring the investigation finished.\n\nWe distinguish:\n- Complete\n- Cancelled\n- Parked\n\nThe annotation tells us which.\n\n## 3. A combined example\n\nSuppose we investigate an application of higher category theory to biology.\n\n`⌕⑂{A: DNA categories | B: biological hyperstructures}⑃⧖⤳▣✓`\n\nThat says:\n\n1. Investigate the two approaches independently.\n2. Reconcile their findings.\n3. Construct a geometric comparison.\n4. Explore connections.\n5. Record and verify the result.\n\nThat's a fairly expressive workflow in very little space.\n\n## 4. A few rules to keep us out of trouble\n\nBranches need identities and distinct outputs. Cycles need exit conditions. Await applies to a particular path, not necessarily the entire workflow. Rejoining requires reconciliation, not merely simultaneous completion.\n\nI've recorded these definitions in the protocol and ledger and verified both writes.\n\nI suggest we **test these five operators before adding more**. Nested branches, conditional routing, synchronization barriers, and other structures can wait until we encounter a genuine need for them.\n\n`⌖◉⑂⑃⟳…■⇢`\n\n**PILOT: operators provisionally defined | NEXT: Test notation on an actual research workflow**"

No architecture implementation, automated sampler, human study, or theory promotion is claimed.  \\n**Worker label:** Ariadne. Why this is a crosswalk, not a duplicate architecture\\n\\nThe HsH main branch now contains [The Memory Credenza: a compact model for continuity, attention, and return](../MEMORY_CREDENZA_MODEL_2026-11-19.md). The file describes itself as experimental and explicitly distinguishes the Key, Credenza, and Castle; Compass, Atlas, Work tray, and Watchtower; purpose-specific cubbies; tick/tock; and a possible neglect sampler. It does not claim a universal architecture or an implemented sampler, and it does not authorize a new automation or schedule.\\n\\nThis review does not replace that model.\\n\\nIt also does not duplicate adjacent work:\\n\\n- [Ravel h945:s4, issue #2084](https://github.com/Satobloc/HsH/issues/2084) already treats active-path memory and off-path archive as separate states requiring explicit adoption.\\n- [Orson h946:s0, issue #2085](https://github.com/Satobloc/HsH/issues/2085) already develops generic cognitive evidence geometry, source-fidelity distinctions, and projection/factorization conditions.\\n- [Aster h946:s3, issue #2086](https://github.com/Satobloc/HsH/issues/2086) covers a separate Kelvin-system source and cross-view evidence problem.\\n- [Loom h946:s2, issue #2087](https://github.com/Satobloc/HsH/issues/2087) covers a separate source-identity and chronology correction.\\n- Enheduanna's October 31 review already examined Tak et al., *From Process Loss to Assembly Bonus*. Three non-equivalent failure modes\\n\\n### A. Source memory and contribution attribution\\n\\nZindulka et al., *The AI Memory Gap: Users Misremember What They Created With AI or Without*, CHI 2026, DOI [10.1145/3772318.3791494](https://doi.org/10.1145/3772318.3791494), [arXiv:2509.11851](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.11851).\\n\\nThe study involved 184 participants in a 2x2 within-subject co-writing design. Participants completed ideation and elaboration stages with or without AI assistance, then returned after a one-week delay for source-memory tests. Overall source attribution accuracy was 65.8% for ideas and 72.8% for elaborations.\\n\\nThe paper's model-based predicted probabilities for identifying the source of an idea were:\\n\\n| Ideation / elaboration workflow | Predicted idea-source accuracy |\\n|---|---:|\\n| Human / human | 92.4% |\\n| AI / human | 37.7% |\\n| Human / AI | 64.0% |\\n| AI / AI | 79.3% |\\n\\nThe mixed workflows were the weakest, especially when AI generated the idea and a human elaborated it. In those mixed conditions, confidence did not reliably distinguish correct from incorrect idea-source attribution. The paper also reports overconfidence in source judgments.\\n\\nThis is not a group-deliberation experiment. It is an individual co-writing task using one chatbot/model configuration, GPT-4.1-mini, and a one-week recall interval. It does, however, show that a single project-level \\\"AI used\\\" flag is too coarse to preserve who originated an idea and who transformed it.\\n\\n**Credenza implication:** retain stage-specific contribution lineage. A claim may have a human origin, AI elaboration, human edit, and later group synthesis. Do not assign one author/source label to the whole artifact.\\n\\n### B. Content fidelity and memory distortion\\n\\nSim et al., *AI-Enabled Human Memory Manipulation: Misleading AI-Generated Summaries Distort Human Memory*, [arXiv:2609.28820](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.28820). This is treated as an arXiv preprint; no peer-reviewed publication status is asserted here.\\n\\nThe experiment involved 328 participants in a 2x2 between-subject design, using two short videos and a 24-48 hour delay. The same ChatGPT-generated and researcher-edited summary was presented under an AI or human source label. The summary's actual production history and the displayed label were therefore separate variables.\\n\\nAccuracy on the critical event question was 83.6% in the consistent-information condition and 44.8% in the misleading-information condition. The displayed AI-versus-human label did not significantly moderate the misinformation effect. The authors' audit of 20 candidate summaries found substantial content defects: 51.6% of critical details were omitted, 6.1% were inaccurately described, and 60% of summaries contained at least one hallucinated addition.\\n\\nA summary-level arithmetic check was performed from the published condition sizes and rounded rates:\\n\\n- Consistent condition: 165 participants, approximately 138 correct.\\n- Misleading condition: 163 participants, approximately 73 correct.\\n- Reconstructed Pearson chi-square: 53.9366, matching the paper's reported 53.937 to rounding.\\n- Approximate risk difference: 38.9 percentage points; risk ratio: 1.87; odds ratio: 6.30.\\n\\nThese are reconstructed from rounded published percentages and group sizes, not an independent raw-data reanalysis. The public OSF data locator is [wmjtn](https://osf.io/wmjtn/); the raw files were not downloaded in this run.\\n\\nThis study is limited to two videos, one selected summary per event, and one delayed memory task. Its source-label manipulation is not a naturalistic multi-agent collaboration experiment. Its value here is the separation it makes visible: the displayed source label did not protect participants from misleading content, and the displayed label was not the same thing as the actual human-AI production chain.\\n\\n**Credenza implication:** keep actual producer, displayed label, transformation history, and content verification as separate fields. A source label is not a verification result.\\n\\n### C. Group process, exposure, and uptake\\n\\nTak et al., *From Process Loss to Assembly Bonus: Human-Grounded Diagnosis of Multi-Agent LLM Collaboration*, Findings of EMNLP 2026, [ACL Anthology 2026.findings-emnlp.1341](https://aclanthology.org/2026.findings-emnlp.1341/).\\n\\nThis paper was already reviewed in Enheduanna's October 31 source report. It compares 500 human-only group dialogues with roughly 26,000 LLM-only group conversations across four tasks. It is not a mixed human-LLM group experiment.\\n\\nThe prior review found that LLM group processes showed lower realization of unique information and earlier lock-in in important conditions. Correct minority signals mattered chiefly when they were publicly re-expressed early and carried through to the final answer. The prior review also recorded that interventions were modest and did not eliminate the coordination bottleneck.\\n\\n**Credenza implication:** preserving a minority claim in storage is not the same as preserving its influence. The event record must distinguish availability, exposure, re-expression, uptake, and final decision use.\\n\\n## 3. A compact linked record, not another top-level drawer\\n\\nThe three studies point to three separate outcome families:\\n\\n1. **Source memory:** who originated or transformed a contribution?\\n2. **Content fidelity:** does the retained claim accurately represent its primary evidence?\\n3. **Group uptake:** who had access to the claim, who re-expressed it, and which later decision used it?\\n\\nDecision accuracy, confidence, trust, and accountability remain separate outcomes as well.\\n\\nThe Memory Credenza already has a Sources / Evidence & Provenance cubby and a Findings / Decisions cubby. A small linked **Provenance-Exposure-Uptake (PEU) event ledger** could connect them without adding a new top-level compartment.\\n\\nMinimum record:\\n\\n- claim_version_id\\n- origin_root_ids: primary source, version/hash, and exact locator\\n- contribution_chain: actor/model/tool, operation (create, edit, summarize, translate, merge), parent claim version, and timestamp\\n- displayed_source_label: what the recipient was told, separate from actual producer\\n- verification_event: primary-source check, method, reviewer, and status\\n- exposure_events: available, delivered, opened, acknowledged, quoted, or adopted, but only where each state has evidence\\n- uptake_events: later claim or decision that references or transforms this version\\n- minority_signal_state: proposed, surfaced, re-expressed, retained, rejected, or lost, with event times\\n- decision_ref: final outcome, confidence, rationale, and accountable decision-maker\\n\\nFor LLMs, prompt inclusion is observable; internal attention is not. Do not equate a claim's presence in a prompt or transcript with demonstrated use. For humans, message availability is not proof of attention. Use explicit acknowledgment or consented interface measures where needed.\\n\\nKeep the visible Credenza card small: claim/version, origin root, provenance status, last verification, exposure/uptake state, open-when trigger, and return cue. Load the detailed event graph only when the task needs it.\\n\\nPreserve UNKNOWN as a first-class state. The existing HsH formalization in [Orson PR #1115](https://github.com/Satobloc/HsH/pull/1115), particularly HumanAIQuestionnaireProvenance.lean, demonstrates how a three-way Human / AI / Unsure judgment loses information when projected to a Boolean. Do not silently collapse uncertain source attribution into false or true.\\n\\nThe Credenza's tick remains a place marker. A tock means a bounded operation has produced a durable result and next cursor. Neither a tick nor a tock means that a claim has been verified, adopted, or accepted.\\n\\n### Crosswalk with branch-aware memory\\n\\nThese are complementary operational layers, not equivalents:\\n\\n- **Branch-aware memory** selects the active history and preserves off-path alternatives. An explicit adoption event is required to move an off-path item into active state.\\n- **Memory Credenza** organizes retrieval routes, cubbies, open-when triggers, and return cues.\\n- **PEU ledger** preserves claim-level origin, contribution, exposure, uptake, verification, and decision events.\\n\\nComposition requires stable branch_id, claim_version_id, and source_root_id mappings across all three layers. A cubby index must not silently convert an off-path claim into an active claim. A final summary must not replace the event lineage that produced it.\\n\\nThe neglect sampler could sample not only under-inspected cubbies, but also distinct source roots, unresolved claim versions, off-path branches, incomplete verification chains, and minority signals that were never re-expressed. Record the sampling frame/version, method/seed where practical, selected item, selection reason, inspection extent, result, action, and next cursor. Sampling is an invitation to inspect, not evidence of importance or completeness.\\n\\n## 4. Formal identifiability boundary\\n\\nLet H be complete interaction histories, O the retained Credenza record, and T a target such as actual authorship, source-root independence, decision-time exposure, or uptake.\\n\\nA deterministic reconstruction g satisfying T = g composed with O exists exactly when T is constant on every fiber of O:\\n\\nO(h1) = O(h2) implies T(h1) = T(h2).\\n\\nThis is the existing generic projection/factorization result in [Orson PR #1115](https://github.com/Satobloc/HsH/pull/1115), especially ObservableProjection.lean. The relevant files compile and their #print axioms commands are part of the build. The PR remains open, draft, and unmerged.\\n\\nNo new Lean module, theorem, #eval, source-specific instantiation, or CI run was created. This review reuses an existing abstract proof primitive; it does not claim that the two new studies or the Memory Credenza have been formalized or empirically validated. The theorem establishes a conditional identifiability boundary, not the truth of the empirical premises.\\n\\n## 5. Falsifiable mixed human-LLM group experiment\\n\\nA bounded next experiment could use groups of two human participants and one LLM peer, with multiple independent groups and objective tasks whose evidence and answer can be adjudicated independently.\\n\\nUse a preregistered 2x2 group-level design:\\n\\n- **Lineage detail:** source label only versus stage-level origin and transformation lineage.\\n- **Minority-signal surfacing:** ordinary chronological transcript versus an explicit early re-expression of the initial minority claim.\\n\\nEach participant first records an independent response before group discussion. The group then deliberates and submits a final decision. Source labels remain truthful; deception is not needed. Any later source-label deception would require ethics approval and debriefing.\\n\\nMeasure separately:\\n\\n- content recall and fidelity to primary evidence\\n- source and contributor attribution\\n- decision accuracy\\n- confidence calibration\\n- minority-signal survival and re-expression timing\\n- actual decision use of a claim\\n- accountability attribution\\n- time and cognitive load\\n\\nUse the group/session as the inferential unit, not message count. Determine sample size through a preregistered power analysis at the group level. Use blinded adjudication of claim fidelity and task outcomes. Record model/version/prompt/context and human-visible interface events with consent. Do not infer attention or subjective mental states from message presence.\\n\\nThe proposal is falsified or needs simplification if stage-level lineage does not improve source attribution, if early re-expression does not improve minority-signal retention, or if any gain is outweighed by cognitive load and delay. If lineage improves attribution but not content accuracy, that is partial support for a narrower function, not validation of the whole Credenza.\\n\\nNo participants, model/API trials, or experiments were conducted in this run.\\n\\n## 6.             "[L1] {\n[L2]   \"content\": \"# The Memory Credenza: a compact model for continuity, attention, and return\\n\\n**Date:** 2026-11-19  \\n**Status:** Experimental, transferable design model. This is a navigation and workflow metaphor, not a claim that a universal architecture or automated sampler is already implemented.\\n\\n## The three scales\\n\\nThe **Key** is the tiny continuity kernel or boot capsule: identity/role where useful, current remit, re-entry instruction, immediate place marker, and a pointer to the Credenza. It must remain small enough to be carried reliably between finite contexts. It is not an encyclopedia.\\n\\nThe **Memory Credenza** is the compact, adaptive control model of the larger memory environment. It keeps a few useful routes, access cues, statuses, and return points close at hand. Its compartments may be added, divided, combined, renamed, or retired as the work teaches us what is useful. A cubby is an access point with a job, not necessarily a folder or a place where all its material is stored.\\n\\nThe **Castle** is the full repository-backed environment: source records, histories, databases, project modules, tools, scripts, methods, workflows, and the deeper structures to which the Credenza points. The Credenza models how to navigate and maintain the Castle; it does not duplicate the Castle.\\n\\n## The Credenza's working surface\\n\\nKeep the visible surface compact:\\n\\n- **Compass:** purpose, boundaries, and controlling priorities.\\n- **Atlas:** principal projects, branches, repositories, and cross-links.\\n- **Work tray:** the current `PIN | NOW | NEXT | RETURN`.\\n- **Watchtower:** pending changes, dependencies, overdue review, and neglected areas.\\n\\nPotential cubbies include: sources/evidence and provenance; questions and competing hypotheses; findings and decisions; tools and instruments; methods and quality controls; entities and cross-branch connections; neglected or underexplored areas; experiments and capability development; and deferred, superseded, or retired work.\\n\\nA compartment card should contain only what helps someone decide whether and how to open it: **purpose, route, open-when trigger, status, last meaningful inspection, and return cue**. Add fields such as owner, source version/hash, coverage due, or review stratum only where they support a real operation. Deep instructions remain in linked modules and are loaded only when needed.\\n\\n## How the tick and tock fit\\n\\nThe Credenza gives the attention/continuity rhythm a navigable place to point. Keep the meanings distinct:\\n\\n- **Tick:** the small, repeatable place marker. It makes the active position and return route visible, typically as `PIN | NOW | NEXT | RETURN`. It is a breadcrumb, not a work-completion claim.\\n- **Tock:** a completed bounded operation that has produced a durable, recorded result. Advance an operation counter only after the result and its next cursor are recorded; a chat turn or tool call alone is not a tock.\\n- **Heartbeat:** a project-specific signal of meaningful human-directed activity or contact. It can inform when a dormant workflow may need attention, but it is not proof that substantive work occurred.\\n- **Attention cycle:** an optional rotation across different parts of the Credenza. It may advance on completed operations, turns, calendar triggers, or another explicit rule. These mechanisms are not interchangeable, and different workflows may need different rhythms or no ticker at all.\\n\\nThe active drawer should not monopolize attention. The pin keeps the immediate task recoverable; the wider Credenza keeps other branches, tools, methods, and source collections visible enough to be rediscovered.\\n\\n## The neglect sampler\\n\\nA future sampler may help detect systematic inattention by combining two selection modes:\\n\\n1. **Coverage rotation:** surface compartments, source strata, questions, or capabilities whose meaningful-inspection date or coverage state indicates that they are due.\\n2. **Stratified random sampling:** select from a defined inventory across branches, source types, dates, geographies, entities, methods, or other useful strata, including an explicit stratum for inventory that is incomplete or poorly understood.\\n\\nA sample is an invitation to inspect, not a finding. Inspect the actual source or artifact, record exactly what was examined and how far, preserve provenance and version/hash, distinguish unexamined from unreadable or absent, and route the result to a bounded operation only when warranted. A null result or no-op may be useful when recorded accurately. Random selection does not establish importance, and a sampler cannot prove completeness.\\n\\nFor auditability, retain the sampling frame/version, selection method and seed where practical, item selected, selection reason, inspection extent, result, action taken, and next review cue. Keep the process inspectable, interruptible, and manually overridable. Evaluate useful discoveries and durable state changes against missed work, duplication, false triggers, source-cursor errors, drift, and overhead. Use coverage debt as a prompt for attention, not as a measure of evidentiary importance.\\n\\n## The caretaker and adoption path\\n\\nA lightweight caretaker periodically inspects the Credenza itself: broken or stale pointers, drawers with unclear purposes, important new tools or modules not yet routed, neglected branches, duplication, missing return cues, sampling-frame bias, and maintenance overhead. It may recommend changes; it should not silently change priorities, conclusions, ownership, or schedules.\\n\\nA sensible build sequence is: (1) create a small registry and human-readable router; (2) connect existing project maps, queues, checkpoints, evidence catalogs, and capability guides; (3) test the cards and return cues during ordinary work; (4) build a sampler only when the inventory is sufficiently structured; and (5) automate only after a bounded pilot demonstrates useful state change. No new automation or schedule is authorized by this design note.\\n\\nThis is a model to experiment with, compare, and revise. Preserve workflow-specific variation. Promote components that improve orientation, rediscovery, coverage, and recovery after interruption; simplify or retire those that add ceremony without useful results.\\n\\n**Nathan's requested sign-off, reproduced verbatim as a textual reference to his signet:**\\n\\n> --NM 19NOV2026 [OWL]\\n\",\n[L3]   \"encoding\": \"utf-8\",\n[L4]   \"sha\": \"86497cd43dc2e36a74dfb4b3983a2071e0e47cd8\",\n[L5]   \"display_url\": \"https://github.com/Satobloc/HsH/blob/main/WORKSPACES/COMMON/MEMORY_CREDENZA_MODEL_2026-11-19.md\",\n[L6]   \"display_title\": \"MEMORY_CREDENZA_MODEL_2026-11-19.md\"\n[L7] }"

            "Yes. I think the Credenza and our Unicode workflow notation could work particularly well together. They solve different problems, and combining them gives us something more capable than either alone.\n\nI've located and read the original **Memory Credenza** model dated November 19, 2026, in the HsH repository, along with its empirical crosswalk.\n\nThe important thing is that we shouldn't reinvent the Credenza from memory. It already has a fairly developed architecture.\n\n## 1. The Credenza: our navigational and continuity system\n\nThe original model distinguishes three scales:\n\n| Element | Function |\n|---|---|\n| **Key** | Small continuity packet carried between contexts |\n| **Credenza** | Compact organization of routes, priorities, compartments, and return points |\n| **Castle** | The complete repository-backed environment containing the actual materials, tools, histories, and project structures |\n\nThink of the Credenza as the control surface, not the storage system itself.\n\nIts working surface has four principal elements:\n\n| Component | Purpose |\n|---|---|\n| Compass | Purpose, boundaries, controlling priorities |\n| Atlas | Projects, branches, repositories, cross-links |\n| Work tray | Immediate position and next action |\n| Watchtower | Pending changes, dependencies, neglected areas |\n\nIts compartments, or cubbies, provide access to deeper resources.\n\nA cubby isn't necessarily a folder. It's an access point with a purpose, an opening condition, a status, and a return cue.\n\n## 2. Unicode notation: our execution system\n\nOur experimental notation describes the structure and progress of an operation.\n\nThe Credenza tells us where the resources and responsibilities are. The glyph notation tells us what we're doing with them.\n\nI see the relationship this way:\n\n| Credenza | Unicode workflow |\n|---|---|\n| Compass | Orient |\n| Atlas | Select branch |\n| Work tray | Current workflow position |\n| Watchtower | Await, review, or alert |\n| Cubbies | Resources and capabilities |\n| Return cues | Workflow resumption |\n| Neglect sampler | Initiate an inspection workflow |\n\nThe two systems are complementary, not competing.\n\n## 3. The particularly useful idea: Tick and Tock\n\nThis deserves special attention.\n\nThe original Credenza model makes an important distinction:\n\n**Tick:** A small place marker. It tells us where we are and how to return.\n\n**Tock:** A completed bounded operation that has produced a durable result.\n\nA conversation turn isn't necessarily a tock. Neither is a tool call. The operation must actually produce something recorded and recoverable.\n\nThat distinction could prevent a lot of false progress reporting.\n\nFor our pilot, I'd propose:\n\n- The Unicode signature is our **Tick**.\n- A completed, recorded, verified work bite is a **Tock**.\n- The Credenza maintains the larger continuity and attention structure.\n\nA compact work-tray record could look like:\n\n`PIN: BIO-SCIENCE | NOW: DNA categories | NEXT: Geometric reconstruction | RETURN: nLab biology note`\n\nWe don't need to repeat all of that in every response. The signature handles the immediate position; the Credenza handles recovery and navigation.\n\n## 4. The neglected-work problem\n\nOne of the most interesting parts of the Credenza is its proposed *neglect sampler*.\n\nIt has two modes:\n\n**Coverage rotation:** Identify compartments, branches, or sources that haven't received meaningful attention recently.\n\n**Stratified random sampling:** Occasionally select something from the wider inventory, including less-explored material.\n\nThis is important because our attention naturally gravitates toward whatever is already active.\n\nWe might spend several sessions on higher category theory while overlooking a biological application, an important historical source, or a useful computational technique sitting elsewhere in the archive.\n\nThe sampler is intended to counteract that tendency.\n\nIt doesn't automatically declare something important. It simply invites inspection.\n\nI'd keep this manual for now. We need enough experience with the Credenza to know what belongs in its inventory before automating selection.\n\n## 5. Tentative combined architecture\n\nHere's how I'd organize the experiment:\n\n```text\n                  THE CASTLE\n          Complete information environment\n                       │\n                       ▼\n                 THE CREDENZA\n        ┌──────────┬──────────┬──────────┐\n        │ Compass  │  Atlas   │Watchtower│\n        └──────────┴──────────┴──────────┘\n                       │\n                  ┌────┴────┐\n                  │ Worktray│\n                  └────┬────┘\n                       │\n                 UNICODE TICK\n                Current position\n                       │\n                       ▼\n                WORKFLOW OPERATORS\n              ⌖ ◉ ⌕ ⧖ ⤳ ▣ ✓ ⇢\n                  ⑂ ⑃ ⟳ … ■\n                       │\n                       ▼\n                 BOUNDED WORK\n                       │\n                       ▼\n                 DURABLE RESULT\n                       │\n                       ▼\n                   TOCK\n                       │\n                       ▼\n              Update Credenza\n              Advance position\n```\n\nThis is a proposed integration, not an existing implemented architecture.\n\n## 6. How we'll implement it\n\nI suggest three experimental stages.\n\n**Stage A: Manual integration.** Use the signature, current work-tray position, and repository ledger together. Keep the Credenza small.\n\n**Stage B: Adaptive compartments.** As we encounter recurring needs, establish cubbies for sources, geometry, biological applications, historical research, computational tools, and experiments. Don't create compartments just because we can.\n\n**Stage C: Attention and continuity experiments.** Test coverage rotation, neglected-work inspection, return cues, and eventually the possibility of a small sampler.\n\nWe should also preserve an important distinction from the Credenza's empirical crosswalk: remembering a claim, knowing where it came from, verifying it, and actually using it in a decision are separate things. The system shouldn't conflate them.\n\n---\n\n### My proposed working arrangement\n\nThe Credenza manages *where our attention can go and how we recover it*.\n\nThe Unicode notation manages *the structure and state of the work we're doing*.\n\nTick marks position. Tock records completed work. The ledger preserves durable history.\n\nWe'll experiment with the integration locally and revise it when actual use exposes weaknesses.
