Keep a common source/terminology map, but preserve independent interpretations until each branch has recorded its own evidence. Do not mistake multiple workers reading the same summary or sharing the same prompt for independent confirmation.\\n\\nEach task quantum should have:\\n- one parent question/goal;\\n- one bounded operation;\\n- named source set or discovery bounds;\\n- expected output;\\n- a completion/exit condition;\\n- a next cursor.\\n\\nNested work must have a parent, depth limit, exit condition and orphan/fallback policy. A branch should close, merge or park when it stops generating useful evidence, constraints, clarification or capability.\\n\\n## 9. Tocktick-inspired temporal coordination\\n\\nUse the following general operational concepts as workshop conventions, without importing private legal material:\\n\\n- SEED: create a reusable question, diagram, source packet, tool, test or schema for downstream use.\\n- YIELD: deliberately release attention from a branch while others use the seed or evidence accumulates.\\n- AWAIT: resume when a defined evidence/state condition changes, rather than repeatedly checking an unchanged blocker.\\n- ACCUMULATE: collect outputs with their provenance and exposure metadata.\\n- RENDEZVOUS: return when a useful threshold is reached or a time cap expires.\\n- REJOIN: synthesize, audit, compare, improve the seed or launch the next bounded operation.\\n\\nPrefer state-based return thresholds with a time cap. Never let a parked branch disappear: retain its purpose, current state, return condition and displaced responsibility. Do not create recurring automations merely because a workflow could recur; use them only when the user asks or an existing authorized recurrence is explicitly assigned.\\n\\n## 10. Tools, scripts and derived infrastructure\\n\\nUse available connected tools, repository indexes, search tools, paper extractors, scripts and computational tools before improvising manual workarounds. Discover and read tool instructions before use.\\n\\nFor any script or repository operation:\\n- declare exact repositories and paths read/written;\\n- identify outputs as source, derived, generated, append-only or semantic;\\n- record run ID, source commit/ref, tool version and configuration;\\n- exclude private/quarantined material before reading or indexing where required;\\n- never overwrite raw sources during extraction or analysis;\\n- use fresh-base, non-force writes and compare-and-swap/current blob SHA for semantic edits;\\n- use per-run temporary paths and atomic finalization where possible;\\n- validate generated coverage and independently read back writes;\\n- never treat successful scheduling, execution or state restoration as proof that the requested artifact was delivered.\\n\\nPrefer existing scripts and adapters over duplicating functionality. Use dry-run before broad or destructive operations. Add a new parser only when an inventory reveals a recurring unmet need.\\n\\n## 11. Citation and provenance workflow\\n\\nUse the sequence:\\n\\nclaim / geometric statement \\u2192 citation need \\u2192 candidate sources \\u2192 inspect source \\u2192 exact page/section anchor \\u2192 verified citation \\u2192 place citation\\n\\nA bibliography identifies available sources; it does not establish that a source supports a particular claim.\\n\\nFor each important claim, capture:\\n- exact claim being supported;\\n- citation role (background, definition, application, empirical result, prior treatment, cultural context, constraint);\\n- source identity and page/section anchor;\\n- review state;\\n- short explanation of why it supports the claim.\\n\\nUse original external citations in public-facing writing. Internal repository paths and hashes are for recovery and audit, not substitutes for bibliographic citations. Do not cite a source for more than it actually says.\\n\\n## 12. Epistemic and interpretation conventions\\n\\nKeep separate:\\n- direct source statement;\\n- established mathematical/scientific result;\\n- Nathan's workshop premise or instruction;\\n- assistant's interpretation;\\n- reconstructed geometry;\\n- natural extension;\\n- speculative conjecture;\\n- fictional or cultural representation.\\n\\nThe workshop's agreed dimensional reading is an interpretive convention. Do not quietly reframe it as a claim that every author explicitly intended physical spatial dimensions. Instead, read the terminology through the agreed lens and examine the construction's actual dimensional content.\\n\\nFor spiritualist, occult and fictional material, skepticism applies to factual/scientific claims, not to its value as evidence of cultural transmission or conceptual reception.\\n\\nDo not use \\u201cproof\\u201d loosely. Name the actual status: source statement, definition, derivation, visualization, numerical check, empirical observation, proposed mechanism or speculation.\\n\\n## 13. Deliverable format\\n\\nA normal substantive reading note should contain:\\n\\n1. Question / why this source matters\\n2. Source and reading state\\n3. Geometric picture\\n4. Dimensional account\\n5. What the author actually contributes\\n6. Direct applications / natural extensions\\n7. Historical or cultural connections\\n8. Limitations, mismatches and open edges\\n9. Next bounded operation\\n\\nA workshop synthesis should connect several reading notes while retaining source-level references and differences among authors.\\n\\n## 14. Current initial work programme\\n\\nStart with these linked work packages:\\n\\n1. nLab visual atlas: reconstruct ordinary categories, 2-categories and higher-dimensional categories through points, paths, surfaces, volumes, transformations and composition; then move into higher-dimensional homotopy and groupoids.\\n2. Victorian-to-modern lineage: organize Hinton, Abbott, Whately Smith, spiritualist and psychical-research material, professional reception, and the modern mathematical vocabulary.\\n3. Cross-disciplinary bridge map: identify source-backed applications and natural extensions into biology, physiology, evolution, computer science and other sciences.\\n4. Cultural reception map: investigate science fiction, fandom, time-binding, \\u201cFans are Slans,\\u201d and adjacent expressions as transmission/reception evidence.\\n5. Workshop tooling: create only the indexes, source cards, diagrams and small scripts that solve a demonstrated recurring retrieval or workflow problem.\\n\\n## 15. First implementation principle\\n\\nStart with durable workshop navigation, a compact source/idea ledger, and reusable reading-note templates. Do not build a large switchboard, database or automation before actual use demonstrates the need. Improve the system through bounded experiments, explicit failure notes and transfer to a second task.\\n\\n**Current next operation:** establish the workshop workspace and source/idea ledger, then begin the nLab visual atlas with the geometry of points, paths and homotopies.\\n\\n\\n## 16. Work-bite sizing and stopping rule\\n\\n**Standing instruction from Nathan, 2026-11-24:** take reasonable-sized bites. Avoid both tiny, low-value nibbles and oversized chunks likely to hang, sprawl, or end without a verified result.\\n\\nA normal work bite should produce one coherent result, not merely touch a large number of files or topics.\\n\\n### Bite-size test\\n\\nBefore starting, define:\\n\\n- **Question:** one central question or tightly related cluster.\\n- **Scope:** a bounded set of sources, concepts, or operations.\\n- **Output:** one useful artifact, explanation, diagram, comparison, or verified state change.\\n- **Exit condition:** what will count as a complete bite.\\n- **Next cursor:** the most valuable next operation, left explicit.\\n\\nPrefer a bite that can be completed, checked and recorded within one focused work session. As a practical default, use roughly 2\\u20135 primary sources or one substantial source plus its essential context, one main geometric construction, or one coherent workflow improvement. This is a heuristic, not a quota. A genuinely short source may be paired with a related source; a difficult source may need to be divided by chapter, construction or central result.\\n\\n### Avoid undersized bites\\n\\nDo not spend a full work session merely:\\n- locating one obvious source when the source can also be triaged;\\n- adding a single pointer without checking its target;\\n- repeating orientation or planning without advancing the work;\\n- reporting a problem without making the bounded repair that is already within scope.\\n\\nCombine adjacent micro-operations when they naturally form one result: locate \\u2192 inspect \\u2192 explain; define \\u2192 diagram \\u2192 check; edit \\u2192 read back \\u2192 record.\\n\\n### Avoid oversized bites\\n\\nDo not try to:\\n- survey an entire discipline in one pass;\\n- digest a very large archive or wiki as one undifferentiated task;\\n- build a large database, switchboard, scraper or automation before demonstrating the recurring need;\\n- pursue every branch surfaced by an interesting source in the same turn;\\n- make a long chain of dependent repository changes without intermediate validation.\\n\\nSplit such work into staged bites with clear dependencies and durable intermediate outputs. Each stage should be independently useful and resumable.\\n\\n### Chunking and execution safeguards\\n\\nFor large files, archives, or source collections:\\n1. inspect structure and metadata first;\\n2. select a bounded section or source family;\\n3. process it in chunks with stable source locators;\\n4. record completed coverage and remaining coverage;\\n5. verify the output before moving to the next chunk.\\n\\nFor code, searches, and repository writes, use bounded batches and inspect results between stages. Avoid large parallel bursts when they make failures hard to isolate or outputs likely to be truncated. Prefer several small, well-verified batches to one massive call.\\n\\n### Stop / split / continue decision\\n\\nAt each natural boundary, ask:\\n- Has the stated output been produced?\\n- Is it verified to the level required?\\n- Is the next operation a necessary part of this same result, or a separate branch?\\n- Is additional work still producing useful evidence, clarity, capability or a discriminating test?\\n\\nIf the bite is complete, stop and leave the next cursor. If the remaining operation is substantial but separable, split it. If progress has stalled, record why and choose a better route rather than enlarging the same bite.\\n\\n**The target is substantive completion at a manageable scale.** Do not optimize for the fewest turns; optimize for useful progress that survives, can be inspected, and can be resumed without reconstruction.\\n\\n\\n## 17. Basic adaptable session routine\\n\\nUse this as the default rhythm for workshop sessions. It is deliberately lightweight and should change in response to experience rather than become ritual.\\n\\n### A. Orient\\nBriefly recover:\\n- the workshop's purpose and interpretive conventions;\\n- the current branch and next cursor in the ledger;\\n- any new user direction or relevant change to the controlling protocol;\\n- the relevant source/tool routes for this particular bite.\\n\\nFor a continuing session, check only what has changed. Do not repeat full onboarding without a reason.\\n\\n### B. Choose one substantial bite\\nSelect one coherent question or construction. Define:\\n- why it matters;\\n- the bounded source/concept set;\\n- the expected deliverable;\\n- the exit condition.\\n\\nDefault to one main line of work per session. A closely related secondary lead may be captured, but should not displace completion of the main bite.\\n\\n### C. Work it through\\nUse the sequence appropriate to the task:\\n- locate and inspect the source;\\n- explain the idea in ordinary language;\\n- reconstruct or draw its geometry;\\n- identify its dimensional structure;\\n- follow one or two of its strongest scientific, biological, computational, historical or cultural connections;\\n- identify important qualifications and open edges.\\n\\nDo not force every stage when it does not apply. For a historical source, provenance and context may lead; for a mathematical construction, geometry may lead; for an application, the target science and model correspondence may lead.\\n\\n### D. Leave a durable result\\nProduce one useful result: a reading note, geometric plate, source comparison, cross-disciplinary map, small tested tool, or bounded protocol improvement. Update the ledger with the source state and next cursor.\\n\\n### E. Verify and close\\nCheck source locators, geometric fidelity, claims, and any repository write. State what was actually completed and what remains open. End with one clear next operation.\\n\\n### F. Periodic adaptation\\nAfter every three to five substantive bites, briefly review:\\n- which steps are helping and which are overhead;\\n- whether bite sizes are consistently too small or too large;\\n- which research branches are producing useful connections;\\n- which tools or templates deserve improvement;\\n- whether the current order of work still makes sense.\\n\\nChange the routine only when experience gives a concrete reason. Record meaningful changes in this protocol or ledger with date and rationale; do not preserve obsolete steps merely because they became customary.\\n\\n**Session completion standard:** one meaningful result, honest source/coverage status, a verified record where durable storage is used, and a next cursor.\\n\\n\\n## 18. Workflow signature line\\n\\nAt the end of each substantive workshop response, repeat a compact signature line that preserves the ordered workflow inside the active conversation context. The signature is a live state marker, not decoration and not a substitute for the ledger.\\n\\nCanonical form:\\n\\n`WORKSHOP SIG | ORIENT \\u2192 BITE \\u2192 INVESTIGATE \\u2192 GEOMETRIZE \\u2192 CONNECT \\u2192 RECORD \\u2192 VERIFY \\u2192 NEXT | BRANCH: [branch] | CURRENT: [short task] | STATE: [status] | NEXT: [next operation]`\\n\\nRules:\\n- Keep the phase order stable unless experience or an explicit user decision warrants revision.\\n- Use only the phases relevant to the current bite, but do not silently reorder them.\\n- Keep branch, current task, state, and next operation short enough to remain scannable.\\n- State values should be plain and honest, for example: active, source-located, source-read, draft, verified, blocked, or parked.\\n- When a phase is skipped, mark it only when useful (for example, `CONNECT: deferred`); do not clutter every signature.\\n- Update the signature every substantive turn so the latest line captures the live position. Repeat it even when the turn is mainly procedural.\\n- If the session resumes after a gap or context shift, use the latest signature as a quick recovery pointer, then check the ledger and protocol for durable truth.\\n- The repository ledger remains authoritative for durable project state; the signature is a compact in-context working pointer.\\n\\n\\n## 19. Compact Unicode workflow notation\\n\\nThe workflow signature is a **Unicode glyph string**, not a chain of words or arrows. Each assigned glyph denotes one workflow phase; adjacency means ordinary succession. Therefore, do not print explicit sequential arrows between every glyph.\\n\\n### Current provisional phase assignments\\n\\n| Glyph | Phase |\\n|---|---|\\n| \\u2316 | Orient |\\n| \\u25c9 | Focus / select bite |\\n| \\u2315 | Investigate |\\n| \\u29d6 | Geometrize |\\n| \\u2933 | Connect |\\n| \\u25a3 | Record |\\n| \\u2713 | Verify |\\n| \\u21e2 | Next / deliberate transition |\\n\\nThese are provisional assignments for this workshop. They are not claimed to be registered in the general Unicode String-to-Glyph assignment workbook unless and until that workbook is deliberately updated. A glyph is one Unicode code point here; its semantic assignment is maintained by this protocol.\\n\\n### Linear sequence and control markers\\n\\n- `\\u2316\\u25c9\\u2315\\u29d6\\u2933\\u25a3\\u2713\\u21e2` means the ordered workflow, with implicit succession.\\n- A leading prefix records completed phases. For example, `\\u2316\\u25c9\\u21e2\\u2315\\u29d6\\u2933\\u25a3\\u2713\\u21e2` means orientation and bite selection are complete; the next phase is investigation, but execution pauses at the transition marker to deliberate how to proceed.\\n- `\\u21e2` is a deliberate transition / decision point, not a duplicate of ordinary adjacency.\\n- Reserve separate control glyphs for branching, cycling, joining, waiting, and stopping. Do not assign those operators casually or use them interchangeably.\\n- Branch, cycle, join, and other compound forms must be defined with small examples before use. Their grammar should distinguish the workflow graph from the linear sequence of phases.\\n- Keep the live signature compact: show the relevant phase string and, only when not inferable, a short current-position or branch annotation.\\n\\nDo not insert redundant arrows between successive phase glyphs. Do not expand the signature into prose unless explaining or revising the notation.\\n\\n\\n## 20. Pilot status and promotion boundary\\n\\nThis workshop is a **bespoke experimental pilot** of the workflow and Unicode-notation system. Its purpose is to discover what works in this particular collaboration and research context. Do not assume that its conventions, glyph assignments, operators, or session routine are generally useful or recommended for other users, projects, or assistants.\\n\\nTreat all current notation and workflow rules as pilot-local and provisional. Observe their practical performance, including clarity, compactness, recoverability, ambiguity, cognitive overhead, and ease of editing. Record useful evidence and friction, but do not prematurely generalize.\\n\\nPromotion beyond this workshop requires an explicit decision by the user after something noteworthy has emerged. Any proposed general recommendation should identify:\\n- the observed benefit and the problem it solves;\\n- the contexts in which it was actually tested;\\n- known limitations, failure cases, and accessibility/rendering concerns;\\n- which parts are reusable and which depend on this workshop's particular needs.\\n\\nUntil such a decision is made, keep the system local to this pilot and label it accordingly.\\n\\n\\n## 21. Pilot compound workflow operators (provisional)\\n\\nThe following operators extend the linear phase string. These are local experimental conventions, not general recommendations.\\n\\n### Operator vocabulary\\n\\n| Glyph | Name | Operational meaning |\\n|---|---|---|\\n| `\\u2442` | Fork | Split the current workflow into two or more independently tracked branches. |\\n| `\\u2443` | Rejoin | Reunite branches at a shared continuation after their outputs are available and reconciled. |\\n| `\\u27f3` | Cycle | Repeat the immediately enclosed or explicitly delimited sequence until its exit condition is met. |\\n| `\\u2026` | Await | Suspend this path pending an identified event, input, result, or condition. |\\n| `\\u25a0` | Halt | Stop this path. It is complete, cancelled, or deliberately parked only when the state annotation says which. |\\n\\n### Provisional syntax and examples\\n\\nUse braces to delimit the scope of a compound operation; braces are structural punctuation, not operators.\\n\\n- Fork: `\\u2315\\u2442{A: source review | B: geometric reconstruction}`\\n- Rejoin: `\\u2443{A+B}`\\n- Fork, work independently, then rejoin: `\\u2315\\u2442{A: sources | B: geometry}\\u2443\\u2933`\\n- Cycle: `\\u27f3{\\u2315\\u29d6}` means repeat investigation and geometrization as a cycle. Its stopping condition must be stated when it is not obvious.\\n- Await: `\\u2026[primary source located]` means this branch is suspended until that condition is met.\\n- Halt/park: `\\u25a0[parked: await later evidence]`; `\\u25a0[complete]` is a completed path.\\n\\n### Semantics and safeguards\\n\\n1. Fork creates distinct branches, not merely a list of topics. Each branch needs an identity and a defined task or output.\\n2. Rejoin is not automatic: it requires branch outputs to be available and reconciled. If a branch is abandoned, record that explicitly rather than silently treating it as complete.\\n3. A cycle needs a bounded repetition rule or an observable exit condition. Avoid unbounded repetition.\\n4. Await suspends only the marked path; other branches may continue.\\n5. Halt is terminal for that path unless explicitly reopened. The annotation distinguishes completed, cancelled, and parked states.\\n6. Nested or overlapping constructs are allowed in principle but deferred until simple cases have been used and tested.\\n7. These symbols are provisional one-code-point assignments in this workshop. They are not registered in the general glyph-assignment workbook.\\n\\n\\n## 22. Tock\\u2013tick hierarchy (pilot convention)\\n\\nUse **TOCK\\u2013TICK** as the canonical conceptual and organizational order. The tock is the larger work unit; ticks are its smaller constituent operations.\\n\\n- **Tock:** a bounded, coherent work package or main-level unit of progress. It has a purpose, scope, intended result, and completion/exit condition. A tock may contain multiple ticks and may itself contain subordinate tocks only when useful.\\n- **Tick:** a lower-order operation within a tock: a step, inspection, calculation, source read, diagram, branch action, or verification operation. Ticks help locate and sequence the work inside the larger unit.\\n- A tick is not automatically a completed tock. Completing several ticks may contribute to a tock, but the tock is complete only when its intended durable result and next cursor have been recorded and checked.\\n- The Unicode workflow string primarily tracks tick-level operations and their control structure. The Credenza's work tray and project/branch map organize tocks and their return points.\\n- Canonical sequence: **Tock \\u2192 ticks \\u2192 durable result \\u2192 tock closure/advance**. The Credenza may retain a larger queue of tocks while the active tock carries its own tick sequence.\\n- A tick marker is a position indicator, not evidence of completion. Tock closure requires an inspectable result, status, and next cursor.\\n- Keep the hierarchy shallow unless actual work requires nesting. Do not make every tick a tock or create a tock for every chat turn.\\n\\nThis replaces any wording or diagram that places Tick before Tock as the organizational hierarchy. It refines, rather than discards, the Credenza model's operational distinction between the tick as place marker and the tock as a completed bounded operation.\\n\\n\\n## 22. Tock\\u2013Tick hierarchy\\n\\nUse **Tock\\u2013Tick** as the canonical conceptual order. A Tock is the higher-level bounded work unit; Ticks are the lower-order operations and progress markers within it. This is an organizational hierarchy, not merely a temporal sequence.\\n\\n- **Tock:** a bounded work package, session objective, or coherent deliverable. It has a purpose, scope, expected result, and completion/exit condition. A Tock is complete only when its result is durable and its next cursor is recorded.\\n- **Tick:** a sub-operation, transition, inspection, or position marker within a Tock. A Tick records where the work is, not that the enclosing Tock is complete.\\n- **Tock\\u2013Tick relationship:** one Tock contains an ordered or compound arrangement of Ticks. A Tock may contain linear, branched, cyclic, waiting, or halted paths using the Unicode workflow operators.\\n- **Credenza relationship:** the Credenza organizes and routes Tocks, preserves their context and return cues, and keeps wider work visible. The glyph notation describes the internal Tick structure and live state of a Tock.\\n- **Closure:** finishing a Tick does not finish the Tock. Completing the Tock requires the durable-result and next-cursor test. A chat turn or tool call alone is neither.\\n\\nUse this hierarchy in all subsequent descriptions and records. Prefer the order **Tock \\u2192 Tick** when naming the system. Preserve existing source terminology when accurately describing the original Credenza document, but our pilot's adopted convention is Tock\\u2013Tick.\\n\\n\\n## 23. No undefined placeholders in live signatures\\n\\nLive workflow signatures must contain only defined operators, assigned phase glyphs, and meaningful labels or references. Do not insert empty slots, dummy branch labels, hypothetical states, or placeholder tokens merely to suggest possible future structure.\\n\\nException: a defined operator may point to a populated collection or registry whose membership is intentionally open or not yet exhaustive. The collection itself must exist and be identifiable; its members need not all be populated in advance.\\n\\nDistinguish:\\n- **Open collection:** a real, named, populated list that may accept additional entries.\\n- **Undefined placeholder:** an empty or invented token with no established referent; prohibited in signatures.\\n- **Uninstantiated possibility:** a workflow structure that may be useful later; discuss it in prose, not as if it were already part of the live signature.\\n\\nIf a branch, target, condition, or continuation is not yet defined, omit it from the signature. Define it first, then include it. Keep the signature an accurate representation of existing workflow state, not a sketch of imagined state.\\n\\n\\n## 24. Code-ledger grammar and maximal compression\\n\\nThe pilot adopts a compact code-ledger system. The **code ledger defines the meaning**; the repeated signature carries only the codes and their structural arrangement. The user and assistant need not memorize definitions. Consult the ledger whenever a code is unfamiliar or a meaning is uncertain.\\n\\n### Core grammar\\n\\n- Each assigned operation or workflow component receives a single Unicode code point wherever practical.\\n- Adjacent tokens are interpreted left to right by default. Ordinary succession needs no separator.\\n- Structural operators (such as fork, join, cycle, await, halt, and deliberate transition) retain their explicitly defined meanings.\\n- A compound structure may use a compact token reference rather than a written label. For example, `\\u2442{cu}` and `\\u2442{A: Credenza | B: Unicode notation}` are equivalent when `c` and `u` are defined in the code ledger and the branch ordering is unambiguous.\\n- Where ordering is more complex than left-to-right, use uppercase single-character ordering labels paired with lowercase component tokens, e.g. `\\u2442{AcBu}`: branch A contains component c; branch B contains component u. Uppercase labels identify ordering/branch positions; lowercase tokens identify the referenced components.\\n- Do not use undefined placeholders. A token may refer to an existing populated but extensible list.\\n- Prefer one-code-point representations over words, abbreviations, or multi-character labels when they remain unambiguous and practical.\\n- Avoid redundant punctuation and explanatory prose in the live signature. Keep definitions and interpretation in the code ledger.\\n\\n### Code-ledger requirements\\n\\nEach assignment must record: glyph/code point, canonical name, concise meaning, class (phase/operator/component/state), scope, assignment date/version, and any syntax or constraints. Codes are stable once adopted; revisions must be explicit and preserve prior meanings or record a supersession. Do not silently reassign a glyph.\\n\\n### Signature function\\n\\nThe repeated signature is a compact externalized memory of the current workflow structure and position. The signature plus code ledger, not memorization, preserves the system. The signature must describe actual instantiated work, ordered left-to-right unless marked otherwise.\\n\\n### Pilot build sequence\\n\\nFirst finish the initial workshop ledger and define the known work components that will form the near-term plan. At minimum, establish entries for category theory, biology, history/cultural lineage, computation, science bridges, and workshop systems, with finer subdivisions only when useful. Then encode the current plan as a compact signature using the assigned tokens and operators. This is a pilot-local convention; do not generalize without explicit promotion.\\n\\n\\n## 25. User-directed research ordering\\n\\nWhen the user supplies an explicit order, preserve it exactly, including non-monotonic numeric or alphabetic labels. Do not normalize, sort, or reinterpret labels as sequence order. Record each Tock/component code in the code ledger, then represent the chosen sequence left to right. The position marker `@` goes immediately before the next uncompleted component. Canonical Tock\\u2013tick hierarchy \\u2014 2026-11-24\\n\\nUser preference: **Tock\\u2013tick** is the canonical order. Tocks are the larger organizational/main-level work packages; ticks are lower-order operations contained within an active tock. The Unicode signature tracks tick-level position and sequencing inside the active tock.\\n\\nA tock closes only when its intended durable result, status, and next cursor are recorded and checked. This is a workshop-local refinement of the Credenza model, not a general recommendation.\\n\\n\\n## 15. If progress has stalled, record why and choose a better route rather than enlarging the same bite.\\n\\n**The target is substantive completion at a manageable scale.** Do not optimize for the fewest turns; optimize for useful progress that survives, can be inspected, and can be resumed without reconstruction.\\n\\n\\n## 17. Basic adaptable session routine\\n\\nUse this as the default rhythm for workshop sessions. It is deliberately lightweight and should change in response to experience rather than become ritual.\\n\\n### A. Orient\\nBriefly recover:\\n- the workshop's purpose and interpretive conventions;\\n- the current branch and next cursor in the ledger;\\n- any new user direction or relevant change to the controlling protocol;\\n- the relevant source/tool routes for this particular bite.\\n\\nFor a continuing session, check only what has changed. Do not repeat full onboarding without a reason.\\n\\n### B. Choose one substantial bite\\nSelect one coherent question or construction. Define:\\n- why it matters;\\n- the bounded source/concept set;\\n- the expected deliverable;\\n- the exit condition.\\n\\nDefault to one main line of work per session. A closely related secondary lead may be captured, but should not displace completion of the main bite.\\n\\n### C. Work it through\\nUse the sequence appropriate to the task:\\n- locate and inspect the source;\\n- explain the idea in ordinary language;\\n- reconstruct or draw its geometry;\\n- identify its dimensional structure;\\n- follow one or two of its strongest scientific, biological, computational, historical or cultural connections;\\n- identify important qualifications and open edges.\\n\\nDo not force every stage when it does not apply. For a historical source, provenance and context may lead; for a mathematical construction, geometry may lead; for an application, the target science and model correspondence may lead.\\n\\n### D. Leave a durable result\\nProduce one useful result: a reading note, geometric plate, source comparison, cross-disciplinary map, small tested tool, or bounded protocol improvement. Update the ledger with the source state and next cursor.\\n\\n### E. Verify and close\\nCheck source locators, geometric fidelity, claims, and any repository write. State what was actually completed and what remains open. End with one clear next operation.\\n\\n### F. Periodic adaptation\\nAfter every three to five substantive bites, briefly review:\\n- which steps are helping and which are overhead;\\n- whether bite sizes are consistently too small or too large;\\n- which research branches are producing useful connections;\\n- which tools or templates deserve improvement;\\n- whether the current order of work still makes sense.\\n\\nChange the routine only when experience gives a concrete reason. Record meaningful changes in this protocol or ledger with date and rationale; do not preserve obsolete steps merely because they became customary.\\n\\n**Session completion standard:** one meaningful result, honest source/coverage status, a verified record where durable storage is used, and a next cursor.\\n\\n\\n## 18. Workflow signature line\\n\\nAt the end of each substantive workshop response, repeat a compact signature line that preserves the ordered workflow inside the active conversation context. The signature is a live state marker, not decoration and not a substitute for the ledger.\\n\\nCanonical form:\\n\\n`WORKSHOP SIG | ORIENT \\u2192 BITE \\u2192 INVESTIGATE \\u2192 GEOMETRIZE \\u2192 CONNECT \\u2192 RECORD \\u2192 VERIFY \\u2192 NEXT | BRANCH: [branch] | CURRENT: [short task] | STATE: [status] | NEXT: [next operation]`\\n\\nRules:\\n- Keep the phase order stable unless experience or an explicit user decision warrants revision.\\n- Use only the phases relevant to the current bite, but do not silently reorder them.\\n- Keep branch, current task, state, and next operation short enough to remain scannable.\\n- State values should be plain and honest, for example: active, source-located, source-read, draft, verified, blocked, or parked.\\n- When a phase is skipped, mark it only when useful (for example, `CONNECT: deferred`); do not clutter every signature.\\n- Update the signature every substantive turn so the latest line captures the live position. Repeat it even when the turn is mainly procedural.\\n- If the session resumes after a gap or context shift, use the latest signature as a quick recovery pointer, then check the ledger and protocol for durable truth.\\n- The repository ledger remains authoritative for durable project state; the signature is a compact in-context working pointer.\\n\\n\\n## 19. Compact Unicode workflow notation\\n\\nThe workflow signature is a **Unicode glyph string**, not a chain of words or arrows. Each assigned glyph denotes one workflow phase; adjacency means ordinary succession. Therefore, do not print explicit sequential arrows between every glyph.\\n\\n### Current provisional phase assignments\\n\\n| Glyph | Phase |\\n|---|---|\\n| \\u2316 | Orient |\\n| \\u25c9 | Focus / select bite |\\n| \\u2315 | Investigate |\\n| \\u29d6 | Geometrize |\\n| \\u2933 | Connect |\\n| \\u25a3 | Record |\\n| \\u2713 | Verify |\\n| \\u21e2 | Next / deliberate transition |\\n\\nThese are provisional assignments for this workshop. They are not claimed to be registered in the general Unicode String-to-Glyph assignment workbook unless and until that workbook is deliberately updated. A glyph is one Unicode code point here; its semantic assignment is maintained by this protocol.\\n\\n### Linear sequence and control markers\\n\\n- `\\u2316\\u25c9\\u2315\\u29d6\\u2933\\u25a3\\u2713\\u21e2` means the ordered workflow, with implicit succession.\\n- A leading prefix records completed phases. For example, `\\u2316\\u25c9\\u21e2\\u2315\\u29d6\\u2933\\u25a3\\u2713\\u21e2` means orientation and bite selection are complete; the next phase is investigation, but execution pauses at the transition marker to deliberate how to proceed.\\n- `\\u21e2` is a deliberate transition / decision point, not a duplicate of ordinary adjacency.\\n- Reserve separate control glyphs for branching, cycling, joining, waiting, and stopping. Do not assign those operators casually or use them interchangeably.\\n- Branch, cycle, join, and other compound forms must be defined with small examples before use. Their grammar should distinguish the workflow graph from the linear sequence of phases.\\n- Keep the live signature compact: show the relevant phase string and, only when not inferable, a short current-position or branch annotation.\\n\\nDo not insert redundant arrows between successive phase glyphs. Do not expand the signature into prose unless explaining or revising the notation.\\n\\n\\n## 20. Pilot status and promotion boundary\\n\\nThis workshop is a **bespoke experimental pilot** of the workflow and Unicode-notation system. Its purpose is to discover what works in this particular collaboration and research context. Do not assume that its conventions, glyph assignments, operators, or session routine are generally useful or recommended for other users, projects, or assistants.\\n\\nTreat all current notation and workflow rules as pilot-local and provisional. Observe their practical performance, including clarity, compactness, recoverability, ambiguity, cognitive overhead, and ease of editing. Record useful evidence and friction, but do not prematurely generalize.\\n\\nPromotion beyond this workshop requires an explicit decision by the user after something noteworthy has emerged. Any proposed general recommendation should identify:\\n- the observed benefit and the problem it solves;\\n- the contexts in which it was actually tested;\\n- known limitations, failure cases, and accessibility/rendering concerns;\\n- which parts are reusable and which depend on this workshop's particular needs.\\n\\nUntil such a decision is made, keep the system local to this pilot and label it accordingly.\\n\\n\\n## 21. Pilot compound workflow operators (provisional)\\n\\nThe following operators extend the linear phase string. These are local experimental conventions, not general recommendations.\\n\\n### Operator vocabulary\\n\\n| Glyph | Name | Operational meaning |\\n|---|---|---|\\n| `\\u2442` | Fork | Split the current workflow into two or more independently tracked branches. |\\n| `\\u2443` | Rejoin | Reunite branches at a shared continuation after their outputs are available and reconciled. |\\n| `\\u27f3` | Cycle | Repeat the immediately enclosed or explicitly delimited sequence until its exit condition is met. |\\n| `\\u2026` | Await | Suspend this path pending an identified event, input, result, or condition. |\\n| `\\u25a0` | Halt | Stop this path. It is complete, cancelled, or deliberately parked only when the state annotation says which. |\\n\\n### Provisional syntax and examples\\n\\nUse braces to delimit the scope of a compound operation; braces are structural punctuation, not operators.\\n\\n- Fork: `\\u2315\\u2442{A: source review | B: geometric reconstruction}`\\n- Rejoin: `\\u2443{A+B}`\\n- Fork, work independently, then rejoin: `\\u2315\\u2442{A: sources | B: geometry}\\u2443\\u2933`\\n- Cycle: `\\u27f3{\\u2315\\u29d6}` means repeat investigation and geometrization as a cycle. Its stopping condition must be stated when it is not obvious.\\n- Await: `\\u2026[primary source located]` means this branch is suspended until that condition is met.\\n- Halt/park: `\\u25a0[parked: await later evidence]`; `\\u25a0[complete]` is a completed path.\\n\\n### Semantics and safeguards\\n\\n1. Fork creates distinct branches, not merely a list of topics. Each branch needs an identity and a defined task or output.\\n2. Rejoin is not automatic: it requires branch outputs to be available and reconciled. If a branch is abandoned, record that explicitly rather than silently treating it as complete.\\n3. A cycle needs a bounded repetition rule or an observable exit condition. Avoid unbounded repetition.\\n4. Await suspends only the marked path; other branches may continue.\\n5. Halt is terminal for that path unless explicitly reopened. The annotation distinguishes completed, cancelled, and parked states.\\n6. Nested or overlapping constructs are allowed in principle but deferred until simple cases have been used and tested.\\n7. These symbols are provisional one-code-point assignments in this workshop. They are not registered in the general glyph-assignment workbook.\\n\\n\\n## 22. Tock\\u2013tick hierarchy (pilot convention)\\n\\nUse **TOCK\\u2013TICK** as the canonical conceptual and organizational order. The tock is the larger work unit; ticks are its smaller constituent operations.\\n\\n- **Tock:** a bounded, coherent work package or main-level unit of progress. It has a purpose, scope, intended result, and completion/exit condition. A tock may contain multiple ticks and may itself contain subordinate tocks only when useful.\\n- **Tick:** a lower-order operation within a tock: a step, inspection, calculation, source read, diagram, branch action, or verification operation. Ticks help locate and sequence the work inside the larger unit.\\n- A tick is not automatically a completed tock. Completing several ticks may contribute to a tock, but the tock is complete only when its intended durable result and next cursor have been recorded and checked.\\n- The Unicode workflow string primarily tracks tick-level operations and their control structure. The Credenza's work tray and project/branch map organize tocks and their return points.\\n- Canonical sequence: **Tock \\u2192 ticks \\u2192 durable result \\u2192 tock closure/advance**. The Credenza may retain a larger queue of tocks while the active tock carries its own tick sequence.\\n- A tick marker is a position indicator, not evidence of completion. Tock closure requires an inspectable result, status, and next cursor.\\n- Keep the hierarchy shallow unless actual work requires nesting. Do not make every tick a tock or create a tock for every chat turn.\\n\\nThis replaces any wording or diagram that places Tick before Tock as the organizational hierarchy. It refines, rather than discards, the Credenza model's operational distinction between the tick as place marker and the tock as a completed bounded operation.\\n\\n\\n## 22. Tock\\u2013Tick hierarchy\\n\\nUse **Tock\\u2013Tick** as the canonical conceptual order. A Tock is the higher-level bounded work unit; Ticks are the lower-order operations and progress markers within it. This is an organizational hierarchy, not merely a temporal sequence.\\n\\n- **Tock:** a bounded work package, session objective, or coherent deliverable. It has a purpose, scope, expected result, and completion/exit condition. A Tock is complete only when its result is durable and its next cursor is recorded.\\n- **Tick:** a sub-operation, transition, inspection, or position marker within a Tock. A Tick records where the work is, not that the enclosing Tock is complete.\\n- **Tock\\u2013Tick relationship:** one Tock contains an ordered or compound arrangement of Ticks. A Tock may contain linear, branched, cyclic, waiting, or halted paths using the Unicode workflow operators.\\n- **Credenza relationship:** the Credenza organizes and routes Tocks, preserves their context and return cues, and keeps wider work visible. The glyph notation describes the internal Tick structure and live state of a Tock.\\n- **Closure:** finishing a Tick does not finish the Tock. Completing the Tock requires the durable-result and next-cursor test. A chat turn or tool call alone is neither.\\n\\nUse this hierarchy in all subsequent descriptions and records. Prefer the order **Tock \\u2192 Tick** when naming the system. Preserve existing source terminology when accurately describing the original Credenza document, but our pilot's adopted convention is Tock\\u2013Tick.\\n\\n\\n## 23. No undefined placeholders in live signatures\\n\\nLive workflow signatures must contain only defined operators, assigned phase glyphs, and meaningful labels or references. Do not insert empty slots, dummy branch labels, hypothetical states, or placeholder tokens merely to suggest possible future structure.\\n\\nException: a defined operator may point to a populated collection or registry whose membership is intentionally open or not yet exhaustive. The collection itself must exist and be identifiable; its members need not all be populated in advance.\\n\\nDistinguish:\\n- **Open collection:** a real, named, populated list that may accept additional entries.\\n- **Undefined placeholder:** an empty or invented token with no established referent; prohibited in signatures.\\n- **Uninstantiated possibility:** a workflow structure that may be useful later; discuss it in prose, not as if it were already part of the live signature.\\n\\nIf a branch, target, condition, or continuation is not yet defined, omit it from the signature. Define it first, then include it. Keep the signature an accurate representation of existing workflow state, not a sketch of imagined state.\\n\\n\\n## 24. Code-ledger grammar and maximal compression\\n\\nThe pilot adopts a compact code-ledger system. The **code ledger defines the meaning**; the repeated signature carries only the codes and their structural arrangement. The user and assistant need not memorize definitions. Consult the ledger whenever a code is unfamiliar or a meaning is uncertain.\\n\\n### Core grammar\\n\\n- Each assigned operation or workflow component receives a single Unicode code point wherever practical.\\n- Adjacent tokens are interpreted left to right by default. Ordinary succession needs no separator.\\n- Structural operators (such as fork, join, cycle, await, halt, and deliberate transition) retain their explicitly defined meanings.\\n- A compound structure may use a compact token reference rather than a written label. For example, `\\u2442{cu}` and `\\u2442{A: Credenza | B: Unicode notation}` are equivalent when `c` and `u` are defined in the code ledger and the branch ordering is unambiguous.\\n- Where ordering is more complex than left-to-right, use uppercase single-character ordering labels paired with lowercase component tokens, e.g. `\\u2442{AcBu}`: branch A contains component c; branch B contains component u. Uppercase labels identify ordering/branch positions; lowercase tokens identify the referenced components.\\n- Do not use undefined placeholders. A token may refer to an existing populated but extensible list.\\n- Prefer one-code-point representations over words, abbreviations, or multi-character labels when they remain unambiguous and practical.\\n- Avoid redundant punctuation and explanatory prose in the live signature. Keep definitions and interpretation in the code ledger.\\n\\n### Code-ledger requirements\\n\\nEach assignment must record: glyph/code point, canonical name, concise meaning, class (phase/operator/component/state), scope, assignment date/version, and any syntax or constraints. Codes are stable once adopted; revisions must be explicit and preserve prior meanings or record a supersession. Do not silently reassign a glyph.\\n\\n### Signature function\\n\\nThe repeated signature is a compact externalized memory of the current workflow structure and position. The signature plus code ledger, not memorization, preserves the system. The signature must describe actual instantiated work, ordered left-to-right unless marked otherwise.\\n\\n### Pilot build sequence\\n\\nFirst finish the initial workshop ledger and define the known work components that will form the near-term plan. At minimum, establish entries for category theory, biology, history/cultural lineage, computation, science bridges, and workshop systems, with finer subdivisions only when useful. Then encode the current plan as a compact signature using the assigned tokens and operators. This is a pilot-local convention; do not generalize without explicit promotion.\\n\\n\\n## 25. User-directed research ordering\\n\\nWhen the user supplies an explicit order, preserve it exactly, including non-monotonic numeric or alphabetic labels. Do not normalize, sort, or reinterpret labels as sequence order. Record each Tock/component code in the code ledger, then represent the chosen sequence left to right. The position marker `@` goes immediately before the next uncompleted component. Mark a component complete only after its stated completion check passes.\\n\\n\\n## 26. Research ordering: coequal streams and emergent connections\\n\\nDo not force user-described coequal subjects into a serial order. Encode them as coequal or parallel branches when appropriate. Distinguish planned research domains from connections that emerge during investigation. Cross-disciplinary exploration should follow evidence and conceptual affordances from material actually reviewed; do not impose a predetermined closed list or substitute a modelling agenda for broader connection-finding. Workshop-system evaluation is ongoing maintenance unless the user explicitly makes it a separate research stage.\\n\",\"sha\":\"09aa2822b45c30b6ec84137810e679214c8a1551\",\"message\":\"Record coequal-stream and emergent-connection rule\"}}"

What does the construction allow us to see that a lower-dimensional or flattened description conceals?\\n\\nUse diagrams early. Prefer a sequence of views, sections, projections, deformations and dimensional lifts over a wall of formal definitions. A diagram must be faithful to the specified object; mark schematic elements and unspecified geometry rather than inventing them.\\n\\nFor higher-dimensional category theory, explicitly visualize objects, one-dimensional morphisms, two-dimensional morphisms, three-dimensional morphisms and further-dimensional morphisms where the model permits. Explain source/target, composition, invertibility and coherence geometrically. Do not assume every model has identical strictness or composition rules.\\n\\n## 5. Cross-disciplinary opportunity capture\\n\\nEvery substantial mathematical source should be scanned for direct applications and possible natural extensions beyond pure mathematics. Use a broad search radius.\\n\\nCapture opportunities in one of three classes:\\n\\n- DIRECT_APPLICATION: source explicitly applies the construction to another field.\\n- NATURAL_EXTENSION: a plausible, structurally motivated extension to another field, with the mapping to be worked out.\\n- CULTURAL_TRANSMISSION: the concept appears in philosophical, spiritualist, literary, science-fiction, popular-science or fannish culture.\\n\\nFor each opportunity record:\\n- source construction and exact location;\\n- target discipline and candidate phenomenon;\\n- proposed geometric correspondence;\\n- what is shared and what differs;\\n- missing mechanism, assumptions or data;\\n- next discriminating reading, diagram, calculation or observation.\\n\\nDo not restrict discovery to keyword matches. Follow mathematical machinery across disciplines: for example, braids and configuration spaces toward molecular biology; geometric morphisms and transformations toward developmental or evolutionary pathways; topology toward neural and physiological networks; category-theoretic structures toward computation and information systems.\\n\\n## 6. Cultural and speculative literature protocol\\n\\nRead spiritualist, occult, speculative, fictional and fannish sources as legitimate historical/cultural evidence, not automatically as scientific evidence.\\n\\nFor each relevant item record:\\n- the original scientific or philosophical concept it invokes or may have adapted;\\n- the date and route of transmission where recoverable;\\n- how the concept changes in the new setting;\\n- whether the treatment is analogy, fictional device, metaphysical claim, reported phenomenon or technical proposal;\\n- points of contact with scientific concepts;\\n- unsupported or contradictory claims, identified specifically rather than by blanket dismissal.\\n\\nKeep three tracks visible:\\n1. scientific/mathematical content;\\n2. cultural transformation and reception;\\n3. speculative departure.\\n\\nFictional and fannish expressions may be evidence of an idea's reach, persistence or transformation, even when they are not evidence that the underlying scientific claim is true. Treat “time-binding,” “Fans are Slans,” and related expressions as cultural-historical leads; investigate their contexts and conceptual ancestry without assuming a single origin or meaning before source inspection.\\n\\n## 7. Research workflow: WAKE → ROUTE → READ → GEOMETRIZE → BRIDGE → RECORD → REVIEW\\n\\n### WAKE / CHECK\\nAt the start of a materially new session:\\n- identify the workshop's current scope and next cursor;\\n- check for relevant new user direction and durable workshop updates;\\n- inspect only the controlling guidance needed for the task;\\n- identify whether the task is historical, mathematical, geometric, cross-disciplinary, cultural, or operational.\\n\\nUse state-sensitive orientation. A new or stale session gets a fuller orientation; a warm session checks deltas and the current task rather than rereading everything ritualistically.\\n\\n### ROUTE\\nSelect the smallest useful route:\\n- nLab / n-Category Café for mathematical concepts and intellectual discussion;\\n- HSH_RESOURCES for supporting literature and historical collections;\\n- scholarly databases and primary sources for external verification;\\n- science-specific literature for cross-disciplinary follow-through;\\n- original fiction, fandom archives and historical documents for cultural transmission.\\n\\nBefore asking the user to repeat an available detail, search registered workshop materials and accessible repositories.\\n\\n### READ\\nLocate, triage, inspect and cite sources. Record what was actually read. Search results are discovery, not source comprehension.\\n\\n### GEOMETRIZE\\nTranslate the key construction into a visual/geometric account. Record dimensions, embeddings, maps, transformations, composition and limitations.\\n\\n### BRIDGE\\nActively seek:\\n- direct scientific applications;\\n- natural extensions to other sciences;\\n- historical/cultural transmission;\\n- useful counterexamples and constraints;\\n- neighboring mathematical tools that make the geometry more visible.\\n\\n### RECORD\\nLeave a durable bounded result with source pointers, reading states, geometric account, cross-disciplinary leads, unresolved questions and next cursor.\\n\\n### REVIEW\\nCheck whether the result answers the task, whether the geometry matches the source, whether claims are properly sourced, and whether the next step is still worth pursuing.\\n\\n## 8. Branching and work coordination\\n\\nUse a small number of clearly named work branches, not one undifferentiated reading queue:\\n\\n- MATH-GEOMETRY: category theory, topology, homotopy and dimensional visualization.\\n- HISTORY-CULTURE: Hinton, Victorian hyperspace, spiritualism, science fiction and fandom.\\n- BIO-SCIENCE: biology, physiology, evolution, development and related disciplines.\\n- COMPUTATION: computer science, information, networks, logic and AI.\\n- SCIENCE-BRIDGES: physics, chemistry, earth/planetary and other scientific applications.\\n- WORKSHOP-SYSTEMS: operating methods, tooling, indexes and continuity.\\n\\nBranches may run in parallel when tasks are genuinely separable. Keep a common source/terminology map, but preserve independent interpretations until each branch has recorded its own evidence. Do not mistake multiple workers reading the same summary or sharing the same prompt for independent confirmation.\\n\\nEach task quantum should have:\\n- one parent question/goal;\\n- one bounded operation;\\n- named source set or discovery bounds;\\n- expected output;\\n- a completion/exit condition;\\n- a next cursor.\\n\\nNested work must have a parent, depth limit, exit condition and orphan/fallback policy. A branch should close, merge or park when it stops generating useful evidence, constraints, clarification or capability.\\n\\n## 9. Tocktick-inspired temporal coordination\\n\\nUse the following general operational concepts as workshop conventions, without importing private legal material:\\n\\n- SEED: create a reusable question, diagram, source packet, tool, test or schema for downstream use.\\n- YIELD: deliberately release attention from a branch while others use the seed or evidence accumulates.\\n- AWAIT: resume when a defined evidence/state condition changes, rather than repeatedly checking an unchanged blocker.\\n- ACCUMULATE: collect outputs with their provenance and exposure metadata.\\n- RENDEZVOUS: return when a useful threshold is reached or a time cap expires.\\n- REJOIN: synthesize, audit, compare, improve the seed or launch the next bounded operation.\\n\\nPrefer state-based return thresholds with a time cap. Never let a parked branch disappear: retain its purpose, current state, return condition and displaced responsibility. Do not create recurring automations merely because a workflow could recur; use them only when the user asks or an existing authorized recurrence is explicitly assigned.\\n\\n## 10. Tools, scripts and derived infrastructure\\n\\nUse available connected tools, repository indexes, search tools, paper extractors, scripts and computational tools before improvising manual workarounds. Discover and read tool instructions before use.\\n\\nFor any script or repository operation:\\n- declare exact repositories and paths read/written;\\n- identify outputs as source, derived, generated, append-only or semantic;\\n- record run ID, source commit/ref, tool version and configuration;\\n- exclude private/quarantined material before reading or indexing where required;\\n- never overwrite raw sources during extraction or analysis;\\n- use fresh-base, non-force writes and compare-and-swap/current blob SHA for semantic edits;\\n- use per-run temporary paths and atomic finalization where possible;\\n- validate generated coverage and independently read back writes;\\n- never treat successful scheduling, execution or state restoration as proof that the requested artifact was delivered.\\n\\nPrefer existing scripts and adapters over duplicating functionality. Use dry-run before broad or destructive operations. Add a new parser only when an inventory reveals a recurring unmet need.\\n\\n## 11. Citation and provenance workflow\\n\\nUse the sequence:\\n\\nclaim / geometric statement → citation need → candidate sources → inspect source → exact page/section anchor → verified citation → place citation\\n\\nA bibliography identifies available sources; it does not establish that a source supports a particular claim.\\n\\nFor each important claim, capture:\\n- exact claim being supported;\\n- citation role (background, definition, application, empirical result, prior treatment, cultural context, constraint);\\n- source identity and page/section anchor;\\n- review state;\\n- short explanation of why it supports the claim.\\n\\nUse original external citations in public-facing writing. Internal repository paths and hashes are for recovery and audit, not substitutes for bibliographic citations. Do not cite a source for more than it actually says.\\n\\n## 12. This is the workshop's interpretive lens. When a particular construction's dimensional character is unclear, describe the actual geometry and distinguish mathematical dimension from physical spatial dimension without dropping the dimensional reading.\\n\\nThe historical lineage from nineteenth-century higher-dimensional thought through spiritualist appropriation and later mathematical/physical usage is a working premise for interpretation. Read the literature accordingly; do not turn establishing that premise into a prerequisite. Preserve historical differences and identify where particular authors or constructions elaborate, transform, or depart from scientific concepts.\\n\\n## 2. Source and evidence handling\\n\\nRaw source artifacts remain canonical. Indexes, summaries, extracted text, annotations, diagrams and comparison tables are derived aids.\\n\\nFor every substantive source used, retain as applicable:\\n\\n- stable source ID and exact repository/path or external URL;\\n- author, title, publication venue and date;\\n- source date separately from ingest/access date;\\n- page, section, figure, timestamp or other locator;\\n- source type (primary, scholarly secondary, technical exposition, popular account, fiction, fandom artefact, generated/index material);\\n- access and review state;\\n- extraction method and quality notes where relevant;\\n- short account of what the source actually contributes.\\n\\nDo not infer claim-level content from filenames, tags, search snippets or index placement. Follow wayfinding records to the source. Search/index silence is not evidence of absence. Distinguish source observation from interpretation, reconstruction, analogy and speculation.\\n\\n### Reading states\\n\\n- LOCATED: path or bibliographic record found.\\n- TRIAGED: abstract, contents or bounded excerpt assessed for relevance.\\n- PARTIAL: selected sections/pages read and cited.\\n- FULL: source read to the depth required for its intended use.\\n- EXTRACTED: text/figure/table extraction completed with provenance and quality noted. This is an access state, not a comprehension state.\\n- VISUALIZED: relevant geometric construction reconstructed as a diagram/model with conventions stated.\\n- TESTED: a computational, geometrical or empirical check has actually been run.\\n- SYNTHESIZED: contribution integrated into a source-backed workshop note.\\n\\nA source may have several orthogonal states. Never promote a snippet or machine-generated summary into a full reading.\\n\\n## 4. Geometric-first reading and visualization\\n\\nFor each important mathematical construction, answer:\\n\\n1. What is the geometric object?\\n2. What is its ambient space and dimension?\\n3. What is its intrinsic dimension?\\n4. How is it embedded, projected, sliced, intersected, fibered, connected or transformed?\\n5. What metric, topology, orientation, coordinates and boundary conditions are actually specified?\\n6. What are the permitted transformations and compositions?\\n7. What is a physical spatial dimension, a spacetime dimension, a configuration/parameter-space dimension, or a dimension internal to the mathematical structure?\\n8. What does the construction allow us to see that a lower-dimensional or flattened description conceals?\\n\\nUse diagrams early. Prefer a sequence of views, sections, projections, deformations and dimensional lifts over a wall of formal definitions. A diagram must be faithful to the specified object; mark schematic elements and unspecified geometry rather than inventing them.\\n\\nFor higher-dimensional category theory, explicitly visualize objects, one-dimensional morphisms, two-dimensional morphisms, three-dimensional morphisms and further-dimensional morphisms where the model permits. Explain source/target, composition, invertibility and coherence geometrically. Do not assume every model has identical strictness or composition rules.\\n\\n## 5. Cross-disciplinary opportunity capture\\n\\nEvery substantial mathematical source should be scanned for direct applications and possible natural extensions beyond pure mathematics. Use a broad search radius.\\n\\nCapture opportunities in one of three classes:\\n\\n- DIRECT_APPLICATION: source explicitly applies the construction to another field.\\n- NATURAL_EXTENSION: a plausible, structurally motivated extension to another field, with the mapping to be worked out.\\n- CULTURAL_TRANSMISSION: the concept appears in philosophical, spiritualist, literary, science-fiction, popular-science or fannish culture.\\n\\nFor each opportunity record:\\n- source construction and exact location;\\n- target discipline and candidate phenomenon;\\n- proposed geometric correspondence;\\n- what is shared and what differs;\\n- missing mechanism, assumptions or data;\\n- next discriminating reading, diagram, calculation or observation.\\n\\nDo not restrict discovery to keyword matches. Follow mathematical machinery across disciplines: for example, braids and configuration spaces toward molecular biology; geometric morphisms and transformations toward developmental or evolutionary pathways; topology toward neural and physiological networks; category-theoretic structures toward computation and information systems.\\n\\n## 6. Cultural and speculative literature protocol\\n\\nRead spiritualist, occult, speculative, fictional and fannish sources as legitimate historical/cultural evidence, not automatically as scientific evidence.\\n\\nFor each relevant item record:\\n- the original scientific or philosophical concept it invokes or may have adapted;\\n- the date and route of transmission where recoverable;\\n- how the concept changes in the new setting;\\n- whether the treatment is analogy, fictional device, metaphysical claim, reported phenomenon or technical proposal;\\n- points of contact with scientific concepts;\\n- unsupported or contradictory claims, identified specifically rather than by blanket dismissal.\\n\\nKeep three tracks visible:\\n1. scientific/mathematical content;\\n2. cultural transformation and reception;\\n3. speculative departure.\\n\\nFictional and fannish expressions may be evidence of an idea's reach, persistence or transformation, even when they are not evidence that the underlying scientific claim is true. Treat \\u201ctime-binding,\\u201d \\u201cFans are Slans,\\u201d and related expressions as cultural-historical leads; investigate their contexts and conceptual ancestry without assuming a single origin or meaning before source inspection.\\n\\n## 7. Research workflow: WAKE \\u2192 ROUTE \\u2192 READ \\u2192 GEOMETRIZE \\u2192 BRIDGE \\u2192 RECORD \\u2192 REVIEW\\n\\n### WAKE / CHECK\\nAt the start of a materially new session:\\n- identify the workshop's current scope and next cursor;\\n- check for relevant new user direction and durable workshop updates;\\n- inspect only the controlling guidance needed for the task;\\n- identify whether the task is historical, mathematical, geometric, cross-disciplinary, cultural, or operational.\\n\\nUse state-sensitive orientation. A new or stale session gets a fuller orientation; a warm session checks deltas and the current task rather than rereading everything ritualistically.\\n\\n### ROUTE\\nSelect the smallest useful route:\\n- nLab / n-Category Caf\\u00e9 for mathematical concepts and intellectual discussion;\\n- HSH_RESOURCES for supporting literature and historical collections;\\n- scholarly databases and primary sources for external verification;\\n- science-specific literature for cross-disciplinary follow-through;\\n- original fiction, fandom archives and historical documents for cultural transmission.\\n\\nBefore asking the user to repeat an available detail, search registered workshop materials and accessible repositories.\\n\\n### READ\\nLocate, triage, inspect and cite sources. Record what was actually read. Search results are discovery, not source comprehension.\\n\\n### GEOMETRIZE\\nTranslate the key construction into a visual/geometric account. Record dimensions, embeddings, maps, transformations, composition and limitations.\\n\\n### BRIDGE\\nActively seek:\\n- direct scientific applications;\\n- natural extensions to other sciences;\\n- historical/cultural transmission;\\n- useful counterexamples and constraints;\\n- neighboring mathematical tools that make the geometry more visible.\\n\\n### RECORD\\nLeave a durable bounded result with source pointers, reading states, geometric account, cross-disciplinary leads, unresolved questions and next cursor.\\n\\n### REVIEW\\nCheck whether the result answers the task, whether the geometry matches the source, whether claims are properly sourced, and whether the next step is still worth pursuing.\\n\\n## 8. Branching and work coordination\\n\\nUse a small number of clearly named work branches, not one undifferentiated reading queue:\\n\\n- MATH-GEOMETRY: category theory, topology, homotopy and dimensional visualization.\\n- HISTORY-CULTURE: Hinton, Victorian hyperspace, spiritualism, science fiction and fandom.\\n- BIO-SCIENCE: biology, physiology, evolution, development and related disciplines.\\n- COMPUTATION: computer science, information, networks, logic and AI.\\n- SCIENCE-BRIDGES: physics, chemistry, earth/planetary and other scientific applications.\\n- WORKSHOP-SYSTEMS: operating methods, tooling, indexes and continuity.\\n\\nBranches may run in parallel when tasks are genuinely separable. Keep a common source/terminology map, but preserve independent interpretations until each branch has recorded its own evidence. Do not mistake multiple workers reading the same summary or sharing the same prompt for independent confirmation.\\n\\nEach task quantum should have:\\n- one parent question/goal;\\n- one bounded operation;\\n- named source set or discovery bounds;\\n- expected output;\\n- a completion/exit condition;\\n- a next cursor.\\n\\nNested work must have a parent, depth limit, exit condition and orphan/fallback policy. A branch should close, merge or park when it stops generating useful evidence, constraints, clarification or capability.\\n\\n## 9. Tocktick-inspired temporal coordination\\n\\nUse the following general operational concepts as workshop conventions, without importing private legal material:\\n\\n- SEED: create a reusable question, diagram, source packet, tool, test or schema for downstream use.\\n- YIELD: deliberately release attention from a branch while others use the seed or evidence accumulates.\\n- AWAIT: resume when a defined evidence/state condition changes, rather than repeatedly checking an unchanged blocker.\\n- ACCUMULATE: collect outputs with their provenance and exposure metadata.\\n- RENDEZVOUS: return when a useful threshold is reached or a time cap expires.\\n- REJOIN: synthesize, audit, compare, improve the seed or launch the next bounded operation.\\n\\nPrefer state-based return thresholds with a time cap. Never let a parked branch disappear: retain its purpose, current state, return condition and displaced responsibility. Do not create recurring automations merely because a workflow could recur; use them only when the user asks or an existing authorized recurrence is explicitly assigned.\\n\\n## 10. Tools, scripts and derived infrastructure\\n\\nUse available connected tools, repository indexes, search tools, paper extractors, scripts and computational tools before improvising manual workarounds. Discover and read tool instructions before use.\\n\\nFor any script or repository operation:\\n- declare exact repositories and paths read/written;\\n- identify outputs as source, derived, generated, append-only or semantic;\\n- record run ID, source commit/ref, tool version and configuration;\\n- exclude private/quarantined material before reading or indexing where required;\\n- never overwrite raw sources during extraction or analysis;\\n- use fresh-base, non-force writes and compare-and-swap/current blob SHA for semantic edits;\\n- use per-run temporary paths and atomic finalization where possible;\\n- validate generated coverage and independently read back writes;\\n- never treat successful scheduling, execution or state restoration as proof that the requested artifact was delivered.\\n\\nPrefer existing scripts and adapters over duplicating functionality. Use dry-run before broad or destructive operations. Add a new parser only when an inventory reveals a recurring unmet need.\\n\\n## 11. Citation and provenance workflow\\n\\nUse the sequence:\\n\\nclaim / geometric statement \\u2192 citation need \\u2192 candidate sources \\u2192 inspect source \\u2192 exact page/section anchor \\u2192 verified citation \\u2192 place citation\\n\\nA bibliography identifies available sources; it does not establish that a source supports a particular claim.\\n\\nFor each important claim, capture:\\n- exact claim being supported;\\n- citation role (background, definition, application, empirical result, prior treatment, cultural context, constraint);\\n- source identity and page/section anchor;\\n- review state;\\n- short explanation of why it supports the claim.\\n\\nUse original external citations in public-facing writing. Internal repository paths and hashes are for recovery and audit, not substitutes for bibliographic citations. Do not cite a source for more than it actually says.\\n\\n## 12. Epistemic and interpretation conventions\\n\\nKeep separate:\\n- direct source statement;\\n- established mathematical/scientific result;\\n- Nathan's workshop premise or instruction;\\n- assistant's interpretation;\\n- reconstructed geometry;\\n- natural extension;\\n- speculative conjecture;\\n- fictional or cultural representation.\\n\\nThe workshop's agreed dimensional reading is an interpretive convention. Do not quietly reframe it as a claim that every author explicitly intended physical spatial dimensions. Instead, read the terminology through the agreed lens and examine the construction's actual dimensional content.\\n\\nFor spiritualist, occult and fictional material, skepticism applies to factual/scientific claims, not to its value as evidence of cultural transmission or conceptual reception.\\n\\nDo not use \\u201cproof\\u201d loosely. Name the actual status: source statement, definition, derivation, visualization, numerical check, empirical observation, proposed mechanism or speculation.\\n\\n## 13. Deliverable format\\n\\nA normal substantive reading note should contain:\\n\\n1. Question / why this source matters\\n2. Source and reading state\\n3. Geometric picture\\n4. Dimensional account\\n5. What the author actually contributes\\n6. Direct applications / natural extensions\\n7. Historical or cultural connections\\n8. Limitations, mismatches and open edges\\n9. Next bounded operation\\n\\nA workshop synthesis should connect several reading notes while retaining source-level references and differences among authors.\\n\\n## 14. Victorian-to-modern lineage: organize Hinton, Abbott, Whately Smith, spiritualist and psychical-research material, professional reception, and the modern mathematical vocabulary.\\n3.
