Victorian-to-modern lineage: organize Hinton, Abbott, Whately Smith, spiritualist and psychical-research material, professional reception, and the modern mathematical vocabulary.\\n3. First implementation principle\\n\\nStart with durable workshop navigation, a compact source/idea ledger, and reusable reading-note templates. Do not build a large switchboard, database or automation before actual use demonstrates the need. Improve the system through bounded experiments, explicit failure notes and transfer to a second task.\\n\\n**Current next operation:** establish the workshop workspace and source/idea ledger, then begin the nLab visual atlas with the geometry of points, paths and homotopies.\\n\\n\\n## 16. Work-bite sizing and stopping rule\\n\\n**Standing instruction from Nathan, 2026-11-24:** take reasonable-sized bites. Avoid both tiny, low-value nibbles and oversized chunks likely to hang, sprawl, or end without a verified result.\\n\\nA normal work bite should produce one coherent result, not merely touch a large number of files or topics.\\n\\n### Bite-size test\\n\\nBefore starting, define:\\n\\n- **Question:** one central question or tightly related cluster.\\n- **Scope:** a bounded set of sources, concepts, or operations.\\n- **Output:** one useful artifact, explanation, diagram, comparison, or verified state change.\\n- **Exit condition:** what will count as a complete bite.\\n- **Next cursor:** the most valuable next operation, left explicit.\\n\\nPrefer a bite that can be completed, checked and recorded within one focused work session. As a practical default, use roughly 2\\u20135 primary sources or one substantial source plus its essential context, one main geometric construction, or one coherent workflow improvement. This is a heuristic, not a quota. A genuinely short source may be paired with a related source; a difficult source may need to be divided by chapter, construction or central result.\\n\\n### Avoid undersized bites\\n\\nDo not spend a full work session merely:\\n- locating one obvious source when the source can also be triaged;\\n- adding a single pointer without checking its target;\\n- repeating orientation or planning without advancing the work;\\n- reporting a problem without making the bounded repair that is already within scope.\\n\\nCombine adjacent micro-operations when they naturally form one result: locate \\u2192 inspect \\u2192 explain; define \\u2192 diagram \\u2192 check; edit \\u2192 read back \\u2192 record.\\n\\n### Avoid oversized bites\\n\\nDo not try to:\\n- survey an entire discipline in one pass;\\n- digest a very large archive or wiki as one undifferentiated task;\\n- build a large database, switchboard, scraper or automation before demonstrating the recurring need;\\n- pursue every branch surfaced by an interesting source in the same turn;\\n- make a long chain of dependent repository changes without intermediate validation.\\n\\nSplit such work into staged bites with clear dependencies and durable intermediate outputs. Each stage should be independently useful and resumable.\\n\\n### Chunking and execution safeguards\\n\\nFor large files, archives, or source collections:\\n1. inspect structure and metadata first;\\n2. select a bounded section or source family;\\n3. process it in chunks with stable source locators;\\n4. record completed coverage and remaining coverage;\\n5. verify the output before moving to the next chunk.\\n\\nFor code, searches, and repository writes, use bounded batches and inspect results between stages. Avoid large parallel bursts when they make failures hard to isolate or outputs likely to be truncated. Prefer several small, well-verified batches to one massive call.\\n\\n### Stop / split / continue decision\\n\\nAt each natural boundary, ask:\\n- Has the stated output been produced?\\n- Is it verified to the level required?\\n- Is the next operation a necessary part of this same result, or a separate branch?\\n- Is additional work still producing useful evidence, clarity, capability or a discriminating test?\\n\\nIf the bite is complete, stop and leave the next cursor. If the remaining operation is substantial but separable, split it. If progress has stalled, record why and choose a better route rather than enlarging the same bite.\\n\\n**The target is substantive completion at a manageable scale.** Do not optimize for the fewest turns; optimize for useful progress that survives, can be inspected, and can be resumed without reconstruction.\\n\\n\\n## 17. Basic adaptable session routine\\n\\nUse this as the default rhythm for workshop sessions. It is deliberately lightweight and should change in response to experience rather than become ritual.\\n\\n### A. Orient\\nBriefly recover:\\n- the workshop's purpose and interpretive conventions;\\n- the current branch and next cursor in the ledger;\\n- any new user direction or relevant change to the controlling protocol;\\n- the relevant source/tool routes for this particular bite.\\n\\nFor a continuing session, check only what has changed. Do not repeat full onboarding without a reason.\\n\\n### B. Choose one substantial bite\\nSelect one coherent question or construction. Define:\\n- why it matters;\\n- the bounded source/concept set;\\n- the expected deliverable;\\n- the exit condition.\\n\\nDefault to one main line of work per session. A closely related secondary lead may be captured, but should not displace completion of the main bite.\\n\\n### C. Work it through\\nUse the sequence appropriate to the task:\\n- locate and inspect the source;\\n- explain the idea in ordinary language;\\n- reconstruct or draw its geometry;\\n- identify its dimensional structure;\\n- follow one or two of its strongest scientific, biological, computational, historical or cultural connections;\\n- identify important qualifications and open edges.\\n\\nDo not force every stage when it does not apply. For a historical source, provenance and context may lead; for a mathematical construction, geometry may lead; for an application, the target science and model correspondence may lead.\\n\\n### D. Leave a durable result\\nProduce one useful result: a reading note, geometric plate, source comparison, cross-disciplinary map, small tested tool, or bounded protocol improvement. Update the ledger with the source state and next cursor.\\n\\n### E. Verify and close\\nCheck source locators, geometric fidelity, claims, and any repository write. State what was actually completed and what remains open. End with one clear next operation.\\n\\n### F. Periodic adaptation\\nAfter every three to five substantive bites, briefly review:\\n- which steps are helping and which are overhead;\\n- whether bite sizes are consistently too small or too large;\\n- which research branches are producing useful connections;\\n- which tools or templates deserve improvement;\\n- whether the current order of work still makes sense.\\n\\nChange the routine only when experience gives a concrete reason. Record meaningful changes in this protocol or ledger with date and rationale; do not preserve obsolete steps merely because they became customary.\\n\\n**Session completion standard:** one meaningful result, honest source/coverage status, a verified record where durable storage is used, and a next cursor.\\n\\n\\n## 18. Workflow signature line\\n\\nAt the end of each substantive workshop response, repeat a compact signature line that preserves the ordered workflow inside the active conversation context. The signature is a live state marker, not decoration and not a substitute for the ledger.\\n\\nCanonical form:\\n\\n`WORKSHOP SIG | ORIENT \\u2192 BITE \\u2192 INVESTIGATE \\u2192 GEOMETRIZE \\u2192 CONNECT \\u2192 RECORD \\u2192 VERIFY \\u2192 NEXT | BRANCH: [branch] | CURRENT: [short task] | STATE: [status] | NEXT: [next operation]`\\n\\nRules:\\n- Keep the phase order stable unless experience or an explicit user decision warrants revision.\\n- Use only the phases relevant to the current bite, but do not silently reorder them.\\n- Keep branch, current task, state, and next operation short enough to remain scannable.\\n- State values should be plain and honest, for example: active, source-located, source-read, draft, verified, blocked, or parked.\\n- When a phase is skipped, mark it only when useful (for example, `CONNECT: deferred`); do not clutter every signature.\\n- Update the signature every substantive turn so the latest line captures the live position. Repeat it even when the turn is mainly procedural.\\n- If the session resumes after a gap or context shift, use the latest signature as a quick recovery pointer, then check the ledger and protocol for durable truth.\\n- The repository ledger remains authoritative for durable project state; the signature is a compact in-context working pointer.\\n\\n\\n## 19. Compact Unicode workflow notation\\n\\nThe workflow signature is a **Unicode glyph string**, not a chain of words or arrows. Each assigned glyph denotes one workflow phase; adjacency means ordinary succession. Therefore, do not print explicit sequential arrows between every glyph.\\n\\n### Current provisional phase assignments\\n\\n| Glyph | Phase |\\n|---|---|\\n| \\u2316 | Orient |\\n| \\u25c9 | Focus / select bite |\\n| \\u2315 | Investigate |\\n| \\u29d6 | Geometrize |\\n| \\u2933 | Connect |\\n| \\u25a3 | Record |\\n| \\u2713 | Verify |\\n| \\u21e2 | Next / deliberate transition |\\n\\nThese are provisional assignments for this workshop. They are not claimed to be registered in the general Unicode String-to-Glyph assignment workbook unless and until that workbook is deliberately updated. A glyph is one Unicode code point here; its semantic assignment is maintained by this protocol.\\n\\n### Linear sequence and control markers\\n\\n- `\\u2316\\u25c9\\u2315\\u29d6\\u2933\\u25a3\\u2713\\u21e2` means the ordered workflow, with implicit succession.\\n- A leading prefix records completed phases. For example, `\\u2316\\u25c9\\u21e2\\u2315\\u29d6\\u2933\\u25a3\\u2713\\u21e2` means orientation and bite selection are complete; the next phase is investigation, but execution pauses at the transition marker to deliberate how to proceed.\\n- `\\u21e2` is a deliberate transition / decision point, not a duplicate of ordinary adjacency.\\n- Reserve separate control glyphs for branching, cycling, joining, waiting, and stopping. Do not assign those operators casually or use them interchangeably.\\n- Branch, cycle, join, and other compound forms must be defined with small examples before use. Their grammar should distinguish the workflow graph from the linear sequence of phases.\\n- Keep the live signature compact: show the relevant phase string and, only when not inferable, a short current-position or branch annotation.\\n\\nDo not insert redundant arrows between successive phase glyphs. Do not expand the signature into prose unless explaining or revising the notation.\\n\\n\\n## 20. Pilot status and promotion boundary\\n\\nThis workshop is a **bespoke experimental pilot** of the workflow and Unicode-notation system. Its purpose is to discover what works in this particular collaboration and research context. Do not assume that its conventions, glyph assignments, operators, or session routine are generally useful or recommended for other users, projects, or assistants.\\n\\nTreat all current notation and workflow rules as pilot-local and provisional. Observe their practical performance, including clarity, compactness, recoverability, ambiguity, cognitive overhead, and ease of editing. Record useful evidence and friction, but do not prematurely generalize.\\n\\nPromotion beyond this workshop requires an explicit decision by the user after something noteworthy has emerged. Any proposed general recommendation should identify:\\n- the observed benefit and the problem it solves;\\n- the contexts in which it was actually tested;\\n- known limitations, failure cases, and accessibility/rendering concerns;\\n- which parts are reusable and which depend on this workshop's particular needs.\\n\\nUntil such a decision is made, keep the system local to this pilot and label it accordingly.\\n\\n\\n## 21. Pilot compound workflow operators (provisional)\\n\\nThe following operators extend the linear phase string. These are local experimental conventions, not general recommendations.\\n\\n### Operator vocabulary\\n\\n| Glyph | Name | Operational meaning |\\n|---|---|---|\\n| `\\u2442` | Fork | Split the current workflow into two or more independently tracked branches. |\\n| `\\u2443` | Rejoin | Reunite branches at a shared continuation after their outputs are available and reconciled. |\\n| `\\u27f3` | Cycle | Repeat the immediately enclosed or explicitly delimited sequence until its exit condition is met. |\\n| `\\u2026` | Await | Suspend this path pending an identified event, input, result, or condition. |\\n| `\\u25a0` | Halt | Stop this path. It is complete, cancelled, or deliberately parked only when the state annotation says which. |\\n\\n### Provisional syntax and examples\\n\\nUse braces to delimit the scope of a compound operation; braces are structural punctuation, not operators.\\n\\n- Fork: `\\u2315\\u2442{A: source review | B: geometric reconstruction}`\\n- Rejoin: `\\u2443{A+B}`\\n- Fork, work independently, then rejoin: `\\u2315\\u2442{A: sources | B: geometry}\\u2443\\u2933`\\n- Cycle: `\\u27f3{\\u2315\\u29d6}` means repeat investigation and geometrization as a cycle. Its stopping condition must be stated when it is not obvious.\\n- Await: `\\u2026[primary source located]` means this branch is suspended until that condition is met.\\n- Halt/park: `\\u25a0[parked: await later evidence]`; `\\u25a0[complete]` is a completed path.\\n\\n### Semantics and safeguards\\n\\n1. Fork creates distinct branches, not merely a list of topics. Each branch needs an identity and a defined task or output.\\n2. Rejoin is not automatic: it requires branch outputs to be available and reconciled. If a branch is abandoned, record that explicitly rather than silently treating it as complete.\\n3. A cycle needs a bounded repetition rule or an observable exit condition. Avoid unbounded repetition.\\n4. Await suspends only the marked path; other branches may continue.\\n5. Halt is terminal for that path unless explicitly reopened. The annotation distinguishes completed, cancelled, and parked states.\\n6. Nested or overlapping constructs are allowed in principle but deferred until simple cases have been used and tested.\\n7. These symbols are provisional one-code-point assignments in this workshop. They are not registered in the general glyph-assignment workbook.\\n\\n\\n## 22. Tock\\u2013tick hierarchy (pilot convention)\\n\\nUse **TOCK\\u2013TICK** as the canonical conceptual and organizational order. The tock is the larger work unit; ticks are its smaller constituent operations.\\n\\n- **Tock:** a bounded, coherent work package or main-level unit of progress. It has a purpose, scope, intended result, and completion/exit condition. A tock may contain multiple ticks and may itself contain subordinate tocks only when useful.\\n- **Tick:** a lower-order operation within a tock: a step, inspection, calculation, source read, diagram, branch action, or verification operation. Ticks help locate and sequence the work inside the larger unit.\\n- A tick is not automatically a completed tock. Completing several ticks may contribute to a tock, but the tock is complete only when its intended durable result and next cursor have been recorded and checked.\\n- The Unicode workflow string primarily tracks tick-level operations and their control structure. The Credenza's work tray and project/branch map organize tocks and their return points.\\n- Canonical sequence: **Tock \\u2192 ticks \\u2192 durable result \\u2192 tock closure/advance**. The Credenza may retain a larger queue of tocks while the active tock carries its own tick sequence.\\n- A tick marker is a position indicator, not evidence of completion. Tock closure requires an inspectable result, status, and next cursor.\\n- Keep the hierarchy shallow unless actual work requires nesting. Do not make every tick a tock or create a tock for every chat turn.\\n\\nThis replaces any wording or diagram that places Tick before Tock as the organizational hierarchy. It refines, rather than discards, the Credenza model's operational distinction between the tick as place marker and the tock as a completed bounded operation.\\n\\n\\n## 22. Tock\\u2013Tick hierarchy\\n\\nUse **Tock\\u2013Tick** as the canonical conceptual order. A Tock is the higher-level bounded work unit; Ticks are the lower-order operations and progress markers within it. This is an organizational hierarchy, not merely a temporal sequence.\\n\\n- **Tock:** a bounded work package, session objective, or coherent deliverable. It has a purpose, scope, expected result, and completion/exit condition. First historical 4D-biology reconnaissance \\u2014 2026-11-24\\n\\n### Strongest primary historical finding: C. H. Hinton, *The Fourth Dimension* (1904)\\n\\n- Repository source: `HISTORICAL/HINTON \\u2014 4TH DIMENSION*` (exact corpus file(s) still to be inventoried); external full text: Project Gutenberg, `https://www.gutenberg.org/files/67153/old/67153-h/67153-h.htm`.\\n- Key location: Chapter III, \\u201cThe Significance of a Four-Dimensional Existence\\u201d (around printed pp. 18\\u201323) and Chapter VII, \\u201cThe Evidences for a Fourth Dimension\\u201d (around printed pp. 76\\u201379).\\n- Hinton explicitly discusses organic beings' bilateral/right-left symmetry and asks whether a four-dimensional folding or movement of minute constituents of living matter could produce corresponding right- and left-handed structures. He states that one general characteristic of organismal forms might be accounted for by four-dimensional motion in the process of life.\\n- Crucial qualification: Hinton explicitly says he does **not** mean that life can be explained as four-dimensional movement; he resists reducing life and volition to matter and motion. He treats the symmetry argument as inconclusive and frames the possible motion as occurring in minute constituents, not gross bodies. He also discusses germ structure and heredity as unresolved difficulties.\\n- Classification: **EXPLICIT 4D BIOLOGICAL SPECULATION**, not established biology. Strong historical target for close reading because the author directly connects four-dimensional spatial geometry, the microscopic constituents of living matter, organismal bilateral symmetry, life, and volition.\\n\\n### Second historical source: W. Whately Smith, *A Theory of the Mechanism of Survival: The Fourth Dimension and Its Applications* (1920)\\n\\n- Repository source: `HISTORICAL/SMITH \\u2014 4TH DIMENSIONAL APPLIC.txt`; online Project Gutenberg source: `https://www.gutenberg.org/files/64055/64055-h/64055-h.htm`.\\n- Key locations: Chapter V, \\u201cVitality and Will\\u201d (printed pp. 113 onward), Chapter VII, \\u201cThe Connecting Link\\u201d (pp. 136 onward), plus Chapter II and IV for the overall hypothesis.\\n- Smith explicitly extends higher-space concepts to vitality and the relation between life and the body. He contrasts a productive view (life as a product of bodily processes) with a transmissive view (the body as a means through which life manifests). He speculates that life could exist apart from ordinary physical matter and affect it from a region of higher space. In Chapter VII he suggests the nervous system as a possible connecting mechanism between a three-dimensional physical body and a four-dimensional vehicle of consciousness.\\n- Crucial qualification: The book's preface calls its hypotheses speculative and extrapolatory. Its argument is strongly entangled with psychical research, survival, and a separate four-dimensional vehicle of consciousness. Smith expressly rejects the notion that the three-dimensional body is merely a section of a four-dimensional whole. Do not conflate this with Hinton's more tentative microscopic symmetry argument or with modern biology.\\n- Classification: **EXPLICIT FOUR-DIMENSIONAL VITALIST / PSYCHICAL SPECULATION**, biologically adjacent rather than empirical biological theory.\\n\\n### Third historical source: Edwin A. Abbott, *Flatland* (1884)\\n\\n- Repository source: `HISTORICAL/ABBOTT \\u2014 FLATLAND.txt`; Project Gutenberg eBook 45506.\\n- Its principal biological relevance in this initial inspection is analogical and literary: inhabitants are represented as living two-dimensional figures with anatomy-like forms, sensory limitations, development, heredity/social class metaphors, and a higher-dimensional observer's access to structures inaccessible to them.\\n- Classification: **BIOLOGICAL ANALOGY / ORGANISMAL WORLD-BUILDING**, not a direct claim that organisms are four-dimensional. Requires a separate literary reading to distinguish biological analogy from social satire.\\n\\n### Modern retrospective control points (not historical sources)\\n\\n1. Geoffrey B. West, James H. This is a metaphorical/effective internal network dimension embedded in ordinary three-dimensional organisms, not an extra independently navigable spatial axis. Primary text found online; not yet fully analyzed.\\n2. They propose combining organismal space with generation/lifetime as a **fourth temporal dimension** in metabolic-scaling analysis. Their abstract explicitly distinguishes this literal temporal fourth dimension from the metaphorical extra spatial dimension in WBE-type network accounts.\\n3. Modern process philosophy of organisms offers another temporal four-dimensional framing: organisms as temporally extended processes rather than momentary three-dimensional bodies. This is a later conceptual comparison, not evidence of historical influence on Hinton or Smith.\\n\\n### Initial synthesis\\n\\nThe archive and external literature already reveal at least four distinct senses of \\u201cfour-dimensional biology\\u201d that must not be collapsed:\\n\\n- **A. Extra spatial dimensionality:** living matter or its constituents participate in a genuinely additional spatial direction (Hinton's speculative proposal).\\n- **B. Higher-space vital vehicle:** life or consciousness is said to operate through a four-dimensional organism/vehicle related to a three-dimensional body (Smith's psychical-vitalist proposal).\\n- **C. Effective/fractal internal dimension:** three-dimensional biological transport networks behave as though they occupy an additional spatial dimension (West\\u2013Brown\\u2013Enquist).\\n- **D. They form a promising historical-to-modern comparison, but not a continuous lineage unless source evidence establishes one.\\n\\n### Next source operations\\n\\n- Inventory and inspect the exact Hinton corpus file in HSH_RESOURCES, checking edition and text against Gutenberg.\\n- Read Hinton Chapters III and VII closely, preserving printed page locators and his explicit caveats.\\n- Read Smith Chapter V and the relevant parts of VII, separating biological/vitality claims from psychical-survival arguments.\\n- Inspect the relevant sections of *Flatland* as a biological analogy and social satire, not as a scientific proposal.\\n- Retrieve and analyze West\\u2013Brown\\u2013Enquist (1999) and Ginzburg\\u2013Damuth (2008) as distinct modern comparators.\\n\\n\\n## 26. Close reading: Hinton and Whately Smith \\u2014 2026-11-24\\n\\n### Hinton, *The Fourth Dimension* (1904), Chapters III and VII\\n\\nPrimary text: Project Gutenberg eBook 67153, https://www.gutenberg.org/files/67153/old/67153-h/67153-h.htm . Repository text exact Hinton file still needs edition/path verification.\\n\\n**Chapter III, \\u201cThe Significance of a Four-Dimensional Existence\\u201d (printed pp. 15\\u201322):**\\n- Hinton develops an analogy between a plane-dwelling being's inability to perceive out-of-plane movement and our possible inability to perceive motions in a fourth spatial direction.\\n- He considers minute constituents of matter that may have more freedom of motion than bulk bodies and suggests a four-dimensional \\u201cether\\u201d as a speculative possibility.\\n- He directly connects organic right-left symmetry with possible four-dimensional folding or motion in microscopic material constituents.\\n- He states that one broad characteristic of organismal form might be accounted for by four-dimensional motion involved in life.\\n- He explicitly refuses the claim that life is thereby explained as four-dimensional movement. The precise status is speculative explanatory analogy / hypothesis, not observation or accepted biology. Its most specific target is organismal bilateral symmetry and a possible microscopic process of living matter. It is not a worked-out account of embryogenesis, heredity, physiology, or evolutionary dynamics.\\n\\n### Smith, *A Theory of the Mechanism of Survival* (1920), Chapters V and VII\\n\\nPrimary text: Project Gutenberg eBook 64055, https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/64055/pg64055-images.html ; repository copy is `HISTORICAL/SMITH \\u2014 4TH DIMENSIONAL APPLIC.txt`.\\n\\n**Chapter V, \\u201cVitality and Will\\u201d (printed pp. 113\\u2013121):**\\n- Smith sets out a productive account of life (life as bodily physiological/chemical outcome) against a transmissive account (body as vehicle or channel through which life manifests).\\n- He aligns himself with the transmissive position and draws on Bergson, William James, Hereward Carrington, and A. First recover SAT/H(s)H precedent and Nathan's intent, then compare outside work without importing assumptions by resemblance. *No Hopf/spherical carrier is imported by default.* The searcher's automatic `PRIOR_ART`/`QUARANTINE` exclusions remain intentionally unchanged as **public-index and exposure controls**, not research-access prohibitions. Do not bypass them to publish private or unreviewed material. The nLab Mersearch port is stand-alone, not an interoperability bridge.\\n\\n\\n## The 15-second rule\\n\\n**Default: search ALL THREE permitted repositories together.**\\n\\n1. `Satobloc/SAT_THEORY_ARCHIVE_2023-25` (original SAT / GLASS)\\n2. `Satobloc/HsH` (H(s)H, full conversations and current work)\\n3. `Satobloc/HSH_RESOURCES` (private/internal reference resources and toolkit; **not** a public search corpus or theory authority)\\n\\nTreat `PRIOR_ART` and `QUARANTINE` as excluded. Do not silently limit a historical search to one archive. If one source is unavailable, **state which repository was missing** and report that results are **partial**. Repository names alone do not establish access rights; follow actual permissions and source classification.\\n\\n### Choose the search interface you actually have\\n\\n| You can… | Use | Status |\\n| --- | --- | --- |\\n| Run Python against checked-out archives | Pinned `mersearch-stable-1.0`, invoked over all three roots | Available now; stable Boolean/NEAR/math notation, not chronology inference |\\n| Use the HsH GitHub connector but cannot run Python | `.github/workflows/mersearch-request-bridge.yml` via `WORKSPACES/COMMON/MERSEARCH_REQUEST.json` on `main` | **Three-root bridge activated 2026-10-09**; inspect the published manifest before asserting coverage |\\n| Work on the chronology/multi-archive development branch | `mersearch-chronology-20261007`: run `python tools/search_archive_content.py --capabilities`, `--help`, `--examples`, `--coverage` | Candidate 1.2, tested on synthetic fixtures; **not** the pinned stable release |\\n| Only have GitHub code search | Query each of the three repositories independently and disclose caps/limitations | Fallback, **not** a verified Mersearch run |\\n\\n**Do not confuse the human Pages interface with research search.** The public web page is a curated conversation-*title/path* catalog until a separately reviewed public full-text index goes live. It does not expose the whole research corpus.\\n\\n> **2026-10-26 publication containment and recursion control (live):** All four bridge workflows now publish only `RUN_MANIFEST.json`, `SEARCH_RECEIPT.json`, and `SEARCH_RECEIPT.md`. New raw `SEARCH_RESULTS.json/.md` are withheld in temporary job storage, not durable public artifacts; older runs may still have raw results and remain a separate exposure-remediation problem. This preserves public-safe bounded navigation but **does not satisfy an exhaustive full-hit inventory request**. The bridge also passes stable Mersearch's existing `--exclude mersearch_requests` option, preventing prior generated request outputs from recursively dominating fresh source searches. The manifest records `bridge_exclusions`. First post-containment execution observed: Lane 2 run #44818799476 (attempt 1, completed successfully) records `bridge_exclusions: [\\\"mersearch_requests\\\"]` and publishes only the three compact artifacts. Job logs confirm that raw `SEARCH_RESULTS.json/.md` remained in temporary Actions job storage and were not copied to `main`. This verifies the containment/exclusion path for this one run only, not every lane, exhaustive hit retrieval, or semantic completeness. The run used a runtime-only hotfix injecting `TOOL_NAME` and `TOOL_VERSION`; the `mersearch-stable-1.0` branch remained unchanged, and the stable/runtime script hashes are separately recorded in the manifest. The lane request remains `requested`; the lane is not released. For exhaustive, access-controlled results, use a local pinned checkout or obtain an approved restricted artifact path; do not overwrite occupied lanes or claim full results from a compact receipt.\\n\\n## GitHub connector route: parallel request lanes\\n\\n**Updated 2026-10-24:** the former single-slot bridge has been expanded to **four independent request lanes**. All lanes run the same pinned `mersearch-stable-1.0` searcher over the same three permitted roots and publish request-scoped outputs into `indexes/mersearch_requests/<request_id>/`.\\n\\nAvailable request files:\\n- Lane 1 / legacy: `WORKSPACES/COMMON/MERSEARCH_REQUEST.json`\\n- Lane 2: `WORKSPACES/COMMON/MERSEARCH_REQUEST_LANE_2.json`\\n- Lane 3: `WORKSPACES/COMMON/MERSEARCH_REQUEST_LANE_3.json`\\n- Lane 4: `WORKSPACES/COMMON/MERSEARCH_REQUEST_LANE_4.json`\\n\\nEach lane has its own GitHub Actions workflow and its own concurrency group, so searches on different lanes can run in parallel subject to the repository/account's available GitHub Actions runner concurrency.\\n\\n**Do not duplicate the Mersearch code itself just to gain throughput.** The bottleneck was the single request file plus single workflow concurrency group, not the search implementation. Keep one pinned implementation and multiply the bridge lanes.\\n\\n1. Inspect the lane request files and choose an idle lane. **Do not overwrite** a lane whose request is still pending/running or whose output has not been verified. If all lanes are occupied, use a local pinned Mersearch checkout or wait/coordinate rather than overwriting another worker's request. Do not pretend connector code search is a Mersearch result.\\n2. When a lane is free, write a fresh globally unique `request_id`, a query using the stable 1.0 language, requester and purpose into that lane's request file. A change to the lane file on `main` starts that lane's workflow.\\n3. Retrieve the request-scoped folder `indexes/mersearch_requests/<request_id>/` and verify `RUN_MANIFEST.json`, `SEARCH_RECEIPT.json` and `SEARCH_RECEIPT.md`. **For post-2026-10-26 containment runs, these are the only three files intentionally published by the bridge**; do not treat absent `SEARCH_RESULTS.json/.md` as a failed run or claim that compact receipts contain all hits. The moving aliases `latest.*` are insufficient provenance.\\n   - **Historical pre-containment runs** may also have public `SEARCH_RESULTS.json` and `SEARCH_RESULTS.md`. Their existence is not authorization to redistribute raw excerpts; assess exposure before reuse. For complete post-containment results, execute pinned Mersearch against an authorized local three-root checkout or use an approved restricted durable artifact route. `RUN_MANIFEST.json` may contain digests for raw outputs generated inside the job even though those outputs were **not** published. Compact receipts are navigation samples; detailed `resources/` matches are intentionally omitted. Confirm the workflow execution and exclusions before claiming coverage.\\n4. Confirm the **actual** searched repositories, exact source SHAs, stable Mersearch implementation ref, exclusions and completion. Failed or incomplete runs are not results. Remember: scan exclusions and large files may limit completeness even if three repositories were checked out.\\n\\n## Execution-to-artifact binding\\n\\nA request ID and compact manifest do not, by themselves, identify the execution attempt that produced the artifacts. For every bridge run, preserve the chain:\\n\\n1. Request file path, request ID, requester, query hash and request-file blob SHA.\\n2. GitHub Actions run ID, run attempt, workflow ID/name, run event, head branch/SHA and status/conclusion.\\n3. Job ID and each checkout step number/name/status, with the actual repository, ref mode, fetch depth and post-checkout commit SHA.\\n4. Stable implementation ref/hash **and** any runtime-only patch/hash, kept distinct.\\n5. Output artifact paths, SHA-256 digests, publication policy, and independent readback of each durable artifact.\\n6. A separate current-run reference, if present. Task-level conversation references and cached-result references must not be promoted to current-run thread bindings.\\n\\nIf the compact manifest omits run/attempt/job/step identifiers, recover them from the Actions run and job logs and append one clone-ledger row per actual checkout event. Do not infer checkout count from repository count, compare a cross-repository checkout SHA with the HsH workflow head, or treat a successful run as proof of exhaustive search. Raw search-result artifacts remain withheld under the post-containment policy.\\n\\n## Local pinned Mersearch usage\\n\\nFrom a stable checkout with sibling archive directories visible (paths here are examples):\\n\\n```bash\\npython tools/search_archive_content.py \\\\\\n  /data/SAT_THEORY_ARCHIVE_2023-25 /data/HsH /data/HSH_RESOURCES \\\\\\n  --expr '(\\\"refractive index\\\" NEAR/12 \\\"phase shift\\\") OR \\\"0.24\\\"' \\\\\\n  --sort date --out /tmp/mersearch-optical\\n```\\n\\nMore queries:\\n\\n```text\\n(\\\"stringing along theory\\\" OR \\\"toy theory\\\") AND (filament OR string)\\n(\\\"Chronophysical\\\" OR \\\"SAT Mark V\\\") AND \\\"phase shift\\\"\\nmath:\\\"B=3/(4*pi)\\\"\\n(name:*LAB* OR path:*PHASE*) AND (optical OR kink)\\nauthor:user AND (worldtube NEAR/12 holonomy)\\n```\\n\\nStable search supports Boolean `AND`/`OR`/`NOT`, parentheses, quoted phrases, `NEAR/n`, `author:`, `role:`, `body:`, `math:`, `title:`, `date:`, `name:`, `path:`, `status:` and path/name globs. The mathematical mode normalizes notation but does **not** prove algebraic equivalence. Search several alternate mathematical forms; don't pretend automatic CAS exists.\\n\\n**LLMs must discover available capabilities.** On the development branch, start with `--capabilities`. On stable 1.0, read `WORKSPACES/COMMON/MERSEARCH_RELEASES.md` and `--help`; do not assume later flags exist. Never guess a filter name.\\n\\n## Required researcher reading and provenance cycle (October 9)\\n\\nEach substantive theory-source pass should consult [FIE](https://github.com/Satobloc/SAT_THEORY_ARCHIVE_2023-25/blob/main/THE%20FUNDAMENTAL%20INTUITIONS%20%E2%80%94%20EXTENDED.pdf) and relevant [RMS primary sources](https://github.com/Satobloc/SAT_THEORY_ARCHIVE_2023-25/blob/main/RMS%20THE%20FRAMEWORK.txt) periodically, plus randomly or systematically sampled **older SAT files**. Search HsH *nested development folders, loose exports, LIVE CONVOS, root files and miscellaneous CONVOS locations*, not only the conventional `SAT_CONVOS_*` folders. Note exactly which documents were *read*, *searched*, *metadata-inventoried* or *unavailable*. Log new source-located equations and share concise cross-worker insights through Common Room. Early terminology and apparently failed constructions must be reconstructed before replacement mechanisms are invented.\\n\\nFor any proposed external crosswalk, maintain this sequence: **SAT source search → exact SAT citations → internal reconstruction/test → nonrestricted prior-art source review → comparator citation only**. The new amendment does not authorize access to the two remaining forbidden classes, indiscriminate private source indexing, or changing public search allowlists.\\n\\n## Historical provenance\\n\\n- Direct message timestamps from structured exports are hard evidence for those messages. Folder/archive dates and dates **mentioned** in text are not interchangeable.\\n- Early use of version names (SAT Mark IV.2, Mark V, SAT X/XY/Z/O, Chronophysical, Stringing Along Theory, toy theory) may date a passage only **tentatively**; retrospective use, renamed concepts and compilations can invalidate simple inferences.\\n- Report **earliest attested**, **earliest estimated**, and **earliest archived** separately. Compare passages from original exports, not merely copied summaries.\\n- For the `0.24 rad` lineage, prioritize early **laboratory optical phase-shift** calculations and related **refractive-index** discussion before imposing later projection-constant interpretations.\\n- Include exact source path, line/message locator, original date if known, query, searched repositories, engine/ref, and limitations with every finding.\\n\\n## Immediate operating rule\\n\\nIf an agent's task involves SAT/H(s)H history, equations, geometry, or the status of a claimed earlier result, **invoke a permitted search route first and inspect original matched context before inventing a replacement**. Do not delay serious calculation once useful sources are found.\\n\\n### Source of truth / more capabilities\\n\\n- [Stable 1.0 instructions](MERSEARCH_RELEASES.md)\\n- [Full search architecture](MERSEARCH_RESEARCH_PLATFORM.md)\\n- [Chronology 1.2 and LLM discovery on development branch](https://github.com/Satobloc/HsH/blob/mersearch-chronology-20261007/WORKSPACES/COMMON/MERSEARCH_AGENT_QUICKSTART.md)\\n- [Development review, **not** stable deployment](https://github.com/Satobloc/HsH/pull/10)\\n- [Human-facing deployment guide](https://github.com/Satobloc/HsH/blob/mersearch-chronology-20261007/CONVERSATION_VIEWER/mersearch/README.md)\\n\\n**Shortcut:** Search three roots; disclose coverage; verify original records; then do the science.\\n\\n\\n## Display-time convention: Nathan Direct (20 November 2026)\\n\\nMersearch and H(s)H operational interfaces must preserve canonical timestamps as timezone-aware machine values, preferably ISO 8601 UTC with a `Z` suffix. **Whenever timestamps are presented to Nathan, convert and display them in the `America/New_York` time zone.** This includes request receipts, queue snapshots, timestamps of requests ahead, event histories, run/status summaries, manifests rendered for the user, and operational reports.\\n\\nUse the IANA zone `America/New_York`, not a fixed `EST` or `EDT` offset. The zone automatically observes the applicable Eastern Standard Time / Eastern Daylight Time rules. Label displayed values as **ET** (or spell out EST/EDT as applicable); do not call all-year local time \\\"EST\\\". Preserve the original UTC timestamp in machine-readable records and, when useful for audit, show it alongside the Eastern rendering. Never rewrite historical event timestamps merely to change their display zone.\\n\\nThis is a presentation-layer preference, not a requirement to store local-time timestamps or to change cross-system ordering, sorting, signatures, hashes, or protocol semantics. If a user-facing interface cannot perform timezone conversion, it must disclose the canonical timezone rather than silently presenting an unlabeled local-looking time.\\n\\n**Signature / attribution:** This directive is recorded at Nathan's request. Raw message IDs pending backfill.\\n\\n## Purpose\\n\\nMersearch is the common query layer for the SAT/H(s)H archive. It should let humans, workers, the Conversation Viewer, and approved public interfaces ask the same query of the same permitted corpus and receive reproducible, provenance-bearing results.\\n\\nThe design rule is **one search semantics, multiple clients**. Do not fork a Sites searcher, Viewer searcher, worker searcher, and CLI searcher with subtly different meanings.\\n\\n## Architecture\\n\\n### 1. Mersearch Core\\n\\nCurrent implementation: `tools/search_archive_content.py` (`Mercer_Searcher_1.0` historical/internal tool identity).\\n\\nCore owns:\\n- query parsing and Boolean semantics;\\n- `AND`, `OR`, `NOT`, parentheses and implicit AND;\\n- quoted phrases;\\n- `NEAR` / `NEAR/n` with auditable token distance;\\n- field predicates;\\n- path/name glob semantics;\\n- record extraction from supported source formats;\\n- conservative notation-normalized math retrieval;\\n- exclusions / corpus boundary enforcement;\\n- provenance-bearing hit construction;\\n- deterministic sorting;\\n- topic enrichment and co-occurrence;\\n- machine-readable result generation.\\n\\nCore must remain usable without a web server or UI.\\n\\n### 2. Mersearch Index\\n\\nTarget layer. Precompute search-oriented representations without replacing source files:\\n- inventory/file manifest;\\n- record/message index;\\n- normalized lexical tokens;\\n- mathematical-expression inventory;\\n- source SHA-256 and source commit/ref;\\n- Viewer/document targets;\\n- conversation-family / duplicate-relation sidecars;\\n- explicit document→text-representation relations where provenance establishes them;\\n- topic/concept indexes;\\n- optional chronology summaries.\\n\\nGenerated indexes are derived state and must be rebuildable. They must never silently confer authority or suppress a source merely because another representation is newer/larger.\\n\\n### 3. Mersearch API / machine adapter\\n\\nTarget layer. A stable machine-facing wrapper over Core/Index for workers, Sites, Viewer and automation.\\n\\nMinimum request:\\n- query expression;\\n- corpus/profile;\\n- sort/order;\\n- pagination;\\n- requested facets;\\n- explain level.\\n\\nMinimum response:\\n- schema/tool/index versions;\\n- exact query and parsed representation;\\n- corpus/profile and exclusions;\\n- source/index commit identity;\\n- coverage counts;\\n- total hits before pagination;\\n- page/cursor;\\n- facets;\\n- hit records;\\n- per-hit provenance;\\n- match/explanation trace;\\n- warnings/limitations.\\n\\nAPI must not accept a client request to bypass quarantine/private-corpus rules merely because the client can name a path.\\n\\n### 4. Mersearch clients\\n\\n**Research frontend:** advanced query bar, filters/facets, chronology, provenance cards, explain-match, source-family handling, equation views, saved queries, export.\\n\\n**Conversation Viewer:** message-level retrieval/jump targets and conversation-local/global search using the same semantics where practical.\\n\\n**Glass Sausage Factory / public site:** public-profile search only. The site is a client, not an independent search authority.\\n\\n**Worker/automation clients:** JSON/JSONL/CSV/CLI/API access for reproducible research, batch archaeology and generated indexes.\\n\\n## Corpus / capability profiles\\n\\nProfiles define permitted corpus and expensive capabilities, not different meanings for the same query.\\n\\n- **public** — only material explicitly available to the public/site.\\n- **viewer** — material legitimately exposed through the Viewer.\\n- **worker** — permitted project corpus for ordinary workers; quarantine and PRIOR_ART remain excluded unless a separately authorized lane/profile exists.\\n- **admin/maintenance** — diagnostics and index maintenance; access still follows repository/quarantine policy.\\n\\nProfile names do not themselves grant access. Enforcement belongs server/index side.\\n\\n## Query language — current\\n\\nUnqualified terms search record body text.\\n\\nCurrent fields:\\n- `body:` — explicit body phrase/term.\\n- `math:` — conservative notation-normalized mathematical substring search.\\n- `name:` — basename; supports shell-style `*`, `?`, character classes.\\n- `path:` — source path; same glob support.\\n- `ext:` — extension, without leading dot.\\n- `type:` / `kind:` — indexed record kind.\\n- `has:` — mechanically established properties such as conversation-source, pdf-source, text-source, message-id, conversation-id, viewer.\\n- `author:` / `speaker:`\\n- `role:`\\n- `title:`\\n- `conversation:` / `cid:`\\n- `date:` including `YYYY-MM-DD..YYYY-MM-DD`\\n- `status:` — lexical status-signal retrieval only.\\n\\nExamples:\\n\\n```text\\nname:*2026.txt\\nname:*26.txt OR name:26*.txt\\n(path:*SAT_CONVOS_20* AND ext:txt) AND body:\\\"star shaped\\\"\\nauthor:Nathan AND (holonomy NEAR/12 glitch)\\nmath:\\\"B=3/(4*pi)\\\"\\n```\\n\\n## Mathematical retrieval roadmap\\n\\n### M0 — notation normalization — IMPLEMENTED\\n\\nNormalize common presentation differences while preserving raw source:\\n- selected Unicode/LaTeX/plain symbol aliases;\\n- multiplication/division glyphs;\\n- Unicode minus / approximation;\\n- whitespace;\\n- simple LaTeX fractions.\\n\\nA notation match is **not algebraic equivalence**. Current negative acceptance control requires `math:\\\"4*pi*B=3\\\"` not to match `B=3/(4*pi)` merely because a human can rearrange it.\\n\\n### M1 — expression extraction\\n\\nIdentify probable equation spans from LaTeX delimiters, display blocks, inline formulas, Unicode/plain equations and code-like math. Store:\\n- exact raw expression;\\n- source locator;\\n- surrounding context;\\n- notation-normalized form;\\n- parse status;\\n- parser/version.\\n\\nNever discard `UNPARSED` expressions.\\n\\n### M2 — structural parsing\\n\\nParse supported expressions into a symbolic AST. Add:\\n- `contains:` structural/subexpression search;\\n- symbol/function/operator facets;\\n- equation-shape fingerprints;\\n- alpha-renaming option only when explicitly requested.\\n\\n### M3 — algebraic relation\\n\\nAdd conservative CAS-backed relationship testing:\\n- `EXACT`\\n- `NORMALIZED-EQUIVALENT`\\n- `ALGEBRAICALLY-EQUIVALENT`\\n- `CONTAINS-SUBEXPRESSION`\\n- `NUMERICALLY-CONSISTENT`\\n- `POSSIBLE-RELATION`\\n- `UNPARSED`\\n\\nTarget query: `equiv:\\\"B=3/(4*pi)\\\"`.\\n\\nCAS transformations must be recorded and bounded. Timeouts/failures remain visible. Do not silently equate expressions under unstated domain assumptions.\\n\\n### M4 — equation genealogy / derivation archaeology\\n\\nTarget `derive:` searches documented archive relationships rather than inventing a derivation. Desired chain:\\n`first known occurrence → reformulation → substitution → numerical evaluation → cross-sector reuse → correction/reversal → latest known occurrence`.\\n\\nChronology alone never establishes supersession. Explicit source language and provenance review control those labels.\\n\\n## Research-power roadmap\\n\\n### High priority\\n\\n1. **Facets and counts:** author, role, year/date, extension, kind, conversation, topic, status signal, source family.\\n2. **File-level inventory mode:** avoid returning one filename match per record/message when the research question is about files.\\n3. **Pagination/cursors and stable total-hit count:** current `--limit` truncates after sorting and should not be confused with total matches.\\n4. **Stable API schema:** separate request, response metadata, facets and hits.\\n5. **Duplicate/snapshot awareness:** attach established conversation-family relation classes; never infer canonical/newest/preferred.\\n6. **Saved/named queries:** versioned query + profile + sort + topic config + index/source identity.\\n7. **Explain-search:** human-readable and structured reason each hit matched.\\n8. **Regex mode:** explicit opt-in, bounded and clearly distinguished from literal search.\\n9. **Case control:** explicit sensitive/insensitive behavior.\\n10. **Prefix/wildcard/fuzzy lexical modes:** explicit, never silently applied.\\n11. **Neighbor-message proximity:** distinguish within-record `NEAR` from message-window proximity.\\n12. **Chronology/history mode:** first/latest occurrence, density and candidate correction/supersession signals without automatic authority inference.\\n13. **Exports:** JSON, JSONL, CSV, Markdown, TSV/plain-text; reproducibility manifest.\\n14. **Source representation graph:** PDF ↔ proven text extraction ↔ rendered/reader version; heuristic candidate relations must be labeled heuristic.\\n15. **Public-safe search profile:** required before live-site backend exposure.\\n\\n### Later / heavier\\n\\n- stemming/lemmatization as opt-in;\\n- multilingual/tokenization improvements;\\n- typo/fuzzy ranking;\\n- semantic/vector retrieval as a separately labeled retrieval mode;\\n- concept graph / topic adjacency;\\n- equation structural and CAS layers;\\n- citation/bibliographic entity search;\\n- image/figure metadata search;\\n- incremental indexing and cache invalidation;\\n- query-performance telemetry without leaking private query/source data;\\n- authenticated research API;\\n- rate limiting and resource budgets;\\n- UI query builder and syntax highlighting.\\n\\n## Provenance / explain contract\\n\\nEvery substantive hit should be able to answer:\\n1. What exact source object matched?\\n2. What corpus/profile allowed it?\\n3. What exact query clause matched?\\n4. Where in the record did it match?\\n5. What normalization/transformation, if any, occurred?\\n6. What source hash/ref/index version was searched?\\n7. Is the displayed source original, extraction, generated representation, or heuristic relation?\\n8. Is any status label lexical, source-authored, reviewed, or inferred?\\n\\nA numeric relevance score without this information is insufficient for research use.\\n\\n## Source relationships\\n\\nDo not infer `PDF → TXT export` solely from similar filenames. Relations may be:\\n- **PROVEN** — explicit manifest/provenance/tool output.\\n- **CONTENT-VERIFIED** — independently compared content establishes the relation.\\n- **CANDIDATE** — basename/path/metadata suggests a relation.\\n- **NONE/UNKNOWN**.\\n\\nClients must be able to distinguish them.\\n\\n## Duplicate / snapshot policy\\n\\nUse the established conversation-relation axes and sidecar work. Search presentation may group related exports, but grouping must not:\\n- delete or hide unique branch material;\\n- call the newest/largest/LIVE copy authoritative;\\n- silently suppress a branch;\\n- convert byte identity into semantic/currentness authority.\\n\\nExpose relation class and allow expand/collapse.\\n\\n## Security / boundary rules\\n\\n- Default exclusions include `QUARANTINE` and `PRIOR_ART`.\\n- Public clients use an allowlisted public corpus/profile, not merely a denylist.\\n- Do not expose filesystem/repository secrets, private paths or hidden source excerpts through error messages/facets.\\n- Regex/CAS/fuzzy/semantic operations require bounded resource budgets.\\n- Query logs, if retained, are operational data and need an explicit retention/privacy rule.\\n- Backend responses must escape/render source text safely; source text is data, never executable markup.\\n- API/client cannot override server-side corpus policy.\\n\\n## Testing\\n\\nThe existing GitHub Actions acceptance gate compiles Core and runs deterministic synthetic semantics tests. Raw message IDs pending backfill.\\n\\n## Purpose\\n\\nMersearch is the common query layer for the SAT/H(s)H archive. It should let humans, workers, the Conversation Viewer, and approved public interfaces ask the same query of the same permitted corpus and receive reproducible, provenance-bearing results.\\n\\nThe design rule is **one search semantics, multiple clients**. Do not fork a Sites searcher, Viewer searcher, worker searcher, and CLI searcher with subtly different meanings.\\n\\n## Architecture\\n\\n### 1. Mersearch Core\\n\\nCurrent implementation: `tools/search_archive_content.py` (`Mercer_Searcher_1.0` historical/internal tool identity).\\n\\nCore owns:\\n- query parsing and Boolean semantics;\\n- `AND`, `OR`, `NOT`, parentheses and implicit AND;\\n- quoted phrases;\\n- `NEAR` / `NEAR/n` with auditable token distance;\\n- field predicates;\\n- path/name glob semantics;\\n- record extraction from supported source formats;\\n- conservative notation-normalized math retrieval;\\n- exclusions / corpus boundary enforcement;\\n- provenance-bearing hit construction;\\n- deterministic sorting;\\n- topic enrichment and co-occurrence;\\n- machine-readable result generation.\\n\\nCore must remain usable without a web server or UI.\\n\\n### 2. Mersearch Index\\n\\nTarget layer. Precompute search-oriented representations without replacing source files:\\n- inventory/file manifest;\\n- record/message index;\\n- normalized lexical tokens;\\n- mathematical-expression inventory;\\n- source SHA-256 and source commit/ref;\\n- Viewer/document targets;\\n- conversation-family / duplicate-relation sidecars;\\n- explicit document→text-representation relations where provenance establishes them;\\n- topic/concept indexes;\\n- optional chronology summaries.\\n\\nGenerated indexes are derived state and must be rebuildable. They must never silently confer authority or suppress a source merely because another representation is newer/larger.\\n\\n### 3. Mersearch API / machine adapter\\n\\nTarget layer. A stable machine-facing wrapper over Core/Index for workers, Sites, Viewer and automation.\\n\\nMinimum request:\\n- query expression;\\n- corpus/profile;\\n- sort/order;\\n- pagination;\\n- requested facets;\\n- explain level.\\n\\nMinimum response:\\n- schema/tool/index versions;\\n- exact query and parsed representation;\\n- corpus/profile and exclusions;\\n- source/index commit identity;\\n- coverage counts;\\n- total hits before pagination;\\n- page/cursor;\\n- facets;\\n- hit records;\\n- per-hit provenance;\\n- match/explanation trace;\\n- warnings/limitations.\\n\\nAPI must not accept a client request to bypass quarantine/private-corpus rules merely because the client can name a path.\\n\\n### 4. Mersearch clients\\n\\n**Research frontend:** advanced query bar, filters/facets, chronology, provenance cards, explain-match, source-family handling, equation views, saved queries, export.\\n\\n**Conversation Viewer:** message-level retrieval/jump targets and conversation-local/global search using the same semantics where practical.\\n\\n**Glass Sausage Factory / public site:** public-profile search only. The site is a client, not an independent search authority.\\n\\n**Worker/automation clients:** JSON/JSONL/CSV/CLI/API access for reproducible research, batch archaeology and generated indexes.\\n\\n## Corpus / capability profiles\\n\\nProfiles define permitted corpus and expensive capabilities, not different meanings for the same query.\\n\\n- **public** — only material explicitly available to the public/site.\\n- **viewer** — material legitimately exposed through the Viewer.\\n- **worker** — permitted project corpus for ordinary workers; quarantine and PRIOR_ART remain excluded unless a separately authorized lane/profile exists.\\n- **admin/maintenance** — diagnostics and index maintenance; access still follows repository/quarantine policy.\\n\\nProfile names do not themselves grant access. Enforcement belongs server/index side.\\n\\n## Query language — current\\n\\nUnqualified terms search record body text.\\n\\nCurrent fields:\\n- `body:` — explicit body phrase/term.\\n- `math:` — conservative notation-normalized mathematical substring search.\\n- `name:` — basename; supports shell-style `*`, `?`, character classes.\\n- `path:` — source path; same glob support.\\n- `ext:` — extension, without leading dot.\\n- `type:` / `kind:` — indexed record kind.\\n- `has:` — mechanically established properties such as conversation-source, pdf-source, text-source, message-id, conversation-id, viewer.\\n- `author:` / `speaker:`\\n- `role:`\\n- `title:`\\n- `conversation:` / `cid:`\\n- `date:` including `YYYY-MM-DD..YYYY-MM-DD`\\n- `status:` — lexical status-signal retrieval only.\\n\\nExamples:\\n\\n```text\\nname:*2026.txt\\nname:*26.txt OR name:26*.txt\\n(path:*SAT_CONVOS_20* AND ext:txt) AND body:\\\"star shaped\\\"\\nauthor:Nathan AND (holonomy NEAR/12 glitch)\\nmath:\\\"B=3/(4*pi)\\\"\\n```\\n\\n## Mathematical retrieval roadmap\\n\\n### M0 — notation normalization — IMPLEMENTED\\n\\nNormalize common presentation differences while preserving raw source:\\n- selected Unicode/LaTeX/plain symbol aliases;\\n- multiplication/division glyphs;\\n- Unicode minus / approximation;\\n- whitespace;\\n- simple LaTeX fractions.\\n\\nA notation match is **not algebraic equivalence**. Current negative acceptance control requires `math:\\\"4*pi*B=3\\\"` not to match `B=3/(4*pi)` merely because a human can rearrange it.\\n\\n### M1 — expression extraction\\n\\nIdentify probable equation spans from LaTeX delimiters, display blocks, inline formulas, Unicode/plain equations and code-like math. Store:\\n- exact raw expression;\\n- source locator;\\n- surrounding context;\\n- notation-normalized form;\\n- parse status;\\n- parser/version.\\n\\nNever discard `UNPARSED` expressions.\\n\\n### M2 — structural parsing\\n\\nParse supported expressions into a symbolic AST. Add:\\n- `contains:` structural/subexpression search;\\n- symbol/function/operator facets;\\n- equation-shape fingerprints;\\n- alpha-renaming option only when explicitly requested.\\n\\n### M3 — algebraic relation\\n\\nAdd conservative CAS-backed relationship testing:\\n- `EXACT`\\n- `NORMALIZED-EQUIVALENT`\\n- `ALGEBRAICALLY-EQUIVALENT`\\n- `CONTAINS-SUBEXPRESSION`\\n- `NUMERICALLY-CONSISTENT`\\n- `POSSIBLE-RELATION`\\n- `UNPARSED`\\n\\nTarget query: `equiv:\\\"B=3/(4*pi)\\\"`.\\n\\nCAS transformations must be recorded and bounded. Timeouts/failures remain visible. Do not silently equate expressions under unstated domain assumptions.\\n\\n### M4 — equation genealogy / derivation archaeology\\n\\nTarget `derive:` searches documented archive relationships rather than inventing a derivation. Desired chain:\\n`first known occurrence → reformulation → substitution → numerical evaluation → cross-sector reuse → correction/reversal → latest known occurrence`.\\n\\nChronology alone never establishes supersession. What exact source object matched?\\n2. What corpus/profile allowed it?\\n3. What exact query clause matched?\\n4. Where in the record did it match?\\n5. What normalization/transformation, if any, occurred?\\n6. What source hash/ref/index version was searched?\\n7. Is the displayed source original, extraction, generated representation, or heuristic relation?\\n8. Mersearch must not make each consumer perform an independent cold archive scan.\\n\\n## Observed baseline\\n\\nDevelopment workflow run `35517040595` established:\\n- Core compiled successfully after newline repair.\\n- Synthetic query-semantics acceptance passed.\\n- First bounded real-corpus inventory smoke began at 14:37:45 UTC and failed at 14:39:46 UTC during output assembly because development constants `TOOL_NAME` / `TOOL_VERSION` were absent.\\n- The failure occurred **after roughly two minutes of cold corpus processing**, before the derivation smoke ran.\\n\\nThe NameError is mechanical and repaired separately. The elapsed cold-scan time is the important systems finding: repeated full scans are not an acceptable steady-state backend for multiple recurrence loops plus interactive clients.\\n\\n## Performance objective\\n\\n**Build/update once; search many times.**\\n\\nQueries should normally read a prepared immutable index. Source crawling, JSON parsing, PDF text extraction, hashing, token normalization and math-expression extraction should happen during index build/update, not independently in every query process.\\n\\n## Proposed architecture\\n\\n### A. Immutable index generations\\n\\nEach successful build produces a generation directory, for example:\\n\\n```text\\nindexes/mersearch/generations/<generation-id>/\\n  manifest.json\\n  files.jsonl\\n  records.jsonl\\n  terms.sqlite\\n  math.jsonl\\n  relations.jsonl\\n```\\n\\nA small pointer/manifest identifies the current green generation.\\n\\nReaders open one generation and never observe a half-written update.\\n\\n### B. Atomic publication\\n\\nBuilder writes to a new temporary/generation location, validates it, then atomically advances the current-generation pointer. Never mutate the active generation in place.\\n\\nConsequences:\\n- many concurrent readers need no global query lock;\\n- a failed rebuild leaves the prior generation usable;\\n- workers can report exact index generation in results;\\n- rollback is pointer-level, not reconstruction.\\n\\n### C. Incremental invalidation\\n\\nManifest stores at least:\\n- source path;\\n- size;\\n- mtime when locally meaningful;\\n- content SHA-256;\\n- parser/extractor version;\\n- record count;\\n- source/ref identity where available.\\n\\nOn update:\\n1. cheap inventory comparison;\\n2. unchanged sources reuse prior derived records;\\n3. changed/new sources are reparsed/rehashed as needed;\\n4. deleted sources disappear only in the new generation;\\n5. normalization/math caches invalidate when their algorithm version changes.\\n\\nFor repository-native operation, Git tree/blob identities can avoid re-reading unchanged blobs where available.\\n\\n### D. SQLite search substrate\\n\\nRecommended first implementation: SQLite, because it is standard, portable, supports concurrent readers, transactional publication/building, indexes and FTS5 in typical builds.\\n\\nCandidate tables:\\n- `sources`\\n- `records`\\n- `record_fts`\\n- `topics`\\n- `record_topics`\\n- `math_expressions`\\n- `source_relations`\\n- `conversation_relations`\\n- `index_metadata`\\n\\nKeep raw source text/provenance sufficient to explain results; SQLite is an index, not the source of truth.\\n\\n### E. Query planning\\n\\nBefore scanning candidate records:\\n- resolve inventory predicates (`name/path/ext/kind/date/author/role`) through indexed columns;\\n- resolve lexical candidates through FTS/token indexes;\\n- apply exact phrase/NEAR/explain logic only to narrowed candidates;\\n- perform expensive math/CAS/regex/fuzzy modes only after cheap candidate reduction.\\n\\nBoolean semantics must remain compatible with stable Mersearch unless version notes explicitly state otherwise.\\n\\n### F. Concurrency classes\\n\\n1. **Interactive** — human/Sites/Viewer query; low latency, bounded page size.\\n2. **Research batch** — recurrence loop / archaeology query; larger result budget.\\n3. **Index maintenance** — single logical builder per corpus generation; never blocks active readers.\\n4. **Heavy math/semantic** — separately budgeted queue; cannot starve ordinary lexical/provenance search.\\n\\nNo worker should need to coordinate a read lock with another worker.\\n\\n### G. Backpressure / resource budgets\\n\\nBackend should enforce:\\n- maximum returned page size;\\n- pagination/cursors;\\n- query timeout;\\n- regex complexity/time budget;\\n- fuzzy expansion cap;\\n- CAS expression/time cap;\\n- semantic retrieval budget;\\n- maximum concurrent heavy jobs;\\n- cancellation;\\n- bounded excerpt generation.\\n\\nIf overloaded, preserve ordinary lexical/provenance service before expensive enrichment.\\n\\n### H. Caching\\n\\nSafe caches:\\n- parsed query AST by exact query+language version;\\n- normalized terms/math strings by normalizer version;\\n- hot result pages keyed by query + profile + index generation + sort;\\n- source/record metadata;\\n- Viewer targets.\\n\\nGeneration ID in cache keys makes invalidation trivial: publish new generation, old cache becomes naturally stale.\\n\\n### I. Recurrence-loop strategy\\n\\nFive round-the-clock loops should **share one index generation**.\\n\\nRecommended behavior:\\n- loops issue read-only queries against current green generation;\\n- each result records generation ID;\\n- loops do not trigger independent rebuilds;\\n- one scheduled/event-driven builder updates the index when source state changes;\\n- if rebuild fails, loops continue reading prior green generation;\\n- an interactive user query receives priority over optional expensive batch enrichment;\\n- saved recurrence queries can be precompiled/cached.\\n\\nA recurrence job that needs exhaustive historical output should request pagination/batch mode rather than an unbounded interactive response.\\n\\n## Targets for 1.1 development\\n\\nBefore promotion:\\n1. repair current development output bugs;\\n2. add timing instrumentation: inventory, parse, evaluate, hash, enrich, serialize;\\n3. implement file-mode/facets/totals cleanly;\\n4. build initial SQLite index prototype;\\n5. compare cold scan vs indexed query on representative corpus;\\n6. run concurrent-reader stress test (at least 8 readers to exceed the stated five-loop baseline);\\n7. run reader-during-rebuild test;\\n8. verify failed rebuild leaves previous generation readable;\\n9. verify exclusions/corpus profiles are enforced during indexing and query;\\n10. verify output includes index generation;\\n11. document performance numbers and hardware/runner context;\\n12. only then consider 1.1 promotion.\\n\\n## Non-goals / cautions\\n\\n- Do not solve load by weakening provenance.\\n- Do not silently truncate exhaustive research queries; report totals/pages/budgets.\\n- Do not let semantic/vector retrieval replace exact search.\\n- Do not put private/quarantined material in a shared public index and hope the API filters it later. Corpus boundary belongs at index/profile construction as well as request enforcement.\\n- Do not use a single mutable JSON artifact as a multi-writer database.\\n- Do not make recurrence loops rebuild the corpus independently.\\n- Do not infer currentness/authority from index freshness.\\n\\n## Performance telemetry\\n\\nRecord per request/build without storing sensitive query text unless explicitly approved:\\n- index generation;\\n- candidate count;\\n- returned count;\\n- elapsed total;\\n- query-plan stages/timings;\\n- cache hit/miss;\\n- timeout/budget events;\\n- error class.\\n\\nAggregate telemetry can guide optimization. Query-content retention needs a separate privacy/retention decision.\\n\\n## Release discipline\\n\\nThis plan does not modify the 1.0 worker greenlight. Development remains on `main` until a later version passes its gate and receives a `MERSEARCH_RELEASES.md` entry.\\n\\n## Live queue position and request observability (Nathan Direct, 2026-11-20)\\n\\nA Mersearch client must be able to determine **where its request is in the queue immediately**, without inferring that state from GitHub Actions run lists or repeatedly polling unrelated workflows.\\n\\n### Required request lifecycle\\n\\nEvery request receives an immutable request ID and a durable status record. The status model must distinguish at least:\\n\\n- `SUBMITTED` — accepted and assigned an ID;\\n- `QUEUED` — waiting for an execution slot;\\n- `CLAIMED` — assigned to a worker/runner;\\n- `RUNNING` — search execution has begun;\\n- `PACKAGING` — results and provenance are being serialized;\\n- `PUBLISHING` — durable result publication is underway;\\n- `COMPLETE` — result payload and manifest are durably readable;\\n- `FAILED` — terminal failure with step, error class and retryability;\\n- `CANCELLED` — explicitly cancelled;\\n- `EXPIRED` — retention policy expired the result (never silently delete).\\n\\nA request must not be reported COMPLETE merely because a workflow was queued, a runner started, a checkout completed, or a process exited. Completion requires durable result readback and manifest verification.\\n\\n### Immediate queue receipt\\n\\nThe submission response should synchronously return a compact receipt containing:\\n\\n- request ID;\\n- current lifecycle state;\\n- **queue position** (1-based) when queued, otherwise null;\\n- number of requests ahead;\\n- estimated/observed service class, not an invented completion-time promise;\\n- selected worker/runner lane and concurrency class;\\n- submitted/accepted timestamp;\\n- last state transition timestamp;\\n- status endpoint or request-scoped status path;\\n- cancellation handle where supported;\\n- query digest and corpus/profile identity.\\n\\nQueue position is a snapshot and must carry an `observed_at` timestamp. It should update on state transitions and be queryable by request ID. Do not derive position from the request-file lane number: lanes are submission slots, not a globally ordered work queue.\\n\\n### Queue architecture\\n\\nUse a durable central request ledger/queue rather than four long-lived mutable request files as the only source of state. Submission should append a request record atomically; workers claim jobs with a lease/heartbeat; stale claims can be recovered without duplicate publication. Preserve idempotency by request ID and make state transitions compare-and-swap or transactionally serialized.\\n\\nThe current four request lanes may remain compatibility ingress adapters during migration, but they should enqueue into the same ledger and return the same queue receipt. Do not overwrite another request to obtain a slot.\\n\\nPriorities should be explicit and fair: interactive user research, ordinary batch, index maintenance, and heavy math/enrichment are separate classes with bounded concurrency and starvation protection. Queue status must say whether a request is waiting for a runner, waiting behind other work, or actively executing. These are different bottlenecks.\\n\\n### User-facing status and observability\\n\\nProvide a status lookup by request ID and an event/receipt path that clients can inspect immediately after submission. Include queue position changes, claim/heartbeat, phase transitions, elapsed time per stage, retry history, worker/runner identity, and terminal outcome. Avoid claiming wall-clock completion estimates until measured service-time distributions support them.\\n\\nThe CLI, GitHub bridge, API and future frontend should expose the same lifecycle semantics. A status display should show a useful result immediately, for example: `QUEUED · position 3 · 2 ahead · interactive class · observed 14:03:22Z`.\\n\\n### Acceptance tests\\n\\n1. Submission returns a request ID and queue state immediately, before runner startup.\\n2. Concurrent submissions receive unique positions in a deterministic order within their priority/fairness policy.\\n3. Queue position changes correctly when jobs are claimed, cancelled, retried or completed.\\n4. A runner crash or expired lease returns the request to a recoverable state without duplicate final publication.\\n5. A status response distinguishes queue wait, runner allocation, checkout, search, packaging and publishing.\\n6. The status record and result manifest are durable and independently readable.\\n7. Compatibility lane adapters report the central queue position, not just a lane number.\\n8. Status/queue visibility does not expose private source excerpts or unauthorized corpus metadata.\\n\\nThis is an architecture requirement and design direction, not an assertion that the central queue/status service is already implemented.\\n\\n### Queue event timestamps and position history (Nathan Direct, 2026-11-20)\\n\\nQueue visibility must include the **timestamp of every request ahead of the current request**, not merely a count or position. The status receipt should expose an ordered, point-in-time snapshot such as:\\n\\n| Position | Request ID | Submitted at | Last state transition |\\n|---:|---|---|---|\\n| 1 | `request-a` | `2026-11-20T13:42:08Z` | `2026-11-20T13:42:08Z` |\\n| 2 | `request-b` | `2026-11-20T13:44:51Z` | `2026-11-20T13:45:02Z` |\\n| 3 | `this-request` | `2026-11-20T13:47:16Z` | `2026-11-20T13:47:16Z` |\\n\\nThe example is illustrative, not actual queue data.\\n\\nFor each request ahead, expose at minimum:\\n- current position within the applicable priority/fairness class;\\n- request ID (or privacy-preserving short identifier);\\n- original accepted/submitted timestamp in an explicit timezone, preferably UTC;\\n- current lifecycle state;\\n- timestamp of its latest state transition;\\n- optionally, accumulated queue-wait duration, computed from timestamps and clearly marked as a live duration.\\n\\nAlso retain an append-only event history for the request itself: submitted, queued, reprioritized, claimed, started, heartbeat, retried, packaged, published, completed, failed, cancelled. Every event has an event timestamp, and state changes record both prior and new state.\\n\\nA queue snapshot must include its own `observed_at` timestamp and identify the ordering/fairness policy used. If requests in another priority class are not ahead under the active scheduling policy, do not misleadingly list them as blocking this request; show class position and any global scheduling context separately. Do not expose sensitive query text or source excerpts from other users' requests. Use opaque IDs and timestamps sufficient to make queue behavior legible.\\n\\nAcceptance tests must verify that timestamps and order are stable, timezone-explicit, and correctly updated after claim, cancellation, retry, reprioritization and completion.\\n\\n### Eastern Time presentation and timestamp integrity (Nathan Direct, 2026-11-20)\\n\\nCanonical timestamps remain timezone-aware UTC values (ISO 8601, normally `Z`) for storage, event ordering, interchange, hashing and audit. **All human-facing timestamps presented to Nathan must be converted to `America/New_York`**: queue submissions ahead, current and prior state transitions, queue-snapshot observation times, runner/workflow events, retries, elapsed-time endpoints, and publication/readback events.\\n\\nUse the IANA zone `America/New_York` so the conversion correctly follows Eastern Standard Time and Eastern Daylight Time as applicable. Raw search-result artifacts remain withheld under the post-containment policy.\\n\\n## Local pinned Mersearch usage\\n\\nFrom a stable checkout with sibling archive directories visible (paths here are examples):\\n\\n```bash\\npython tools/search_archive_content.py \\\\\\n  /data/SAT_THEORY_ARCHIVE_2023-25 /data/HsH /data/HSH_RESOURCES \\\\\\n  --expr '(\\\"refractive index\\\" NEAR/12 \\\"phase shift\\\") OR \\\"0.24\\\"' \\\\\\n  --sort date --out /tmp/mersearch-optical\\n```\\n\\nMore queries:\\n\\n```text\\n(\\\"stringing along theory\\\" OR \\\"toy theory\\\") AND (filament OR string)\\n(\\\"Chronophysical\\\" OR \\\"SAT Mark V\\\") AND \\\"phase shift\\\"\\nmath:\\\"B=3/(4*pi)\\\"\\n(name:*LAB* OR path:*PHASE*) AND (optical OR kink)\\nauthor:user AND (worldtube NEAR/12 holonomy)\\n```\\n\\nStable search supports Boolean `AND`/`OR`/`NOT`, parentheses, quoted phrases, `NEAR/n`, `author:`, `role:`, `body:`, `math:`, `title:`, `date:`, `name:`, `path:`, `status:` and path/name globs. Raw message IDs pending backfill.\\n\\n## Purpose\\n\\nMersearch is the common query layer for the SAT/H(s)H archive. It should let humans, workers, the Conversation Viewer, and approved public interfaces ask the same query of the same permitted corpus and receive reproducible, provenance-bearing results.\\n\\nThe design rule is **one search semantics, multiple clients**. Do not fork a Sites searcher, Viewer searcher, worker searcher, and CLI searcher with subtly different meanings.\\n\\n## Architecture\\n\\n### 1. Mersearch Core\\n\\nCurrent implementation: `tools/search_archive_content.py` (`Mercer_Searcher_1.0` historical/internal tool identity).\\n\\nCore owns:\\n- query parsing and Boolean semantics;\\n- `AND`, `OR`, `NOT`, parentheses and implicit AND;\\n- quoted phrases;\\n- `NEAR` / `NEAR/n` with auditable token distance;\\n- field predicates;\\n- path/name glob semantics;\\n- record extraction from supported source formats;\\n- conservative notation-normalized math retrieval;\\n- exclusions / corpus boundary enforcement;\\n- provenance-bearing hit construction;\\n- deterministic sorting;\\n- topic enrichment and co-occurrence;\\n- machine-readable result generation.\\n\\nCore must remain usable without a web server or UI.\\n\\n### 2. Mersearch Index\\n\\nTarget layer. Precompute search-oriented representations without replacing source files:\\n- inventory/file manifest;\\n- record/message index;\\n- normalized lexical tokens;\\n- mathematical-expression inventory;\\n- source SHA-256 and source commit/ref;\\n- Viewer/document targets;\\n- conversation-family / duplicate-relation sidecars;\\n- explicit document→text-representation relations where provenance establishes them;\\n- topic/concept indexes;\\n- optional chronology summaries.\\n\\nGenerated indexes are derived state and must be rebuildable. A stable machine-facing wrapper over Core/Index for workers, Sites, Viewer and automation.\\n\\nMinimum request:\\n- query expression;\\n- corpus/profile;\\n- sort/order;\\n- pagination;\\n- requested facets;\\n- explain level.\\n\\nMinimum response:\\n- schema/tool/index versions;\\n- exact query and parsed representation;\\n- corpus/profile and exclusions;\\n- source/index commit identity;\\n- coverage counts;\\n- total hits before pagination;\\n- page/cursor;\\n- facets;\\n- hit records;\\n- per-hit provenance;\\n- match/explanation trace;\\n- warnings/limitations.\\n\\nAPI must not accept a client request to bypass quarantine/private-corpus rules merely because the client can name a path.\\n\\n### 4.
